body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I compared a **fp32 CPU** training run against a **fp32 CUDA** training run of the same ResNet50 (torchvision, CIFAR stem: conv1 3x3 stride 1, maxpool replaced by Identity) on identical synthetic deterministic data, single node, with TF32 **disabled** (`torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False`, `torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = False`), `cudnn.benchmark` off, `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` and `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8` — so this is a true fp32-vs-fp32 comparison, not fp32-vs-TF32. Optimizer: AdamW(lr=0.05, betas=(0.0,0.999), weight_decay=0.0), StepLR(step_size=10, gamma=0.1), clip_grad_norm 5.0, 20 steps, batch 2. Both arms start from identical initial weights and consume identical batches. I ran the whole comparison three times; the `RESULT` line is bit-identical across all three runs.

Every **single-step** quantity matches to round-off and the **parameter norm still matches at step 20**, but the **end-state** loss / gradient differ. Note this configuration is numerically unstable — the loss grows from 2.55 at step 0 to 24.0 (CPU) / 31.9 (CUDA) at step 20 — so both arms are in a diverging regime:

| quantity | CPU | CUDA | rel. diff |
|---|---|---|---|
| first forward loss (step 0, single-op) | 2.546584 | 2.546585 | 5.6e-7 |
| first backward grad-norm (step 0, single-op) | 348.023 | 348.011 | 3.4e-5 |
| **final loss (step 20)** | 24.038 | 31.885 | 0.281 |
| **final grad-norm (step 20, pre-clip)** | 93.288 | 133.379 | 0.354 |
| logits norm (step 20) | 267.31 | 285.39 | 0.065 |
| param norm (step 20) | 669.575 | 675.906 | 0.0094 |
| final grad SUM (signed, step 20) | 562.85 | 2582.56 | 1.284 |
| param SUM (signed, step 20) | −38787.6 | +24680.3 | sign flip |

**What I am and am not claiming.** PyTorch's numerical-accuracy notes state that CPU and GPU kernels may use different reduction orders, so I am *not* claiming either backend computes a wrong gradient — the single-step forward loss matches to 5.6e-7, the single-step grad-norm to 3.4e-5, and the parameter norm still agrees to 0.9% at step 20. Because the loss is diverging in this configuration (2.55 → 24/32 over 20 steps), both arms are amplifying tiny round-off through an unstable trajectory. I *am* asking whether an end-state gap of this size (final loss rel. 0.281, pre-clip grad-norm rel. 0.354) is simply the expected amplification of documented CPU-vs-GPU rounding through AdamW in an unstable regime, or whether it indicates a backend-specific interaction worth investigating. I am not asserting a defect.

        print("NO_CUDA"); return
    cpu = run_arm("cpu", args, init_sd, xs, ys)
    gpu = run_arm("cuda", args, init_sd, xs, ys)

    def rel(a, b):
        return abs(a - b) / max(1e-12, (abs(a) + abs(b)) / 2)

    out = {"model": args.model, "optimizer": args.optimizer, "lr": args.lr,
           "momentum": args.momentum, "weight_decay": args.weight_decay,
           "scheduler": args.scheduler, "clip": args.clip, "steps": args.steps,
           "batch": args.batch, "seed": args.seed}
    for k in SUM_KEYS + NORM_KEYS:
        out["cpu_" + k] = cpu[k]; out["gpu_" + k] = gpu[k]; out["rel_" + k] = rel(cpu[k], gpu[k])
        if k in SUM_KEYS and cpu[k] * gpu[k] < 0:
            out["signflip_" + k] = True
    print("RESULT " + json.dumps(out))

    # Human-readable honest summary: sum-only vs norm-level.
    def tag(k):
        r = out["rel_" + k]; sf = out.get("signflip_" + k, False)
        return f"  {k:28s} rel={r:.4g}{'  SIGNFLIP' if sf else ''}{'  DIVERGE' if r > 0.2 else '  match'}"
    print("SUMMARY sums:"); [print(tag(k)) for k in SUM_KEYS]
    print("SUMMARY norms:"); [print(tag(k)) for k in NORM_KEYS]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

title: [ROCm] Sparse COO coalesce returns garbage values when the dense size exceeds one tile
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

The issue was encountered during skipped FBGEMM TBE tests re-enablement on ROCm and became a reason of disabling the unit tests on ROCm CI. `sparse_coo_tensor` output is used there and causes tests to compare against ill-formed reference. CUDA pipeline on the other hand passes.

On ROCm, `coalesce()` of a sparse COO tensor on the GPU returns wrong values whenever the dense part of the values is wider than one kernel tile (warp_size * 4, so 256 on CDNA) and nnz is at least 2. The affected columns are never written, so they contain whatever was in the memory returned by `at::empty`. There is no error. It reproduces for float32, float16, bfloat16 and bool.

```python
import torch

s = torch.sparse_coo_tensor(torch.tensor([[1, 5]]), torch.randn(2, 512), (10, 512))
print((s.cuda().coalesce().to_dense().cpu() - s.coalesce().to_dense()).abs().max())
```

Expected: `tensor(0.)`. Observed on gfx950: a large value; columns 260 to 511 are wrong.

> The following analysis was produced with Claude Code (AI assistant) and reviewed by me:
>
> #158281 moved the feature tile index of `coalesceValuesKernel` from `blockIdx.y` to `blockIdx.z` on ROCm, but the ROCm branch computes the tile offset as `blockIdx.z * nsegments * SZ` instead of `blockIdx.z * blockDim.x * SZ` (aten/src/ATen/native/sparse/cuda/SparseCUDAApplyUtils.cuh, both overloads). The host still sizes `grid.z` in tiles of `warp_size * SZ`, so tiles overlap or leave gaps unless `nsegments == warp_size`. The number of wrong columns measured on gfx950 for nnz in 2..128 and dense sizes 256..1024 matches this model exactly. The same root cause was reported for gfx1201 in a comment on #158281. Using `blockDim.x` like the CUDA branch fixes it: a 1794 case fuzz against CPU coalesce (11 dtypes, nnz up to 70000 including the batched grid path, several dense shapes) passes with that change.

### Versions

Observed with the nightly `torch==2.15.0.dev20260930+rocm10.0` (git 89ac0527b15d5d9e2d5389b4cc56c54ce5320ed0). Code is unchanged on main as of d0b8bbb0151.

title: `torch.conv2d` fp16 on CPU returns wrong results on CPUs with AMX-FP16 (oneDNN `brg_conv_fwd:avx10_1_512_amx_fp16`)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.conv2d` in fp16 on CPU produces incorrect results on Intel Xeon 6736P, with errors as large as the output values themselves.

The issue appears to be in oneDNN's AMX-FP16 convolution kernel and has been reported as uxlfoundation/oneDNN#6151.

It affects both PyTorch 2.14.1 and the 2.15 nightly build (both bundle oneDNN v3.12.0).

I discovered the issue when a test comparing accelerator results against an fp16 CPU reference failed on this machine. As a workaround, I set `ONEDNN_MAX_CPU_ISA=AVX512_CORE_AMX`.

The reproducer and analysis below were prepared with Claude (AI-assisted); I ran and checked each result myself.

> **Reproducer**
>
> ```python
> import torch
>
> torch.manual_seed(0)
> x = torch.randn(1, 6, 128, 128, dtype=torch.float16)
> w = torch.randn(64, 6, 16, 16, dtype=torch.float16)
> b = torch.randn(64, dtype=torch.float16)
>
> conv = lambda x, w, b: torch.conv2d(x, w, b, stride=(16, 16))
> ref32 = conv(x.float(), w.float(), b.float())
> print("max |fp32|        =", ref32.abs().max().item())
> print("max |fp16 - fp32| =", (conv(x, w, b).float() - ref32).abs().max().item())
> ```
>
> **Observed:** `max |fp32| = 145.7`, `max |fp16 - fp32| = 159.3`. The error is as large as the outputs, so this isn't fp16 rounding: the same fp16 inputs give 0.059 when oneDNN avoids the AMX-FP16 kernel.
>
> | torch | bundled oneDNN | max \|fp16 − fp32\| |
> |---|---|---|
> | 2.14.1+cpu | v3.12.0 | **159.3** |
> | 2.15.0.dev20261001+cpu | v3.12.0 | **159.3** |
> | either, `ONEDNN_MAX_CPU_ISA=AVX512_CORE_AMX` | — | 0.059 |
> | either, `torch.backends.mkldnn.flags(enabled=False)` | — | 0.059 |
>
> **Expected:** fp16 conv matching the fp32 result within fp16 accuracy, as with the two settings above.
>
> `ONEDNN_VERBOSE=1` shows the kernel:
>
> ```
> onednn_verbose,v1,info,cpu,isa:Intel AVX10.1 and Intel AMX with bfloat16, float16 and 8-bit integer support
> onednn_verbose,v1,primitive,exec,cpu,convolution,brg_conv_fwd:avx10_1_512_amx_fp16,forward_training,src:f16:a:blocked:acdb::f0 wei:f16:ap:blocked:AcdB16b32a2b::f0 bia:f16:a:blocked:a::f0 dst:f16:a:blocked:acdb::f0,...,mb1_ic6oc64_ih128oh8kh16sh16dh0ph0_iw128ow8kw16sw16dw0pw0
> ```
>
> It reproduces without PyTorch on oneDNN `main` (45e6cb14aae6): benchdnn fails the same case with errors:4066/4096. Details, a benchdnn one-liner and a C++ reproducer are in uxlfoundation/oneDNN#6151. With a 16x16 kernel at stride 16, IC = 6, 8 and 16 fail, while IC = 1, 2, 15, 17, 31, 32, 33 and 64 pass. A 3x3 kernel at stride 1 passed for every IC tried.
>
> **Workaround:** `ONEDNN_MAX_CPU_ISA=AVX512_CORE_AMX` (or `torch.backends.mkldnn.flags(enabled=False)`), at the cost of the AMX-FP16 path.

title: CPU bf16/fp16 `add(other, alpha=)` rounds differently in the vectorized body and the scalar tail (and on x86 vs arm64); alpha is rounded to the tensor dtype
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On CPU, `torch.add(self, other, alpha=a)` for bfloat16 (and float16) gives different results for identical inputs depending on the tensor length and the element's index. Neither result is the one-rounding value that `mul`/`div` give for reduced floats.

```python
import torch
g, p, a = 0.052978515625, -0.53125, 0.1
for n in (31, 32, 33):
    x = torch.full((n,), g, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    y = torch.full((n,), p, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    print(n, sorted(set(x.add(y, alpha=a).tolist())), x.add(y, alpha=a)[-1].item())
```

On x86 (AVX512, `torch.backends.cpu.get_cpu_capability() == 'AVX512'`):

| n  | elements 0..31 | trailing elements |
|----|----------------|-------------------|
| 31 | −0.000244140625 (all) | — |
| 32 | −0.0001983642578125 (all) | — |
| 33 | −0.0001983642578125 | −0.000244140625 |

- Exact `g + a*p` = −0.0001464844; correctly rounded to bf16 = −0.0001468658447265625.
- −0.0001983642578125 = fp32 fma with **alpha rounded to bf16** (0.1 → 0.10009765625).
- −0.000244140625 = `bf16(g + bf16(a*p))`, two bf16 roundings.

On Apple M1 (arm64/NEON) every element takes the two-rounding value, so the same op gives different results on x86 and arm64.

`torch._foreach_add(..., alpha=)` shows the same split. That is the path `torch.optim.Adam`'s L2 weight decay (`grad.add(param, alpha=weight_decay)`) takes for bf16 parameters, and where we hit this. In our differential test, the same optimizer cell, seed and torch version produce different bf16 trajectories on x86 and arm64.

### Cause (v2.14.1, unchanged on main)

- `aten/src/ATen/native/native_functions.yaml` L564-569: `add.out` is a ufunc, `Generic: add (AllAndComplex, BFloat16, Half, ComplexHalf)`, so it is instantiated with `T = BFloat16` and alpha is a `BFloat16`.
- `aten/src/ATen/native/ufunc/add.h` L15-17 (scalar): `self + alpha * other` in `BFloat16` arithmetic gives two roundings.
- `add.h` L22-24 (vector): `vec::fmadd(other, alpha, self)`. On x86 this widens to fp32 and rounds once. On NEON, `vec128_bfloat16_neon.h` L647-663 implements bf16 `fmadd` as `a * b + c` in bf16 (NOTE [BF16 FMA]), giving two roundings.
- By contrast, `cpu/BinaryOpsKernel.cpp` gives `mul`/`div` a reduced-float path that keeps the scalar as `opmath_t` and computes in fp32 (L139-153, L171-185).

### Expected

The same result for every element regardless of position or ISA. Ideally that is `bf16(float(self) + opmath(alpha) * float(other))`, as `mul`/`div` already do for reduced floats. This is a one-ulp-scale effect, but it is layout- and host-dependent, and it is largest under cancellation (`self ≈ −alpha*other`).

(Not yet checked: CUDA behaviour.)

### Versions

torch 2.14.1 (PyPI wheel `2.14.1+cu130`, run on CPU), Python 3.13.14, Linux x86_64, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz (AVX512). Also observed with torch 2.14.1 on macOS arm64 (Apple M1 Pro), Python 3.13.7.

Suggested labels: module: cpu, module: bfloat16

title: Unverified potential RCE / insecure shell usage in script helpers or build workflows
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

File: .ci/magma/Makefile
Issue: Shell execution blocks use dynamic variables like $(shell git rev-parse --show-toplevel) and environment substitutions directly in command strings (DOCKER_RUN) without strict sanitization, which could lead to command injection if repository paths or workspace environments are maliciously controlled. (Unverified in current context).

### Versions

solution: Ensure proper quoting of shell variables and paths, or refactor shell expansions into safer subprocess arrays where applicable.

  Example fix pattern: Ensure proper quoting
  DOCKER_RUN = set -eou pipefail; TOPLEVEL="$$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"; ${DOCKER_CMD} run --rm -i \
      -v "$${TOPLEVEL}/.ci:/builder" \
      -w /builder \
      -e PACKAGE_NAME="${PACKAGE_NAME}${DESIRED_CUDA_SHORT}" \

title: [CD] Remove temporary cuBLAS override for CUDA 13.4 Linux wheels
body:
We are holding the full CUDA 13.4 Update 1 move because its cuSOLVER 12.3.4.7 can cause **link errors when previously built libraries that require versioned cuSOLVER symbols are relinked against it**. This is a specific link-time compatibility issue; it does not mean every build or existing binary fails.

Filing issue per comment https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199269#issuecomment-5933206729 to track the removal of this temporary cuBLAS range, when CTK 13.4U2 is released.

title: [inductor] torch.view_as_complex_copy fails with "Tensor must have a last dimension with stride 1" (fallback lacks the require_contiguous handling view_as_complex got in #100428)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.view_as_complex_copy` works in eager but fails under `torch.compile` (Inductor, CPU) with `Tensor must have a last dimension with stride 1`:

```python
import torch
def f():
    t = torch.zeros(4, 4, 4, 4)
    t = torch.linalg.cholesky_ex(t)[0]
    t = torch.nn.functional.adaptive_max_pool2d(t, (2, 2))
    return torch.view_as_complex_copy(t)
print("eager:", f().shape)
with torch.no_grad():
    torch.compile(f)()
```

```
eager: torch.Size([4, 4, 2])
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: RuntimeError: Tensor must have a last dimension with stride 1
```

The error is raised while Inductor runs the fallback kernel for `view_as_complex_copy` (`lowering.py` handler → `ir.py` `process_kernel` → fake-tensor dispatch). The input it passes has the layout Inductor chose for the `adaptive_max_pool2d` buffer, whose last dimension is not stride-1. In eager (and in fake-tensor propagation of the original graph) the `adaptive_max_pool2d` output has strides `(16, 4, 2, 1)`.

For `view_as_complex`, this was handled in #100428 (fix for #100086), which registers `make_fallback(aten.view_as_complex, require_contiguous)` and special-cases `aten.view_as_complex.default` in `lowering.py`. There is no equivalent for `aten.view_as_complex_copy`, so it falls back without the contiguity requirement. Adding the same `require_contiguous` handling for `view_as_complex_copy` would presumably fix this.

Not the same as #179368 / #176986, which hit the same message on CUDA in the backward pass.

title: Caching allocator: cross-stream memory when running two streams on green contexts
body:
Previously, I opened #195378 related to SM green context memory mapping. This is another question related to memory in the same setup.

Currently, I'm working on LLM prefill and decode running in parallel using green contexts. Each of them runs in a separate stream.

As you know, the caching allocator holds allocated memory only in the stream context in which the memory was allocated. It is intended by design (it is stated in the docs). I wanted to see how costly this can be in the above case and prepared a simple test.

Test 1: allocate 512 MiB of memory on stream 1, free it and allocate 512 MiB again.
- same stream: reserved 512 MiB
- different streams: reserved 1024 MiB

Test 2: allocate and free 8, 7, 8, 7, 8, 7 GiB, alternating between two streams. 8 + 7 GiB cannot be allocated simultaneously on the GPU, but each one separately.
- same stream: 0 retries, less than 0.5 ms per allocation
- different streams: a cache flush and retry on every allocation attempt; roughly 180 - 200 ms per allocation

The Setup: T4 (Colab), PyTorch [version]. Sizes in test 2 are for a ~15 GB GPU, so adjust accordingly.

```python
import time,torch
MB,GB=1024**2,1024**3

def test1(same_stream):
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    s1=torch.cuda.Stream()
    s2=s1 if same_stream else torch.cuda.Stream()
    with torch.cuda.stream(s1):
        a=torch.empty(512*MB,dtype=torch.uint8,device="cuda")
    del a
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    with torch.cuda.stream(s2):
        b=torch.empty(512*MB,dtype=torch.uint8,device="cuda")
    print("same" if same_stream else "different","| reserved MiB",torch.cuda.memory_reserved()//MB)
    del b

def test2(same_stream):
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    s1=torch.cuda.Stream()
    s2=s1 if same_stream else torch.cuda.Stream()
    for i, size in enumerate([8,7,8,7,8,7]):
        s=s1 if i % 2 == 0 else s2
        t0=time.perf_counter()
        with torch.cuda.stream(s):
            a=torch.empty(size*GB,dtype=torch.uint8,device="cuda")
        del a
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        print(i, size, "GiB | retries",torch.cuda.memory_stats()["num_alloc_retries"],"| ms",round((time.perf_counter()-t0)*1000,2))

test1(True);test1(False)
test2(True);test2(False)
```
same | reserved MiB 512
different | reserved MiB 1024
0 8 GiB | retries 10 | ms 345.56
1 7 GiB | retries 10 | ms 0.5
2 8 GiB | retries 10 | ms 0.2
3 7 GiB | retries 10 | ms 0.16
4 8 GiB | retries 10 | ms 0.21
5 7 GiB | retries 10 | ms 0.2

0 8 GiB | retries 10 | ms 196.09
1 7 GiB | retries 11 | ms 199.45
2 8 GiB | retries 12 | ms 175.54
3 7 GiB | retries 13 | ms 199.1
4 8 GiB | retries 14 | ms 179.86
5 7 GiB | retries 15 | ms 201.33


In case of green contexts, Two streams have different memory requirements most of the times, hence the free memory in one stream can not assist the other. When the memory is near to full, this will lead to retries as seen in test 2.

My queries are:
1. Any recommended approach for this situation? For instance, should I allocate everything in one stream and use record_stream? Or should I go for separate memory pools?
2. Any ongoing effort, or thought process, on allowing one stream to use memory freed by another stream somehow, for instance, by waiting for an event from another stream? I know that it reduces overlap and hence may not be a good trade off.

I am more than willing to test out solutions or contribute with a PR if required.

Thanks!

title: [numeric] fp32 CPU vs fp32 CUDA (TF32 off): single-op matches but final loss/grad-norm/logits diverge after 20 deterministic steps (ResNet50, AdamW lr=0.01, grad-accumulation 2, clip 0.1)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I compared a **fp32 CPU** training run against a **fp32 CUDA** training run of the same ResNet50 (torchvision, CIFAR stem: conv1 3x3 stride 1, maxpool replaced by Identity) on identical synthetic deterministic data, single node, with TF32 **disabled** (`torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False`, `torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = False`) and `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` — so this is a true fp32-vs-fp32 comparison, not fp32-vs-TF32. Optimizer: AdamW(lr=0.01, betas=(0.9,0.999), weight_decay=0.0) with clip_grad_norm 0.1 and gradient_accumulation_steps=2. Both arms start from identical initial weights and consume identical batches.

Every **single-step** quantity matches to round-off and the **parameter norm still matches at step 20**, but the **end-state** loss / gradient / logits diverge:

| quantity | CPU | CUDA | rel. diff |
|---|---|---|---|
| first forward loss (step 0, single-op) | 2.43785 | 2.43785 | 1.3e-6 |
| first backward grad-norm (step 0, single-op) | 128.300 | 128.308 | 6.4e-5 |
| **final loss (step 20)** | 2.4377 | 3.7698 | 0.429 |
| **final grad-norm (step 20)** | 8.6718 | 15.4028 | 0.559 |
| **logits norm (step 20)** | 131.013 | 168.446 | 0.250 |
| param norm (step 20) | 364.689 | 364.513 | 0.0005 |

**What I am and am not claiming.** PyTorch's numerical-accuracy notes state that CPU and GPU kernels may use different reduction orders, so I am *not* claiming either backend computes a wrong gradient — the single-step forward/backward agree to ~1e-6 and the parameter norm still agrees to 0.0005 at step 20. I *am* asking whether the **magnitude** of the end-state divergence after only 20 deterministic steps (final loss rel. 0.429, grad-norm rel. 0.559) is within the expected amplification of documented CPU-vs-GPU rounding through the optimizer, or whether it indicates a backend-specific interaction worth investigating.

**Minimal reproducible example** (fully self-contained: random-init torchvision weights and synthetic data, nothing is downloaded). Save as one file and run the command below it; it prints one `RESULT` JSON line.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Self-contained minimal reproducer: fp32 CPU vs fp32 CUDA end-state divergence.

Single node, synthetic deterministic batches (no downloaded data), identical
initial weights, TF32 disabled on the CUDA arm so this is a true fp32-vs-fp32
comparison.  Reports single-step (step 0) and end-state (step N) metrics.

Usage:
  python pt_min_cpu_vs_gpu.py --model resnet18 --optimizer sgd --lr 1.0 \
      --momentum 0.9 --weight-decay 1e-4 --steps 20 --batch 8 --seed 42
"""
import argparse, json, copy
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torchvision.models as tv


def build_model(model_name, num_classes=10):
    m = {"resnet18": tv.resnet18, "resnet34": tv.resnet34, "resnet50": tv.resnet50}[model_name](
        weights=None, num_classes=num_classes)
    m.conv1 = torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False)
    m.maxpool = torch.nn.Identity()
    return m


def make_optimizer(name, model, lr, momentum, weight_decay):
    if name == "sgd":
        return torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr, momentum=momentum,
                               weight_decay=weight_decay)
    if name == "adamw":
        return torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, betas=(momentum, 0.999),
                                 weight_decay=weight_decay)
    raise ValueError(name)


def gen_data(seed, n_micro, batch, input_size):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    xs = torch.randn((n_micro, batch, 3, input_size, input_size), generator=g)
    ys = (torch.arange(batch) % 10).expand(n_micro, batch).clone()
    return xs, ys


def global_norm(grads):
    return torch.linalg.vector_norm(torch.stack([torch.linalg.vector_norm(x) for x in grads]))


def run_arm(device, args, init_sd, xs, ys):
    torch.manual_seed(args.seed)
    model = build_model(args.model).to(device)
    model.load_state_dict(copy.deepcopy(init_sd))
    model.train()
    opt = make_optimizer(args.optimizer, model, args.lr, args.momentum, args.weight_decay)
    metrics = {}
    mi = 0
    for step in range(args.steps):
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        acc_grads = None
        last_loss = last_logits = None
        for k in range(args.grad_accum):
            x = xs[mi].to(device); y = ys[mi].to(device); mi += 1
            logits = model(x)
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y) / args.grad_accum
            loss.backward()
            last_loss = loss.item() * args.grad_accum
            last_logits = logits
        grads = [p.grad for p in model.parameters() if p.grad is not None]
        gnorm = global_norm(grads).item()
        if step == 0:
            metrics["first_forward_loss"] = last_loss
            metrics["first_backward_grad_norm"] = gnorm
        if args.clip:
            torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), args.clip)
        opt.step()
        metrics["final_loss"] = last_loss
        metrics["final_grad_norm"] = gnorm
        metrics["logits_norm"] = torch.linalg.vector_norm(last_logits).item()
    metrics["param_norm"] = global_norm([p for p in model.parameters()]).item()
    return metrics


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--model", default="resnet18")
    p.add_argument("--input-size", type=int, default=32)
    p.add_argument("--optimizer", default="sgd")
    p.add_argument("--lr", type=float, default=1.0)
    p.add_argument("--momentum", type=float, default=0.9)
    p.add_argument("--weight-decay", type=float, default=0.0)
    p.add_argument("--clip", type=float, default=0.0)
    p.add_argument("--grad-accum", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=20)
    p.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=8)
    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    args = p.parse_args()

    # True fp32-vs-fp32: disable TF32 + cudnn autotune, deterministic algorithms.
    torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False
    torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = False
    torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
    torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True, warn_only=True)

    xs, ys = gen_data(args.seed, args.steps * args.grad_accum, args.batch, args.input_size)
    torch.manual_seed(args.seed)
    init_sd = copy.deepcopy(build_model(args.model).state_dict())

    if not torch.cuda.is_available():
        print("NO_CUDA"); return
    cpu = run_arm("cpu", args, init_sd, xs, ys)
    gpu = run_arm("cuda", args, init_sd, xs, ys)

    def rel(a, b):
        return abs(a - b) / max(1e-12, (abs(a) + abs(b)) / 2)
    keys = ["first_forward_loss", "first_backward_grad_norm", "final_loss",
            "final_grad_norm", "logits_norm", "param_norm"]
    out = {"model": args.model, "optimizer": args.optimizer, "lr": args.lr,

title: [numeric] fp32 CPU vs fp32 CUDA (TF32 off): single-op matches but final grad-norm and logits-norm diverge after 20 deterministic steps (ResNet34, AdamW lr=0.1, clip 5.0)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I compared a **fp32 CPU** training run against a **fp32 CUDA** training run of the same ResNet34 (torchvision, CIFAR stem: conv1 3x3 stride 1, maxpool replaced by Identity) on identical synthetic deterministic data, single node, with TF32 **disabled** (`torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False`, `torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = False`) and `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` — so this is a true fp32-vs-fp32 comparison, not fp32-vs-TF32. Optimizer: AdamW(lr=0.1, betas=(0.9,0.999), weight_decay=0.01) with clip_grad_norm 5.0. Both arms start from identical initial weights and consume identical batches.

Every **single-step** quantity matches to round-off and the **parameter norm still matches at step 20**, but the **end-state** loss / gradient / logits diverge:

| quantity | CPU | CUDA | rel. diff |
|---|---|---|---|
| first forward loss (step 0, single-op) | 2.49541 | 2.49541 | 0.0 |
| first backward grad-norm (step 0, single-op) | 35.7857 | 35.7857 | 1.7e-6 |
| **final loss (step 20)** | 2.1643 | 2.1946 | 0.014 |
| **final grad-norm (step 20)** | 0.5151 | 0.9011 | 0.545 |
| **logits norm (step 20)** | 14.637 | 25.648 | 0.547 |
| param norm (step 20) | 2430.09 | 2432.59 | 0.001 |

**What I am and am not claiming.** PyTorch's numerical-accuracy notes state that CPU and GPU kernels may use different reduction orders, so I am *not* claiming either backend computes a wrong gradient — the single-step forward/backward agree to ~1e-6 and the parameter norm still agrees to 0.001 at step 20. I *am* asking whether the **magnitude** of the end-state divergence after only 20 deterministic steps (final loss rel. 0.014, grad-norm rel. 0.545) is within the expected amplification of documented CPU-vs-GPU rounding through the optimizer, or whether it indicates a backend-specific interaction worth investigating.

**Minimal reproducible example** (fully self-contained: random-init torchvision weights and synthetic data, nothing is downloaded). Save as one file and run the command below it; it prints one `RESULT` JSON line.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Self-contained minimal reproducer: fp32 CPU vs fp32 CUDA end-state divergence.

Single node, synthetic deterministic batches (no downloaded data), identical
initial weights, TF32 disabled on the CUDA arm so this is a true fp32-vs-fp32
comparison.  Reports single-step (step 0) and end-state (step N) metrics.

Usage:
  python pt_min_cpu_vs_gpu.py --model resnet18 --optimizer sgd --lr 1.0 \
      --momentum 0.9 --weight-decay 1e-4 --steps 20 --batch 8 --seed 42
"""
import argparse, json, copy
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torchvision.models as tv


def build_model(model_name, num_classes=10):
    m = {"resnet18": tv.resnet18, "resnet34": tv.resnet34, "resnet50": tv.resnet50}[model_name](
        weights=None, num_classes=num_classes)
    m.conv1 = torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False)
    m.maxpool = torch.nn.Identity()
    return m


def make_optimizer(name, model, lr, momentum, weight_decay):
    if name == "sgd":
        return torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr, momentum=momentum,
                               weight_decay=weight_decay)
    if name == "adamw":
        return torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, betas=(momentum, 0.999),
                                 weight_decay=weight_decay)
    raise ValueError(name)


def gen_data(seed, n_micro, batch, input_size):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    xs = torch.randn((n_micro, batch, 3, input_size, input_size), generator=g)
    ys = (torch.arange(batch) % 10).expand(n_micro, batch).clone()
    return xs, ys


def global_norm(grads):
    return torch.linalg.vector_norm(torch.stack([torch.linalg.vector_norm(x) for x in grads]))


def run_arm(device, args, init_sd, xs, ys):
    torch.manual_seed(args.seed)
    model = build_model(args.model).to(device)
    model.load_state_dict(copy.deepcopy(init_sd))
    model.train()
    opt = make_optimizer(args.optimizer, model, args.lr, args.momentum, args.weight_decay)
    metrics = {}
    mi = 0
    for step in range(args.steps):
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        acc_grads = None
        last_loss = last_logits = None
        for k in range(args.grad_accum):
            x = xs[mi].to(device); y = ys[mi].to(device); mi += 1
            logits = model(x)
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y) / args.grad_accum
            loss.backward()
            last_loss = loss.item() * args.grad_accum
            last_logits = logits
        grads = [p.grad for p in model.parameters() if p.grad is not None]
        gnorm = global_norm(grads).item()
        if step == 0:
            metrics["first_forward_loss"] = last_loss
            metrics["first_backward_grad_norm"] = gnorm
        if args.clip:
            torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), args.clip)
        opt.step()
        metrics["final_loss"] = last_loss
        metrics["final_grad_norm"] = gnorm
        metrics["logits_norm"] = torch.linalg.vector_norm(last_logits).item()
    metrics["param_norm"] = global_norm([p for p in model.parameters()]).item()
    return metrics


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--model", default="resnet18")
    p.add_argument("--input-size", type=int, default=32)
    p.add_argument("--optimizer", default="sgd")
    p.add_argument("--lr", type=float, default=1.0)
    p.add_argument("--momentum", type=float, default=0.9)
    p.add_argument("--weight-decay", type=float, default=0.0)
    p.add_argument("--clip", type=float, default=0.0)
    p.add_argument("--grad-accum", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=20)
    p.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=8)
    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    args = p.parse_args()

    # True fp32-vs-fp32: disable TF32 + cudnn autotune, deterministic algorithms.
    torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False
    torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = False
    torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
    torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True, warn_only=True)

    xs, ys = gen_data(args.seed, args.steps * args.grad_accum, args.batch, args.input_size)
    torch.manual_seed(args.seed)
    init_sd = copy.deepcopy(build_model(args.model).state_dict())

    if not torch.cuda.is_available():
        print("NO_CUDA"); return
    cpu = run_arm("cpu", args, init_sd, xs, ys)
    gpu = run_arm("cuda", args, init_sd, xs, ys)

    def rel(a, b):
        return abs(a - b) / max(1e-12, (abs(a) + abs(b)) / 2)
    keys = ["first_forward_loss", "first_backward_grad_norm", "final_loss",
            "final_grad_norm", "logits_norm", "param_norm"]
    out = {"model": args.model, "optimizer": args.optimizer, "lr": args.lr,
           "steps": args.steps, "grad_accum": args.grad_accum, "clip": args.clip,
           "batch": args.batch}
    for k in keys:
        out["cpu_" + k] = cpu[k]; out["gpu_" + k] = gpu[k]; out["rel_" + k] = rel(cpu[k], gpu[k])
    print("RESULT " + json.dumps(out))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import torchvision.models as tv


def build_model(model_name, num_classes=10):
    m = {"resnet18": tv.resnet18, "resnet34": tv.resnet34, "resnet50": tv.resnet50}[model_name](
        weights=None, num_classes=num_classes)
    m.conv1 = torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False)
    m.maxpool = torch.nn.Identity()
    return m


def make_optimizer(name, model, lr, momentum, weight_decay):
    if name == "sgd":
        return torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr, momentum=momentum,
                               weight_decay=weight_decay)
    if name == "adamw":
        return torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, betas=(momentum, 0.999),
                                 weight_decay=weight_decay)
    raise ValueError(name)


def gen_data(seed, n_micro, batch, input_size):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    xs = torch.randn((n_micro, batch, 3, input_size, input_size), generator=g)
    ys = (torch.arange(batch) % 10).expand(n_micro, batch).clone()
    return xs, ys


def global_norm(grads):
    return torch.linalg.vector_norm(torch.stack([torch.linalg.vector_norm(x) for x in grads]))


def run_arm(device, args, init_sd, xs, ys):
    torch.manual_seed(args.seed)
    model = build_model(args.model).to(device)
    model.load_state_dict(copy.deepcopy(init_sd))
    model.train()
    opt = make_optimizer(args.optimizer, model, args.lr, args.momentum, args.weight_decay)
    metrics = {}
    mi = 0
    for step in range(args.steps):
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        acc_grads = None
        last_loss = last_logits = None
        for k in range(args.grad_accum):
            x = xs[mi].to(device); y = ys[mi].to(device); mi += 1
            logits = model(x)
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y) / args.grad_accum
            loss.backward()
            last_loss = loss.item() * args.grad_accum
            last_logits = logits
        grads = [p.grad for p in model.parameters() if p.grad is not None]
        gnorm = global_norm(grads).item()
        if step == 0:
            metrics["first_forward_loss"] = last_loss
            metrics["first_backward_grad_norm"] = gnorm
        if args.clip:
            torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), args.clip)
        opt.step()
        metrics["final_loss"] = last_loss
        metrics["final_grad_norm"] = gnorm
        metrics["logits_norm"] = torch.linalg.vector_norm(last_logits).item()
    metrics["param_norm"] = global_norm([p for p in model.parameters()]).item()
    return metrics


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--model", default="resnet18")
    p.add_argument("--input-size", type=int, default=32)
    p.add_argument("--optimizer", default="sgd")
    p.add_argument("--lr", type=float, default=1.0)
    p.add_argument("--momentum", type=float, default=0.9)
    p.add_argument("--weight-decay", type=float, default=0.0)
    p.add_argument("--clip", type=float, default=0.0)
    p.add_argument("--grad-accum", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=20)
    p.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=8)
    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
    args = p.parse_args()

    # True fp32-vs-fp32: disable TF32 + cudnn autotune, deterministic algorithms.
    torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False
    torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = False
    torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
    torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True, warn_only=True)

    xs, ys = gen_data(args.seed, args.steps * args.grad_accum, args.batch, args.input_size)
    torch.manual_seed(args.seed)
    init_sd = copy.deepcopy(build_model(args.model).state_dict())

    if not torch.cuda.is_available():
        print("NO_CUDA"); return
    cpu = run_arm("cpu", args, init_sd, xs, ys)
    gpu = run_arm("cuda", args, init_sd, xs, ys)

    def rel(a, b):
        return abs(a - b) / max(1e-12, (abs(a) + abs(b)) / 2)
    keys = ["first_forward_loss", "first_backward_grad_norm", "final_loss",
            "final_grad_norm", "logits_norm", "param_norm"]
    out = {"model": args.model, "optimizer": args.optimizer, "lr": args.lr,
           "steps": args.steps, "grad_accum": args.grad_accum, "clip": args.clip,
           "batch": args.batch}
    for k in keys:
        out["cpu_" + k] = cpu[k]; out["gpu_" + k] = gpu[k]; out["rel_" + k] = rel(cpu[k], gpu[k])
    print("RESULT " + json.dumps(out))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

title: [dynamo] funcname_cache gives wrong qualified names after a def/class with a same-line body
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

> _Drafted by Claude (AI) for @egeboy35._
>
> `torch._dynamo.funcname_cache.get_funcname`, which provides the qualified name in the `TORCH_LOGS=trace_source` / `trace_call` headers, keeps a `def`/`class` name on its stack when the body is on the same line (`class E(Exception): pass`, one-line `@overload` stubs). Every later line in that file then gets a wrong name:
>
> ```python
> import tempfile
> from torch._dynamo.funcname_cache import get_funcname
>
> src = "class E(Exception): pass\ndef f():\n    return 1\n"
> with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".py", delete=False) as fp:
>     fp.write(src)
> print(get_funcname(fp.name, 3))  # E.f, expected f
> ```
>
> In torch itself, `torch/nn/modules/module.py` line 1791 on main (`Module._call_impl`) is reported as `Module.to.to.to.to._call_impl`, because of the four one-line `@overload def to(...)` stubs above it. Comparing every statement line of the torch source with `ast`, 47,765 of 510,281 lines in 116 files get a wrong name. A ~10-line fix (pop the name when a `def`/`class` line is not followed by an INDENT) with a test is ready.

### Versions

> Current main (556f9401181). Reproduced by running `torch/_dynamo/funcname_cache.py` on its own under Python 3.12 and 3.14, since it only depends on `tokenize`.

title: [Inductor] Static CUDA launcher and AOTI can't load Triton kernels that need oversized shared memory
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

While tuning FP8/BF16 GEMMs with max-autotune on an sm_107 GPU, I noticed that configs whose Triton kernels use more shared memory than the per-block opt-in limit silently ran with `num_stages=1` (much slower), and that AOTI-compiled models containing such kernels failed to launch.

The details below were drafted with Claude Code; I have reviewed and reproduced them.

> On sm_107 a block can use more shared memory than
> `CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_MAX_SHARED_MEMORY_PER_BLOCK_OPTIN`, but only in the oversized
> shared memory mode (`CU_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_SHARED_MEMORY_MODE` =
> `CU_SHARED_MEMORY_MODE_ALLOW_OVERSIZED_SHARED_MEMORY`, up to
> `CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_MAX_OVERSIZED_SHARED_MEMORY_PER_BLOCK`). Triton compiles and
> launches kernels against the larger limit, but Inductor's launchers only know the
> opt-in limit:
>
> - **Static CUDA launcher:** the kernel fails to load with `OutOfMemoryError`, then
>   `compile_by_disabling_pipelining` recompiles it with `num_stages=1`, so the run
>   silently uses a much slower kernel. Default max-autotune configs are affected,
>   e.g. bf16 mm `(128, 128, 128, 4, 8)`.
> - **AOTI / cpp_wrapper:** the generated `loadKernel` sets
>   `CU_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_MAX_DYNAMIC_SHARED_SIZE_BYTES`, which can't exceed the opt-in
>   limit, so launching the kernel fails with `CUDA driver error: invalid argument`.

Repro (AOTI, sm_107):

```python
import torch, triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def matmul_kernel(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M, N, K,
                  BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr):
    offs_m = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK_M + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M)
    offs_n = tl.program_id(1) * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N)
    offs_k = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K)
    a_ptrs = a_ptr + offs_m[:, None] * K + offs_k[None, :]
    b_ptrs = b_ptr + offs_k[:, None] * N + offs_n[None, :]
    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=tl.float32)
    for _ in range(0, K, BLOCK_K):
        acc += tl.dot(tl.load(a_ptrs), tl.load(b_ptrs))
        a_ptrs += BLOCK_K
        b_ptrs += BLOCK_K * N
    tl.store(c_ptr + offs_m[:, None] * N + offs_n[None, :], acc.to(tl.bfloat16))

# 4 stages of 128x128 bf16 tiles: ~256 KiB of shared memory, above the opt-in limit
matmul = triton.autotune(
    configs=[triton.Config({"BLOCK_M": 128, "BLOCK_N": 128, "BLOCK_K": 128},
                           num_warps=8, num_stages=4)], key=[])(matmul_kernel)
M = N = K = 512

class Model(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, a, b):
        c = torch.empty(M, N, device=a.device, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
        matmul[(M // 128, N // 128)](a, b, c, M, N, K)
        return c

a = torch.randn(M, K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
b = torch.randn(K, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ep = torch.export.export(Model(), (a, b), strict=True)
fn = torch._inductor.aoti_load_package(torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package(ep))
fn(a, b)  # RuntimeError: CUDA driver error: invalid argument
```

### Error logs

```
RuntimeError: CUDA driver error: invalid argument                         # AOTI
OutOfMemoryError: out of resource: triton_tem_fused_mm_0 Required: 262160 Hardware limit:232448
  -> recompiled with num_stages=1                                          # static launcher
```

title: Inductor can use a value-only reduction for abs().max(dim).values
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Context

`.max(...)[0]` currently lowers to `max_with_index` and `amax(...)` lowers to `max2`. Initially, these seem semantically equivalent, and we would think that we can avoid the reduction over indices by lowering `max(...)[0]` to `max2` as well since we aren't using the index part of the tuple, except that when there is a tie between differently signed zeros, the sign of the zero returned could be different in the two cases. So we cannot, and inductor does not, perform this optimisation. This is currently recognized with a test as well: `test/inductor/test_triton_kernels.py:313`.

## However

If there is a `abs()` preceding this `max()`, then the signed zero edge case vanishes, and we don't need to do the extra index reduction.

## Why it may matter

I recently debugged a slowdown of torch.compiled code versus cuda in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/25094, PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59564 that ended up being because of this extra index reduction. Numbers can be found therein.

In that case (a FP8 group quant kernel), we had `.abs().max()[0]`, and saw a 20% speedup in this kernel after manually replacing it with `.amax()`.

It is reasonable that inductor does this automatically. The general optim pattern exists, and considering that we actively _don't_ do this optim today cos of the signed zero edge case, it makes sense that we check if we have .abs()d before.

There is probably no need to take it too far. For instance, I don't want to deal with various `.to()` casts and stuff in between. `.view()` might be OK, I am open to suggestions here. That is, if this change is interesting to the maintainers at all.

## Impl ideas

 - It has to be postgrad since gradients need to be routed to the exact index, we cannot do any opti there.
 - From looking at the rough structure of the lowering, it seems like rewriting `.abs() -> .max() -> .values` to `.amax()` whenever the index part of the tuple is unused, is a fairly simple rewrite IMO. Doing it through `.view()`s will add some code it seems but I don't think will be problematic.

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

title: [MPS] upsample_bilinear2d backward ~25x slower when grad_output is channels_last
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On MPS, the backward of bilinear `F.interpolate` gets ~25x slower when `grad_output` is channels_last instead of contiguous. Calling `.contiguous()` on the grad first and taking the normal path is several times cheaper.

You don't have to ask for channels_last to hit this. It happens in a common segmentation loss pattern: upsample the logits, then `permute(0, 2, 3, 1).reshape(-1, C)` into `cross_entropy`. The gradient then comes back channels_last-strided. On CPU the same grad layout is faster than contiguous (22 vs 80 ms for the first shape below), so this looks MPS-specific.

```python
import time
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def bench(shape, grad_layout):
    times = []
    for i in range(8):
        x = torch.randn(shape, device="mps", requires_grad=True)
        y = F.interpolate(x, size=(640, 640), mode="bilinear", align_corners=False)
        g = torch.ones_like(y)
        if grad_layout == "channels_last":
            g = g.contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
        torch.mps.synchronize()
        t = time.perf_counter()
        y.backward(g)
        torch.mps.synchronize()
        if i:
            times.append(time.perf_counter() - t)
    return sorted(times)[len(times) // 2] * 1000


for shape in [(2, 150, 80, 80), (2, 150, 40, 40)]:
    nchw = bench(shape, "contiguous")
    cl = bench(shape, "channels_last")
    print(f"{shape}: contiguous grad {nchw:.1f} ms, channels_last grad {cl:.1f} ms")
```

M4, macOS 27.0, fp32:

```
torch 2.14.0
(2, 150, 80, 80): contiguous grad 9.6 ms, channels_last grad 249.2 ms
(2, 150, 40, 40): contiguous grad 11.8 ms, channels_last grad 281.8 ms

torch 2.9.1
(2, 150, 80, 80): contiguous grad 9.7 ms, channels_last grad 274.6 ms
(2, 150, 40, 40): contiguous grad 12.4 ms, channels_last grad 280.0 ms
```

With `.contiguous()` on the grad inside the timed region, the first shape costs ~31 ms on 2.14 and ~100 ms on 2.9.1. Both are well below the ~250 ms of the channels_last path. It shows up on 2.9.1 and 2.14.0, so it's not a recent regression.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0
Is debug build: False
CUDA used to build PyTorch: None
OS: macOS 27.0 (arm64)
Clang version: 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)

Is CUDA available: False
CPU: Apple M4
```

Also reproduced with torch 2.9.1 on the same machine.

title: [ROCm][gfx1201/RDNA4] LayerNorm/RMSNorm backward never writes odd-indexed weight/bias grad elements (M >= 128)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On RDNA4 (gfx1201), the backward of `F.layer_norm` / `nn.LayerNorm` never writes the **odd-indexed elements** of the weight and bias gradients when the input has M ≥ 128 rows. They hold whatever was in that memory: 0 in a fresh process, which is what the repro below shows, and stale values in a real run. The even-indexed elements are correct, and so are the input gradient and the forward output. Nothing is NaN or Inf, so training runs and the loss goes down. Half of every LayerNorm's affine gradient is silently dropped.

Reproduces on both gfx1201 cards I have (RX 9070 XT and Radeon AI PRO R9700). It happens in fp32, under bf16 autocast and with bf16 tensors, for every hidden size tried (768, 1024, 4096) and every M ≥ 128 tried (up to 70000). M < 128 is correct. RMSNorm's weight gradient is affected the same way. See the follow-up comment for what looks like the root cause.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

print(torch.__version__, torch.version.hip, torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))
torch.manual_seed(0)
for D in (768, 1024, 4096):
    x, gy = torch.randn(2, 2048, D), torch.randn(2, 2048, D)
    w, b = torch.ones(D), torch.zeros(D)
    grads = {}
    for dev in ("cpu", "cuda"):
        xd, wd, bd = (t.to(dev).clone().requires_grad_() for t in (x, w, b))
        (F.layer_norm(xd, (D,), wd, bd) * gy.to(dev)).sum().backward()
        grads[dev] = (xd.grad.cpu(), wd.grad.cpu(), bd.grad.cpu())
    for name, g, c in zip(("dx", "dw", "db"), grads["cuda"], grads["cpu"]):
        ok = torch.isclose(g, c, rtol=1e-3, atol=1e-3)
        wrong = (~ok).nonzero().flatten()
        print(f"D={D} {name}: correct {ok.sum().item()}/{ok.numel()}, "
              f"exactly zero {(g == 0).sum().item()}, first wrong idx {wrong[:6].tolist()}")
```

Output on RX 9070 XT (identical on the R9700):

```
2.12.1+rocm7.2 7.2.53211 AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT
D=768 dx: correct 3145728/3145728, exactly zero 0, first wrong idx []
D=768 dw: correct 384/768, exactly zero 384, first wrong idx [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]
D=768 db: correct 384/768, exactly zero 384, first wrong idx [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]
D=1024 dx: correct 4194304/4194304, exactly zero 0, first wrong idx []
D=1024 dw: correct 512/1024, exactly zero 512, first wrong idx [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]
D=1024 db: correct 512/1024, exactly zero 512, first wrong idx [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]
D=4096 dx: correct 16777216/16777216, exactly zero 0, first wrong idx []
D=4096 dw: correct 2048/4096, exactly zero 2048, first wrong idx [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]
D=4096 db: correct 2048/4096, exactly zero 2048, first wrong idx [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]
```

With random (non-unit) weights the same thing shows as `cos(grad_gpu, grad_cpu) == |grad_gpu| / |grad_cpu| ≈ 0.707` for both `dw` and `db`, i.e. half the entries missing. In one early run on the R9700 some `dw`/`db` tensors came back with cosine 0.0. That's consistent with the unwritten elements holding stale memory (see the comment below).

Because every other element is dropped, my guess is a vectorized or packed store in the gamma/beta backward kernel (`aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/layer_norm_kernel.cu`) that only writes every other lane on RDNA4. Wave32 versus the wave64 the kernel might assume is one candidate. I haven't confirmed this.

**Impact:** any fine-tuning on these cards that trains LayerNorm parameters, which covers essentially every transformer. On a V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L fine-tune, 49 of 160 trainable tensors (every LayerNorm in the trainable blocks) got wrong gradients while loss curves looked normal. Possibly related: a fp16 ModernBERT fine-tune on the same machine got NaN LayerNorm weight gradients, and the same workaround fixed it.

**Workaround:** compute LayerNorm from elementwise ops (mean, var, rsqrt) so autograd doesn't use the fused backward. That gives exact parity with CPU in fp32.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.12.1+rocm7.2
ROCM used to build PyTorch: 7.2.53211
OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (x86_64)
Python version: 3.13.13 (64-bit runtime)
Kernel: 6.17.0-23-generic
GPU models and configuration: AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT (gfx1201), AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201)
HIP runtime version: 7.2.53211

```

title: torch.compile with functionalize_rng_ops=True: randperm and multinomial return the same result on every call
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `torch._functorch.config.functionalize_rng_ops = True`, a compiled function that calls `torch.randperm` or `torch.multinomial` on CUDA returns the identical result on every call. The generator does not advance between calls for these ops. `torch.rand` and dropout under the same flag do advance. With the flag off, every call differs.

```python
import torch
import torch._functorch.config as fc

fc.functionalize_rng_ops = True
x = torch.empty(1, device="cuda")
f = torch.compile(lambda x: torch.randperm(8, device=x.device), backend="aot_eager")
torch.manual_seed(0)
print([f(x).tolist() for _ in range(3)])   # three identical permutations
```

The same check over 3 seeds × 4 calls, under `aot_eager` and `inductor`:

| functionalize_rng_ops | randperm repeats across calls | multinomial repeats | rand repeats |
|---|---|---|---|
| False | no (3/3 seeds) | no | no |
| True | **yes (3/3 seeds, both backends)** | **yes** | no |

At larger scale, 400 consecutive calls to a compiled `randperm(16)` gave 399 identical consecutive pairs, and the position-uniformity chi-square z-score was 208. Two `randperm` calls *within* one compiled call still differ from each other, so only the cross-call state is stuck.

**Possible cause (a guess, not checked in the source).** RNG functionalization threads explicit seed/offset through philox-based ops (rand, randn, bernoulli) and advances the offset after each call. `randperm` and `multinomial` are not philox-decomposed, so they may read a generator state that is saved and restored around each compiled call, without that state ever being advanced.

`functionalize_rng_ops` is a private config flag and off by default, so impact is limited to users who turn it on, for example for activation-checkpointing RNG replay.

### Versions

```
torch 2.15.0.dev20260928+cu130 (git 68e0ae4967e1a7e39d914179aea0026036cc1a23), CUDA 13.0, driver 580.82.07,
Tesla T4 (sm_75), triton 3.8.0, Python 3.13.15, Ubuntu (Google Colab)
```

title: [inductor] NetworkXError "node source not in graph" when a checkpointed region contains an identity op (x * 1.0, x + 0.0)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.compile` (default Inductor) fails to compile a non-reentrant `torch.utils.checkpoint` region whose body contains an arithmetic identity such as `t * 1.0` or `t + 0.0`. The min-cut partitioner raises `NetworkXError: node source not in graph`. Eager works, and so do non-identity bodies like `t * 2.0` or `sin(t)`.

```python
import torch
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint

def f(x):
    return checkpoint(lambda t: t * 1.0, x, use_reentrant=False)

x = torch.randn(8, 64, requires_grad=True)
torch.compile(f)(x).sum().backward()
```

```
torch._dynamo.exc.BackendCompilerFailed: backend='inductor' raised:
NetworkXError: node source not in graph
```

Which bodies crash:

| checkpointed body | result |
|---|---|
| `t * 1.0` | NetworkXError |
| `t + 0.0` | NetworkXError |
| `sin(t * 1.0)` | NetworkXError |
| `sin(t + 0.0)` | NetworkXError |
| `F.dropout(t * 1.0, 0.3, True)` | NetworkXError |
| `sin(t * 2.0)` | OK |
| `sin(t)` | OK |

A related shape fails differently: `lin(x) + checkpoint(lambda t: F.dropout(t * 1.0, 0.3, True), x, use_reentrant=False)` raises `AssertionError: Node mm_1 was invalid, but is output`. Selective activation checkpointing with `MUST_RECOMPUTE` / `PREFER_RECOMPUTE` on such a region, and `use_reentrant=True` inside `torch.compile`, also hit the NetworkXError. This happens on CPU and CUDA alike.

**Where it fails.** The traceback runs `min_cut_rematerialization_partition` → `choose_saved_values_set` → `solve_min_cut`, and fails at `minimum_cut(nx_graph, "source", "sink")` (`torch/_functorch/partitioners.py:2950` in 2.15.0.dev20260930). The `"source"` node only enters `nx_graph` through `ban_recomputation` (`add_edge("source", ...)`, around line 2729). My guess, which I haven't verified, is that once the identity op is simplified away no node in the region gets banned, so `"source"` never exists and NetworkX rejects the call. If so, `solve_min_cut` could treat a missing `"source"` as "nothing to cut".

PR #197724 (Dinic min-cut replacing NetworkX, closed unmerged 2026-09-19) would have changed this code path, but I haven't checked whether it handles the case.

### Versions

Reproduced on 2.15.0.dev20260930 (CPU, below) and 2.15.0.dev20260928+cu130 (Tesla T4). Also seen on torch 2.14.0 (CPU).

title: torch.cond / while_loop / map / switch backward redraws random ops, so gradients use a different dropout mask than the forward
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When the branch or body of `torch.cond` contains a random op (dropout, `rand_like`, `bernoulli`, ...), the backward pass runs the op again with fresh randomness. The forward output uses one mask and the gradient uses an independent one. The same happens with `torch._higher_order_ops.while_loop`, `map` and `switch`. It happens in plain eager mode, without `torch.compile`, and nothing is raised or warned.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def f(x):
    # both branches apply dropout; the forward keeps one mask, the backward should reuse it
    return torch.cond(x.sum() > 0,
                      lambda t: F.dropout(t, 0.3, training=True),
                      lambda t: F.dropout(t, 0.3, training=True) * 1.0,
                      (x,))

torch.manual_seed(0)
x = (torch.rand(64, 256) + 0.5).requires_grad_()
y = f(x)
y.sum().backward()
# dy/dx is mask/(1-p), so x.grad must be zero exactly where y is zero
print("fwd/bwd mask mismatch:", ((y != 0) != (x.grad != 0)).float().mean().item())
# prints ~0.42 (= 2p(1-p), i.e. independent masks); expected 0.0
```

Output on 2.15.0.dev20260930 and on 2.14.0:

```
fwd/bwd mask mismatch: 0.41802978515625
```

Expected `0.0`. At `p = 0.3`, two independent masks disagree on `2p(1-p) = 0.42` of positions, which matches the output. Plain `F.dropout(x, 0.3)` outside `cond` gives `0.0` in the same process.

The same check across ops and backends, over seeds 0/1/2:

| op | eager | compile(aot_eager) | compile(inductor) |
|---|---|---|---|
| plain dropout (control) | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| `torch.cond` | 0.418 / 0.430 / 0.418 | 0.418 / 0.430 / 0.418 | 0.419 / 0.411 / 0.423 |
| `while_loop` (1 iteration) | 0.418 / 0.430 / 0.418 | 0.418 / 0.430 / 0.418 | 0.418 / 0.430 / 0.418 |
| `map` | 0.418 / 0.430 / 0.418 | 0.418 / 0.430 / 0.418 | InductorError |
| `switch` | 0.418 / 0.430 / 0.418 | 0.418 / 0.430 / 0.418 | 0.419 / 0.411 / 0.423 |
| `scan` (control) | 0.0 | 0.0 | InductorError |
| `nested_compile_region` (control) | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 |

With continuous noise the gradient is plainly wrong, not just masked differently. For `torch.cond(pred, lambda t: t * torch.rand_like(t), ...)`, `dy/dx` should equal `y/x` elementwise. `max|x.grad - y/x|` is `0.994` in eager and `0.996` under inductor.

<details><summary>Full script for the table, and its output</summary>

```python
"""D-28 repro R1: torch.cond / control_flow.map / while_loop / switch backward re-runs the branch with FRESH randomness.
Forward keeps mask m1; backward differentiates an independent mask m2, so grad != d(out)/dx.
Expected mismatch fraction under independent masks: 2p(1-p) = 0.42 for p=0.3. Correct: 0.
CPU only. Usage: python repro.py
"""
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from torch._higher_order_ops.map import map as control_flow_map
from torch._higher_order_ops.while_loop import while_loop
from torch._higher_order_ops.switch import switch
from torch._higher_order_ops.scan import scan

p = 0.3
drop = lambda t: F.dropout(t, p, training=True)


def mismatch(fn, seed):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    x = (torch.rand(64, 256) + 0.5).requires_grad_()
    y = fn(x)
    y.sum().backward()                       # d y / d x = mask / (1-p): zero exactly where y == 0
    return ((y != 0) != (x.grad != 0)).float().mean().item()


cases = {
    "plain dropout (control)": drop,
    "torch.cond(dropout)": lambda x: torch.cond(x.sum() > 0, drop, lambda t: drop(t) * 1.0, (x,)),
    "torch.cond(x * rand_like)": None,
    "control_flow.map(dropout)": lambda x: control_flow_map(lambda r: drop(r), x),
    "while_loop(1 iter, dropout)": lambda x: while_loop(lambda i, a: i < 1, lambda i, a: (i + 1, drop(a)),
                                                        (torch.tensor(0), x))[1],
    "switch(dropout)": lambda x: switch(torch.tensor(1), [lambda t: drop(t) * 1.0, lambda t: drop(t)], (x,)),
    "scan(dropout) (control: saves)": lambda x: scan(lambda c, r: (c + 0, drop(r)), torch.zeros(()), x)[1],
    "nested_compile_region (control)": lambda x: torch.compiler.nested_compile_region(lambda t: drop(t))(x),
}
print(torch.__version__, torch.version.git_version)
for name, fn in cases.items():
    if fn is None:
        continue
    for mode in ["eager", "compile(aot_eager)", "compile(inductor)"]:
        f = fn if mode == "eager" else torch.compile(fn, backend=mode.split("(")[1][:-1])
        try:
            r = [round(mismatch(f, s), 3) for s in range(3)]
        except Exception as e:
            r = f"ERROR {type(e).__name__}"
        torch._dynamo.reset()
        print(f"{name:28s} {mode:20s} mismatch frac per seed = {r}")

# continuous noise: y = x * u, dy/dx must equal u = y/x
for mode in ["eager", "compile(inductor)"]:
    fn = lambda x: torch.cond(x.sum() > 0, lambda t: t * torch.rand_like(t), lambda t: t * 1.0, (x,))
    f = fn if mode == "eager" else torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor")
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    x = (torch.rand(64, 256) + 0.5).requires_grad_()
    y = f(x); y.sum().backward()
    print(f"torch.cond(x*rand_like)      {mode:20s} max|dy/dx - y/x| = {(x.grad - y.detach() / x.detach()).abs().max().item():.3f}")
    torch._dynamo.reset()

**Likely cause.** `CondAutogradOp.forward` (`torch/_higher_order_ops/cond.py:315`) builds `create_bw_fn(true_fn, operands)` and `create_bw_fn(false_fn, operands)` (lines 326 and 330). `backward` materializes that joint graph (`create_bw_fn`, `torch/_higher_order_ops/utils.py:982`, via `create_joint`) and runs it, which re-executes the branch forward to get the intermediates. No RNG state is saved in the forward or restored before the re-execution. `MapAutogradOp` (`map.py:226`), `WhileLoopAutogradOp` (`while_loop.py:844`) and `SwitchAutogradOp` (`switch.py:278`) do the same. `scan` and `nested_compile_region` save the partitioned intermediates and are unaffected. Line numbers are from 2.15.0.dev20260930; the code is the same in 2.14.0.

As a check, saving `torch.get_rng_state()` in `CondAutogradOp.forward` and restoring it inside `torch.random.fork_rng(devices=[])` around the `cond_op` call in `backward` brings the minimal repro to `0.0` on CPU. That patch is diagnostic only; it doesn't handle device generators.

The control-flow tracker (#172568) already notes that the backward fully recomputes the forward, and lists it as a performance item. The random-op consequence doesn't appear there, in the `torch.cond` docstring's restrictions, or in the cond autograd PR (#126911).

Possible fixes, from least to most change: (a) raise when a random op is traced inside a control-flow HOP that requires grad, as the proposed `invoke_subgraph`-based checkpointing does (open PR #192845 rejects RNG in the region); (b) snapshot the generator state in the autograd `forward` and restore it around the backward re-execution, like `torch.utils.checkpoint(preserve_rng_state=True)`; (c) save the random op's output as a residual instead of recomputing it.

Related but distinct: #190758 / #190717 (the memory-budget partitioner recomputes RNG ops with fresh randomness, through `activation_memory_budget`).

title: torch.utils.checkpoint under torch.compile(backend="eager") recomputes dropout with a fresh mask (preserve_rng_state is dropped)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.utils.checkpoint(..., use_reentrant=False)` with the default `preserve_rng_state=True` gives correct gradients in eager and under `backend="aot_eager"`. Under `torch.compile(backend="eager")`, or any custom backend that runs the Dynamo graph directly (e.g. `lambda gm, _: gm.forward`), the recompute in backward draws a new dropout mask. The gradient then corresponds to a different mask from the one used in the forward. Nothing is raised or warned.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint

def block(t):
    return F.dropout(t * 1.0, 0.3, training=True)

def f(x):
    return checkpoint(block, x, use_reentrant=False)  # preserve_rng_state=True (default)

def run(fn):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    x = (torch.rand(64, 256) + 0.5).requires_grad_()
    y = fn(x)
    y.sum().backward()
    return ((y != 0) != (x.grad != 0)).float().mean().item()

print("eager               :", run(f))                                         # 0.0
print("compile(aot_eager)  :", run(torch.compile(f, backend="aot_eager")))     # 0.0
torch._dynamo.reset()
print("compile(eager)      :", run(torch.compile(f, backend="eager")))         # ~0.42, expected 0.0
```

Output on 2.15.0.dev20260930 and on 2.14.0:

```
eager               : 0.0
compile(aot_eager)  : 0.0
compile(eager)      : 0.41802978515625
```

Expected `0.0` for all three. At `p = 0.3`, two independent masks disagree on `2p(1-p) = 0.42` of positions.

Selective activation checkpointing behaves the same way. With a `context_fn` whose policy returns `PREFER_RECOMPUTE` for the dropout, the mismatch is 0.418 / 0.430 / 0.418 over seeds 0-2 under `backend="eager"` and under a custom `gm.forward` backend, and 0.0 in eager and under `aot_eager`.

<details><summary>Full script (AC and SAC, three seeds, four backends) and its output</summary>

```python
"""D-28 repro R2: torch.utils.checkpoint (preserve_rng_state=True, the default) inside
torch.compile(backend="eager") -- or any backend that runs Dynamo's graph without AOTAutograd --
recomputes dropout in backward with a FRESH mask. Plain eager and backend="aot_eager" are correct.
Mechanism (torch/_higher_order_ops/wrap.py, tag_activation_checkpoint eager impl): it forces
kwargs["preserve_rng_state"] = False on the assumption that AOTAutograd/Inductor will functionalize
RNG; with backend="eager" nothing does. CPU only.
"""
import functools
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint, create_selective_checkpoint_contexts, CheckpointPolicy

p = 0.3


def block(t):
    return F.dropout(t * 1.0, p, training=True)


def mismatch(fn, seed):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    x = (torch.rand(64, 256) + 0.5).requires_grad_()
    y = fn(x)
    y.sum().backward()
    return ((y != 0) != (x.grad != 0)).float().mean().item()


def my_backend(gm, example_inputs):  # the canonical "custom backend" from the torch.compile docs
    return gm.forward


ac = lambda x: checkpoint(block, x, use_reentrant=False)  # preserve_rng_state defaults to True
sac_ctx = functools.partial(create_selective_checkpoint_contexts,
                            lambda ctx, op, *a, **k: CheckpointPolicy.PREFER_RECOMPUTE)
sac = lambda x: checkpoint(block, x, use_reentrant=False, context_fn=sac_ctx)

print(torch.__version__, torch.version.git_version)
for name, fn in [("checkpoint", ac), ("selective checkpoint", sac)]:
    for label, f in [("eager (no compile)", fn),
                     ("compile(backend='eager')", torch.compile(fn, backend="eager")),
                     ("compile(custom gm.forward)", torch.compile(fn, backend=my_backend)),
                     ("compile(backend='aot_eager')", torch.compile(fn, backend="aot_eager"))]:
        r = [round(mismatch(f, s), 3) for s in range(3)]
        torch._dynamo.reset()
        print(f"{name:22s} {label:30s} fwd/bwd mask mismatch frac = {r}   (0 = correct, 0.42 = independent)")
```

```

```

</details>

**Likely cause.** Dynamo rewrites the checkpoint call to the `tag_activation_checkpoint` HOP. Its eager implementation, `tag_activation_checkpoint_impl` in `torch/_higher_order_ops/wrap.py`, sets `kwargs["preserve_rng_state"] = False` (line 491) before calling `torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint`. `WrapActivationCheckpoint.__call__` does the same at line 359. The comment explains why:

> This doesn't mean that we don't preserve RNG state. Instead, we will always preserve RNG state regardless of this flag (by doing RNG functionalization via `replace_random_passes` in Inductor instead of in AOTAutograd).

That holds only when AOTAutograd traces the HOP. A backend that executes the Dynamo graph directly calls the eager implementation, so checkpoint runs with RNG preservation off, and nothing downstream restores it. `test/dynamo/test_activation_checkpointing.py` states the guarantee ("Regardless of whether `preserve_rng_state` is True or False, we will always preserve RNG state when using `torch.compile`") but only exercises `aot_autograd`-based backends.

As a check, changing line 491 to `kwargs.setdefault("preserve_rng_state", True)` brings `compile(eager)` in the repro to `0.0`, while eager and `aot_eager` stay at `0.0`. That was on CPU only; I didn't try CUDA, where the `fork_rng` tracing concern in the comment applies. Line numbers are from 2.15.0.dev20260930.

This matters beyond the eager backend itself, because `compile(backend="eager")` is the usual first bisection step for compile accuracy problems. A checkpointed model with dropout diverges under that backend for a reason unrelated to the bug being bisected.

Related:

- #160773 (closed) reported that `backend="eager"` ignored AC entirely. The eager implementation now calls `checkpoint`, but with `preserve_rng_state` forced off.
- Open PR #160883 ("Fallback to eager AC when backend=eager for TagActivationCheckpoint") routes the non-AOT case to plain `checkpoint` with the caller's kwargs, which looks like it would fix this too. Its test checks memory and FLOP parity, not RNG.
- #198866 (closed): fwd/bwd dropout mismatch under checkpoint with the *inductor* backend on CUDA. Its root cause was the 4x-random path (#184377, reverted in #198680). That's a different path: here `aot_eager` is correct, and only backends that skip AOTAutograd fail.
- #190758 / #190717: the memory-budget partitioner recomputes RNG ops with fresh randomness, through AOTAutograd and `activation_memory_budget`.

### Versions

Reproduced on torch 2.14.0 (git 08187d9e) and on the nightly below. CPU only; not tried on CUDA.

title: torch.compile(backend="eager") drops checkpoint RNG preservation, producing incorrect dropout gradients
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Checkpoint should reuse the forward dropout mask when `preserve_rng_state=True`. Under `torch.compile(backend="eager")`, backward draws a different mask and produces incorrect gradients, with no error or warning.

> **AI disclosure:** Codex prepared the following report from supplied reproduction notes.
>
> `torch.utils.checkpoint(..., use_reentrant=False)` defaults to `preserve_rng_state=True`. The following CPU repro gives correct gradients without compilation and with `backend="aot_eager"`, but incorrect gradients with `backend="eager"`:
>
> ```python
> import torch
> import torch.nn.functional as F
> from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint
>
> def block(t):
>     return F.dropout(t * 1.0, 0.3, training=True)
>
> def f(x):
>     return checkpoint(block, x, use_reentrant=False)
>
> def run(fn):
>     torch.manual_seed(0)
>     x = (torch.rand(64, 256) + 0.5).requires_grad_()
>     y = fn(x)
>     y.sum().backward()
>     return ((y != 0) != (x.grad != 0)).float().mean().item()
>
> print("eager               :", run(f))
> print("compile(aot_eager)  :", run(torch.compile(f, backend="aot_eager")))
> torch._dynamo.reset()
> print("compile(eager)      :", run(torch.compile(f, backend="eager")))
> ```
>
> Expected: `0.0` for all three. Inputs are strictly positive, so the zeros in the gradient must match the zeros in the forward dropout output. This compares each backward to its own forward output; it does not require identical random draws between backends.
>
> The same problem occurs with a custom backend returning `gm.forward` and with selective activation checkpointing whose policy returns `CheckpointPolicy.PREFER_RECOMPUTE`:
>
> | Execution | Checkpoint: mismatch for seeds 0 / 1 / 2 | Selective checkpoint: mismatch for seeds 0 / 1 / 2 |
> |---|---|---|
> | Eager, without compilation | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
> | `compile(backend="eager")` | .418 / .430 / .418 | .418 / .430 / .418 |
> | `compile(backend=lambda gm, _: gm.forward)` | .418 / .430 / .418 | .418 / .430 / .418 |
> | `compile(backend="aot_eager")` | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
>
> At dropout probability `p = 0.3`, independent masks disagree on `2p(1-p) = 0.42` of positions, consistent with these results.
>
> A likely cause is the eager implementation of [`tag_activation_checkpoint`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/89ac0527b15d5d9e2d5389b4cc56c54ce5320ed0/torch/_higher_order_ops/wrap.py#L491). It forces `kwargs["preserve_rng_state"] = False` before calling `checkpoint`, relying on downstream RNG functionalization. A backend that executes the Dynamo graph directly does not run that downstream handling. In the supplied CPU diagnostic, changing that assignment to `kwargs.setdefault("preserve_rng_state", True)` reduces the `compile(eager)` mismatch to `0.0`, while the eager and `aot_eager` controls remain `0.0`. This diagnostic was not tested on CUDA.
>
> This also affects debugging: `backend="eager"` is used to isolate compile failures, but checkpointed dropout acquires a gradient error under that backend.
>
> Related:
>
> - #160773 reported that `backend="eager"` ignored activation checkpointing entirely. The tested implementation now calls `checkpoint`, but disables RNG preservation.
> - Open PR #160883 proposes an eager checkpoint fallback for this backend and may address this path. The RNG behavior above provides an additional correctness case to check.
> - #198866 concerns Inductor checkpoint dropout on CUDA. This report concerns CPU execution under backends that skip AOTAutograd; it makes no claim that Inductor passes this repro.
> - #190758 / #190717 concern fresh RNG during memory-budget partitioning. This repro uses the default settings and fails without AOTAutograd.

> compile(aot_eager)  : 0.0

title: torch.cond / while_loop / map / switch backward uses fresh randomness, producing incorrect gradients
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Backward draws a different mask from the one used in forward, producing incorrect gradients. This happens even without `torch.compile`, with no error or warning.

> **AI disclosure:** Codex prepared the following report from supplied reproduction notes.
>
> When a `torch.cond` branch contains dropout, backward uses a different mask from the one used in forward. The gradient therefore does not match the output that was computed. This occurs without an explicit `torch.compile` call, and no error or warning is raised.
>
> Minimal CPU repro:
>
> ```python
> import torch
> import torch.nn.functional as F
>
> def f(x):
>     return torch.cond(
>         x.sum() > 0,
>         lambda t: F.dropout(t, 0.3, training=True),
>         lambda t: F.dropout(t, 0.3, training=True) * 1.0,
>         (x,),
>     )
>
> torch.manual_seed(0)
> x = (torch.rand(64, 256) + 0.5).requires_grad_()
> y = f(x)
> y.sum().backward()
> print("fwd/bwd mask mismatch:", ((y != 0) != (x.grad != 0)).float().mean().item())
> ```
>
> Observed on both 2.14.0 and 2.15.0.dev20260930:
>
> ```text
> fwd/bwd mask mismatch: 0.41802978515625
> ```
>
> Expected: `0.0`. Every input element is positive, and for dropout `dy/dx = mask / (1-p)`. The gradient must be zero exactly where the forward output is zero. At `p = 0.3`, independent masks disagree on `2p(1-p) = 0.42` of positions, consistent with the observed mismatch. Plain `F.dropout` outside `cond` gives `0.0` in the same process.
>
> This checks backward against its own forward output; it does not compare random draws between eager and compiled execution or between releases.
>
> The same mismatch occurs with the private control-flow operators `torch._higher_order_ops.while_loop`, `map`, and `switch`. `torch.cond` is a public prototype API. CPU results for seeds 0, 1, and 2:
>
> | Op | Eager | `compile(aot_eager)` | `compile(inductor)` |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Plain dropout (control) | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
> | `torch.cond` | .418 / .430 / .418 | .418 / .430 / .418 | .419 / .411 / .423 |
> | `while_loop` (one iteration) | .418 / .430 / .418 | .418 / .430 / .418 | .418 / .430 / .418 |
> | `map` | .418 / .430 / .418 | .418 / .430 / .418 | Not measured: `InductorError` |
> | `switch` | .418 / .430 / .418 | .418 / .430 / .418 | .419 / .411 / .423 |
> | `scan` (control) | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 | Not measured: `InductorError` |
> | `nested_compile_region` (control) | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
>
> Continuous noise shows the same problem: for a `cond` branch returning `t * torch.rand_like(t)`, the gradient should equal `y / x`. The measured maximum absolute difference is `0.994` in eager and `0.996` under Inductor.
>
> A likely cause is backward recomputing the branch without replaying its RNG state. At the tested nightly commit, [`CondAutogradOp`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/89ac0527/torch/_higher_order_ops/cond.py#L315) saves operands and constructs backward functions, then materializes and runs those functions in backward without saving or restoring RNG state. A diagnostic CPU-only patch that restores forward RNG state inside `torch.random.fork_rng(devices=[])` reduces the minimal repro mismatch to `0.0`; it is not a proposed device-complete fix.
>
> Related: #172568 tracks forward recomputation as a performance item. #190758 / #190717 report fresh RNG during memory-budget partitioning; this repro requires neither that setting nor an explicit compilation call.
