title: [Feature Request] Make the fake process group and the LocalTensor RNG state path accelerator-agnostic (third-party devices, e.g. Ascend NPU)
body:
### Context

Two hardcoded device whitelists block the DTensor/FSDP test suites on any third-party accelerator (here: Ascend NPU, a renamed PrivateUse1 backend registered through `torch.accelerator`). They are two consecutive blockers on the same code path rather than two independent features, so they are reported together.

This issue was requested in review of #195260 ("our usual process is to discuss on the issue before doing the PR ... make sure that the issue is marked actionable before sending a PR"). The second change is already open as #195261.

## 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Blocker 1 — the fake backend's device whitelist (`torch/testing/_internal/distributed/fake_pg.py`)

```python
dist.Backend.register_backend(
    dist.Backend.FAKE,
    _create_fake_pg,
    extended_api=True,
    devices=["cpu", "cuda", "hpu", "xpu"],   # still the case on main @36a88a5f7945
)
```

For any device type outside that list, `init_process_group(backend="fake")` fails in the umbrella lookup with `No backend type associated with device type npu` (`ProcessGroup.cpp`), even though `FakeProcessGroup` is a device-agnostic C++ no-op. `hpu` and `xpu` were each added one at a time; the next accelerator needs one more core patch for no technical reason.

Consequence: the classes created by `create_local_tensor_test_class` in `test/distributed/tensor/test_random_ops.py` (`DistTensorRandomInitTestWithLocalTensor`, `DistTensorRandomOpTestWithLocalTensor`, `DistTensorRandomOpsTest3DWithLocalTensor`) cannot even construct their process group on such a backend, so the whole single-process multi-rank path is unrunnable there.

### Blocker 2 — the LocalTensor RNG state classification (`torch/distributed/_local_tensor/__init__.py:800`)

```python
if self._device.type in {"cuda", "xpu"}:
    if self._device.index not in any_rank_cuda:
        raise AssertionError
    any_rank_device_state = any_rank_cuda[self._device.index]
else:
    any_rank_device_state = any_rank_cpu
```

Any device type outside `{cuda, xpu}` — hpu, privateuse1, ... — takes the **CPU MT19937 state tensor**, which `_PhiloxState` then misparses as a 16-byte philox layout:

```
RuntimeError: a Tensor with 631 elements cannot be converted to Scalar
```

The collection side in the same file is already device-generic: `_collect_accelerator_rng_states` goes through `torch.accelerator` / `torch.get_device_module()` and returns an accelerator-keyed dict for whatever backend registered it. Only the classification branch above is stale.

### Pitch — two small changes

1. **#195260** (closed, to be re-submitted): register the `devices` argument as a `list` subclass that resolves `torch.accelerator.current_accelerator().type` at **read time** (base list + current accelerator type, deduped, probe wrapped in try/except). Resolving eagerly at import does not work: `fake_pg` is imported while `_import_device_backends()` is still autoloading the vendor backend (the import chain pulls in `dynamo -> fsdp -> _flat_param -> fake_pg`), so `current_accelerator()` raises and the whole backend autoload breaks. `Backend.backend_capability["fake"]` holds a list by reference and it is consumed lazily when `init_process_group` builds its device-to-backend map, which is why read-time resolution is the correct hook. cpu/cuda/hpu/xpu behaviour is byte-for-byte unchanged.
2. **#195261** (open): flip the classification to "`cpu` reads the cpu state; every other device type reads the accelerator states dict keyed by device index", matching the already device-generic collection side. cuda/xpu/cpu behaviour is unchanged; only "other" devices go from misparsing the cpu state to the correct accelerator state.

**Request:** mark this actionable (or point us at the preferred design) so the two changes can be re-submitted / reviewed. Happy to implement a different shape.

## Alternatives

- **Status quo — per-backend static whitelist:** append each new accelerator's device type one by one. Every new backend needs a core patch, and hpu still hits blocker 2.
- **Probe `torch.accelerator` eagerly at import time:** rejected — the module is imported before the vendor backend finishes registering itself, which raises mid-autoload and breaks it (observed: `Failed to load the backend extension`).
- **Make the fake backend device-agnostic by contract** (e.g. `devices` optional / "all device types registered via `torch.accelerator`"): arguably the cleanest fix for blocker 1; we are happy to implement whichever direction maintainers prefer over the lazy list.

## Additional context — real-machine evidence

Host: Ascend NPU machine (CANN 9.2.0-beta.2), torch and torch_npu built from `main @949e0b9476e`, with the two files under test overlaid from the PR branches. Measured 2026-08-29; both whitelists are still present on main as of 2026-10-01 (`fake_pg.py` `7251380a`, `_local_tensor/__init__.py` `8d5085c4`).

| Check | before | after both changes |
|---|---|---|
| `list(Backend.backend_capability["fake"])`, accelerator env | `['cpu','cuda','hpu','xpu']` | `['cpu','cuda','hpu','xpu','npu']` |
| same, CPU-only env (torch_npu not loaded) | `['cpu','cuda','hpu','xpu']` | `['cpu','cuda','hpu','xpu']` (unchanged) |
| `DistTensorRandomInitTestWithLocalTensor.test_init_ops` | error: `No backend type associated with device type npu` | OK |
| `test/distributed/tensor/test_random_ops.py` (full file, WORLD_SIZE=4) | `errors=1` (the only error is this issue) | `Ran 55, OK (skipped=42)`, errors=0 |
| `import torch` (triggers the backend autoload chain) | — | clean; an eager-probe variant of the change breaks here |
| CPU-only env: `init_process_group(backend="fake", world_size=8)` | works | works |

The fake-PG change alone removes the `No backend type ...` error; blocker 2 (`a Tensor with 631 elements cannot be converted to Scalar`) is what surfaces next — which is why the two are reported as one path. Both errors reproduce on unmodified main as well (checked by swapping the two files only).

title: `torch.compile` (inductor) — `Tensor.set_` storage rebind silently miscompiled: a mutation of the OLD storage leaks into the rebound tensor (wrong value); eager and `backend="eager"` are correct
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`Tensor.set_(source)` rebinds `dest`'s storage to `source`'s storage. After the rebind, mutating the *old* storage
must not affect `dest`. Under `torch.compile` with the inductor backend, the compiled function instead still reflects
the old storage's mutation in `dest`, returning a silently wrong value. Eager and `torch.compile(..., backend="eager")`
both return the correct value, so this is **inductor-specific** (the inductor lowering/codegen drops the `set_` storage
aliasing), not a Dynamo tracing or AOTAutograd functionalization issue. Reproduces on CPU and CUDA, deterministically.

## Minimal repro

```python
import torch

def f(dest, src, storage):
    dest.set_(src)        # rebind dest's storage to src's storage
    storage[0] = 10.0     # mutate the OLD storage -> must NOT affect dest
    return dest[0].clone()

def fresh():
    storage = torch.arange(5, dtype=torch.float32)
    return storage[:3], torch.full((3,), 7.0), storage

print(f(*fresh()))                                      # eager:         7.0   (dest[0] == src[0])
torch._dynamo.reset()
print(torch.compile(f, backend="eager")(*fresh()))     # backend=eager: 7.0   -> not a Dynamo/AOTAutograd bug
torch._dynamo.reset()
print(torch.compile(f, backend="inductor")(*fresh()))  # inductor:      10.0  (WRONG: old-storage mutation leaked in)
```

## Isolation

| case | eager | backend="eager" | inductor |
|---|---|---|---|
| `set_` rebind + old-storage mutation, CPU | OK `7` | OK `7` | **WRONG `10`** |
| `set_` rebind + old-storage mutation, CUDA | OK `7` | OK `7` | **WRONG `10`** |

title: [inductor] freezing_discard_parameters=True fails with "only Tensors of floating point dtype can require gradients" for an integer nn.Parameter(requires_grad=False)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `freezing=True` and `freezing_discard_parameters=True`, `torch.compile` fails on a module that has an integer `nn.Parameter` created with `requires_grad=False`. The same module compiles fine with `freezing=True` alone, and eager works.

```python
import torch
from torch._inductor import config

class M(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        # integer, non-trainable parameter (e.g. an index table)
        self.idx = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor([0, 2]), requires_grad=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return x[:, self.idx] * 2

m = M().eval()
x = torch.randn(3, 4)
print("eager:", m(x).shape)

with torch.no_grad():
    with config.patch(freezing=True):
        print("freezing:", torch.compile(m)(x).shape)
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    with config.patch(freezing=True, freezing_discard_parameters=True):
        print("freezing + freezing_discard_parameters:", torch.compile(m)(x).shape)
```

```
eager: torch.Size([3, 2])
freezing: torch.Size([3, 2])
torch._dynamo.exc.BackendCompilerFailed: backend='inductor' raised:
RuntimeError: only Tensors of floating point dtype can require gradients
```

The error is raised in `torch/_inductor/freezing.py`:

```
  File ".../torch/_inductor/freezing.py", line 196, in invalidate_eager_modules
    e_t.requires_grad_(True)
```

`invalidate_eager_modules` and `discard_traced_gm_params` both replace every parameter/buffer with an `ErasedTensor` and, for any `nn.Parameter`, unconditionally call `e_t.requires_grad_(True)`. That fails for non-floating-point parameters, and also changes `requires_grad` for parameters the user created with `requires_grad=False`. Keeping the original tensor's `requires_grad` (e.g. `e_t.requires_grad_(tensor.requires_grad)`) should avoid it.

title: [torch.compile] AssertionError "n=copy_, n.args[0]=dequantize" when a graph input is mutated in place after torch.dequantize on a non-quantized tensor
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Mutating a graph input in place after calling `torch.dequantize` on it (with a regular, non-quantized float tensor) works in eager mode but fails under `torch.compile` with an AOTAutograd functionalization assertion.

```python
import torch

def f(x):
    a = torch.dequantize(x)
    b = torch.trunc_(x)
    return a, b

print("eager:", [t.tolist() for t in f(torch.tensor([1.7]))])
torch.compile(f, backend="inductor")(torch.tensor([1.7]))
```

```
eager: [[1.0], [1.0]]
torch._dynamo.exc.BackendCompilerFailed: backend='inductor' raised:
AssertionError: n=copy_, n.args[0]=dequantize, placeholders={arg0_1}, graph=graph():
    %arg0_1 : [num_users=1] = placeholder[target=arg0_1]
    %dequantize : [num_users=2] = call_function[target=torch.ops.aten.dequantize.self](args = (%arg0_1,), kwargs = {})
    %trunc : [num_users=1] = call_function[target=torch.ops.aten.trunc.default](args = (%dequantize,), kwargs = {})
    %copy_ : [num_users=1] = call_function[target=torch.ops.aten.copy_.default](args = (%dequantize, %trunc), kwargs = {})
```

The assertion comes from `_is_functional_graph` in `torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/functional_utils.py` ("Can only copy_/set_ into an input"): the input mutation from `trunc_` is written back into `%dequantize` rather than into the graph input `%arg0_1`.

In eager, `torch.dequantize` on a non-quantized tensor returns the input itself, so `a` aliases `x` and both outputs are `[1.0]`. That aliasing appears to be the trigger — `dequantize_self` is listed in #60426 as an op whose output shares storage with its input. The same assertion was previously hit through other ops (#136064, #178952, both closed), but this `dequantize` path still fails.

title: torch.isin raises "view size is not compatible" on CPU when test_elements is a non-contiguous multi-dimensional tensor (regression since 1.11)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On CPU, `torch.isin` raises a `RuntimeError` when `test_elements` is a multi-dimensional tensor that can't be flattened without a copy (e.g. a transposed matrix). The same call works with `test_elements.contiguous()`, `numpy.isin` returns the expected result, and it worked in torch 1.10. The docs don't mention any contiguity requirement.

```python
import torch

elements = torch.tensor([0., 5., 9.])
test_elements = torch.arange(4.).reshape(2, 2).t()   # non-contiguous

print(torch.isin(elements, test_elements.contiguous()))  # tensor([ True, False, False])
print(torch.isin(elements, test_elements))               # RuntimeError
```

```
tensor([ True, False, False])
RuntimeError: view size is not compatible with input tensor's size and stride (at least one dimension spans across two contiguous subspaces). Use .reshape(...) instead.
```

| torch version | `torch.isin(elements, test_elements)` |
|---|---|
| 1.10.2+cpu | `tensor([ True, False, False])` |
| 1.11.0+cpu | `RuntimeError: view size is not compatible ...` |
| 2.14.0+cpu, nightly 2.15.0.dev20260925+cpu | `RuntimeError: view size is not compatible ...` |

It only happens on the brute-force path, which is used when `test_elements` is small relative to `elements` (`test_elements.numel() < 10 * elements.numel() ** 0.145`). With a larger `test_elements`, the sorting path is used and the same non-contiguous input works. One-dimensional strided inputs (`x[::2]`, `x[:, 1]`, `expand`) also work.

**Cause:** in `aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/TensorCompareKernel.cpp`, `isin_default_kernel_cpu` flattens with `view`:

```cpp
Tensor test_elements_flat = test_elements.to(common_type).view(-1);
auto test_elements_stride = test_elements_flat.stride(0);
```

This line came from #70659 (the fix for #67432, landed in abe361754ec3), which replaced `.ravel()` with `.view(-1)` plus a stride-aware loop so that 1-D strided inputs are read correctly. `view(-1)` fails for multi-dimensional inputs that can't be viewed as 1-D. `.reshape(-1)` should cover both cases: it returns a view when possible (and the loop already handles its stride) and a copy otherwise.

This also shows up through `torch.isin(x, x)` when `x` is transposed.

title: [inductor] AOTI arrayref (stack-allocation) wrapper tests consistently red on trunk since mid-September
body:
This showed up as red `inductor_aoti_fallback` (unstable) legs on several unrelated PRs of mine, and it reproduces on main itself, so here is a tracker.

**What is failing**

`test/inductor/test_aot_inductor_arrayref.py::AOTInductorTestABICompatibleCpuWithStackAllocation`: 45 distinct tests across the two shards on the latest completed main run I checked (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/36772927145, sha 138b5776f, 2026-09-30). Representative failures:

- `test_aoti_debug_printer_codegen_cpu_with_stack_allocation`: `RuntimeError: Expected to find "before_launch - aoti_torch_cpu_addmm_out" but did not find it`
- `test_aoti_profiler_input_shapes_cpu_with_stack_allocation`: `RuntimeError: Expected to find "aoti_torch_tensor_to_ivalue" but did not find it`
- `test_cond_unbacked_symint_predicate_cpu_with_stack_allocation`: `Failed: Unexpected success`
- `test_constant_folding_cpu_with_stack_allocation` / `test_const_graph_no_autotune_at_compile_time_cpu_with_stack_allocation`: `RuntimeError: Mismatch ...`

**How long**

Both shards are red on every main run I sampled: 35161124625 (09-16), 35970086847 (09-24, predates #179699), 36497560056 (09-28), 36772927145 (09-30, which already includes #179700, so that follow-up does not cover this). The legs are unstable so nothing is blocked, which is probably how it has sat for two weeks.

**Reading**

Every failure describes generated code that no longer matches what these tests check: debug-printer launch lines and profiler ivalue emission missing for extern kernels, a cond test that unexpectedly succeeds, constant-folding output mismatches. They all live on the stack-allocation (arrayref) wrapper path, so one codegen change there would explain the whole set. #179699 and #179700 touched fallback-kernel profiling codegen in this area around the start of the window; I have not bisected, so treat that as a pointer, not an accusation.

**Repro**

```
python test/inductor/test_aot_inductor_arrayref.py AOTInductorTestABICompatibleCpuWithStackAllocation.test_aoti_debug_printer_codegen_cpu_with_stack_allocation
```

on a CPU build of current main.

Verification boundary: CI evidence only. I do not have a local CPU build of main here, so no local repro and no bisect.

title: [AOTAutograd] Dynamic checkpoint input aliases RNG state shape, causing backward assertion
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When compiling a model with checkpoint recomputation and fallback_random=True, the added RNG state tensors can be assigned symbolic shapes that accidentally share a symbol with an input dimension, without a corresponding equality guard. If that input dimension later changes, the compiled backward expects the fixed-size RNG state to change with it, causing a shape assertion failure. I believe the RNG state shape should remain static and independent of the model’s dynamic input shapes.


AI disclosure: The quoted report below was prepared with Codex, which ran the reproducer and controls in the described environment. The submitter’s own assessment belongs above; the quoted text is AI-generated.

> Reproduced on official nightly `2.15.0.dev20260928+cu130` (commit `68e0ae4967e1a7e39d914179aea0026036cc1a23`) with `MUST_RECOMPUTE`, `fallback_random=True`, and the default memory budget (`1.0`). Changing the input from `[16,32]` to `[28,32]` succeeds in forward but fails in backward with `expected size 16==28`.

### Reproducer

>
> Save as `repro_must_recompute.py` and run `python -I repro_must_recompute.py` in a fresh process:
>
> ```python
> import argparse
> from functools import partial
>
> import torch
> import torch._functorch.config
> import torch._inductor.config
> from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint, CheckpointPolicy, create_selective_checkpoint_contexts
>
> parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
> parser.add_argument("--sizes", default="16,28,16")
> args = parser.parse_args()
>
> torch._inductor.config.fallback_random = True
> torch._inductor.config.compile_threads = 1
> # Leave activation_memory_budget at its default.
> print(f"activation_memory_budget={torch._functorch.config.activation_memory_budget}", flush=True)
>
> def recompute_policy(ctx, op, *args, **kwargs):
>     return CheckpointPolicy.MUST_RECOMPUTE
>
> context_fn = partial(create_selective_checkpoint_contexts, recompute_policy)
>
> def model(x):
>     return checkpoint(
>         lambda z: torch.nn.functional.dropout(z, p=0.1, training=True).square(),
>         x,
>         use_reentrant=False,
>         context_fn=context_fn,
>     )
>
> print(f"torch={torch.__version__}, git={torch.version.git_version}", flush=True)
> print(f"CUDA RNG state shape={tuple(torch.cuda.get_rng_state().shape)}", flush=True)
> compiled = torch.compile(model, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True, dynamic=True)
>
> for size in map(int, args.sizes.split(",")):
>     torch.manual_seed(121)
>     x = torch.randn(size, 32, device="cuda", requires_grad=True)
>     ref_x = x.detach().clone().requires_grad_()
>     torch.manual_seed(5678)
>     ref = model(ref_x)
>     ref.sum().backward()
>     torch.manual_seed(5678)
>     out = compiled(x)
>     print(f"size={size}: forward_equal={torch.equal(out, ref)}", flush=True)
>     out.sum().backward()
>     print(f"size={size}: gradient_equal={torch.equal(x.grad, ref_x.grad)}", flush=True)
> ```
>

### Evidence and candidate fix

>
> Generated backward (the actual RNG state is CPU `uint8[16]`):
>
> ```python
> assert_size_stride_grouped(
>     (rng_state_output_0, primals_3),
>     ((s77,), (s77, s27)),
>     ((1,), (s27, 1)),
>     'input',
> )
> ```
>
> Controls:
>
> - Unmodified nightly with `--sizes 17,28,17`: all outputs and gradients exactly match eager.
> - Adding `static_shapes=True` below: `16,28,16` passes with all outputs and gradients exactly matching eager; RNG metadata becomes `[16]`, while input shapes remain dynamic.
>
> Candidate fix in [`functionalize_rng_ops.get_sample_rng_state`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/68e0ae4967e1a7e39d914179aea0026036cc1a23/torch/_functorch/partitioners.py):
>
> ```diff
> - return fake_mode.from_tensor(get_device_rng_state(device))
> - return fake_mode.from_tensor(torch.get_rng_state())
> + return fake_mode.from_tensor(get_device_rng_state(device), static_shapes=True)
> + return fake_mode.from_tensor(torch.get_rng_state(), static_shapes=True)
> ```
>
> The fix was tested in-process on CUDA; the CPU branch was not independently tested.

title: torch.compile moves backward-only RNG into forward with fallback_random=True
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When we use `torch.compile` with `fallback_random=True`, a `torch.randint` call written only in the backward method of an `autograd.Function` is moved into forward during compilation. This means, in this case, compile behavior is different from the eager behavior, because moving the seed draw into forward can change the order of the random ops and thus change the bitwise result of the random operation.

AI assistance: Codex helped prepare and test the minimal reproducer and collect the environment information.

```python
import torch

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
get_state = torch.cuda.get_rng_state if device == "cuda" else torch.get_rng_state

class BackwardRNG(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x):
        return x.clone()

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad):
        seed = torch.randint(0, 2**31, (), device=grad.device)
        return torch.where(seed >= 0, grad, -grad)

def run(fn):
    x = torch.ones(8, device=device, requires_grad=True)
    torch.manual_seed(321)
    y = fn(x)
    between = torch.rand(8, device=device)
    y.sum().backward()
    return between, get_state()

compiled = torch.compile(
    BackwardRNG.apply, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True,
    options={"fallback_random": True, "compile_threads": 1},
)
run(compiled)  # Warm up both forward and backward before measuring.
eager, compiled_result = run(BackwardRNG.apply), run(compiled)
print("between_equal:", torch.equal(eager[0], compiled_result[0]))
print("final_rng_equal:", torch.equal(eager[1], compiled_result[1]))
```


### Error logs


> No exception; silent RNG ordering mismatch. CPU and CUDA both print:

```text
between_equal: False
final_rng_equal: True
```

title: [DTensor] exponential_, log_normal_, geometric_ and multinomial give the same random values on every shard
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When you call a random op on a sharded DTensor, each shard should get different random values. DTensor does this by sending random ops through its RNG tracker, which gives each shard its own part of the random stream.

Four ops are not sent through the tracker: `exponential_`, `log_normal_`, `geometric_` and `multinomial`. They run on each rank's local generator instead. Since every rank uses the same seed, **every shard gets the same values.** No error is raised.

Example: a `(8, 4)` tensor sharded by rows over 2 GPUs. After `dt.exponential_()`, rows 0-3 and rows 4-7 are identical.

**A second, narrower effect:** if the shards are uneven (for example 2 rows on one GPU and 1 row on the other) and large enough, each GPU's generator moves forward by a different amount. After that, a normal tracked op like dropout on a `Replicate` DTensor gives a different mask on each GPU, even though the tensor should be the same everywhere.

### Cause

DTensor decides whether an op is random by checking two hardcoded lists:

- `self._random_ops` in [`torch/distributed/tensor/_dispatch.py`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a9ff16cf2fae5946d5fbe59864e1dd3b7c59e1f2/torch/distributed/tensor/_dispatch.py#L211-L226)
- `is_random_op()` in [`torch/csrc/autograd/python_variable.cpp`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a9ff16cf2fae5946d5fbe59864e1dd3b7c59e1f2/torch/csrc/autograd/python_variable.cpp#L1337-L1371)

The four ops have sharding rules in [`_ops/_random_ops.py`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a9ff16cf2fae5946d5fbe59864e1dd3b7c59e1f2/torch/distributed/tensor/_ops/_random_ops.py#L38-L55), but are missing from both lists.

**Tests didn't catch it**: [`test_init_ops`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/a9ff16cf2fae5946d5fbe59864e1dd3b7c59e1f2/test/distributed/tensor/test_random_ops.py#L73-L82) slices the other rank's shard using the full width instead of the shard width, so the shapes never match and `assertNotEqual` always passes. `test_multinomial_sharded` only checks shape and placement.

### Suggested fix

Add the four ops to both lists. `multinomial` may need a closer look: unlike the other three, it doesn't simply fill a tensor element by element, so it's worth confirming that each shard uses no more random numbers than the tracker reserves for it.

Repro (needs 2 CUDA GPUs; run with `torchrun --nproc-per-node 2 repro.py`):

```python
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.distributed.device_mesh import init_device_mesh
from torch.distributed.tensor import distribute_tensor, Replicate, Shard

dist.init_process_group("nccl")
rank = dist.get_rank()
torch.cuda.set_device(rank)
torch.manual_seed(0)
mesh = init_device_mesh("cuda", (2,))


def sharded(*shape):
    return distribute_tensor(torch.empty(*shape, device="cuda"), mesh, [Shard(0)])


# 1. Each rank holds one row; the two rows should differ
ops = {
    "uniform_ (control)": lambda t: t.uniform_(),
    "exponential_": lambda t: t.exponential_(),
    "log_normal_": lambda t: t.log_normal_(),
    "geometric_": lambda t: t.geometric_(0.5),
    "multinomial": lambda t: torch.multinomial(t.fill_(1 / 16), 16, replacement=True),
}
for name, op in ops.items():
    full = op(sharded(2, 16)).full_tensor()
    if rank == 0:
        print(f"{name:20s} rows equal: {torch.equal(full[0], full[1])}")

# 2. Uneven shards (2 rows vs 1 row), then dropout on a Replicate tensor;
#    the masks should be the same on both ranks
for name in ["uniform_ (control)", "exponential_"]:
    ops[name](sharded(3, 400_000))
    r = distribute_tensor(torch.ones(1000, device="cuda"), mesh, [Replicate()])
    mask = torch.nn.functional.dropout(r, 0.5).to_local()
    masks = [torch.empty_like(mask) for _ in range(2)]
    dist.all_gather(masks, mask)
    if rank == 0:
        print(f"{name:20s} then dropout, masks equal: {torch.equal(*masks)}")

dist.destroy_process_group()
```

Output (2x NVIDIA A10, torch 2.14.0+cu130):

```
uniform_ (control)   rows equal: False
exponential_         rows equal: True
log_normal_          rows equal: True
geometric_           rows equal: True
multinomial          rows equal: True
uniform_ (control)   then dropout, masks equal: True
exponential_         then dropout, masks equal: False
```

Expected: every `rows equal` line is `False`, and both `masks equal` lines are `True`. `uniform_` is already in the lists and shows the correct behavior.

I'd like to submit a fix, adding the four ops to both lists and fixing the test, if that sounds right to the maintainers.

title: [ROCm][Windows] Device-side assert prints no message: C10_USE_ROCM_KERNEL_ASSERT is off in the Windows ROCm wheel
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

In the Windows ROCm wheel `2.11.0+rocm7.13.0a20260416`, a device-side assert prints no message. `C10_USE_ROCM_KERNEL_ASSERT` is undefined in this wheel (`torch/headeronly/macros/cmake_macros.h:12`), so `CUDA_KERNEL_ASSERT` falls back to HIP's `assert`. On Windows, HIP's device `assert` is `__builtin_trap()` with no message: the header says "FIXME: Need `wchar_t` support to generate assertion message" ([hip_assert.h#L19-L24](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-systems/blob/bc176d4b86e86cf5caf5dc44fc2beec442ad6e38/projects/clr/hipamd/include/hip/amd_detail/hip_assert.h#L19-L24)).

```python
import torch
fine = torch.zeros(64, 4, device="cuda")
idx = torch.tensor([3, 10**9, 7], dtype=torch.int64).to("cuda")
fine.view(-1).index_fill_(0, idx, 0.0)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
```

- **ROCm wheel on an AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201):** nothing is printed. On this card the synchronize also never returns. That hang is the HIP runtime's, filed as https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-systems/issues/12572. The script that ran is `oob_hang.py` in https://gist.github.com/ethancawse/733fe8e44cfbc820c5f2a0b9d2417aa8.
- **CUDA wheel on an RTX 3060 Ti in the same machine:** `IndexKernel.cu:154 ... "index out of bounds" failed` is printed, followed by `torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: device-side assert triggered`.

Only the missing message is PyTorch's. Expected: the failing assertion's message is printed, as it is on CUDA.

### Versions

Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26100.9457; PyTorch 2.11.0+rocm7.13.0a20260416 (HIP 7.2.0, `amdhip64_7.dll` 10.0.3581.0); Python 3.14.6; AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700; Adrenalin 32.0.31041.1004; Intel Core i9-13900KS. The CUDA control used PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130.

title: Intel Arc (B70, level_zero): Conv1d/Conv2d/matmul return NaN in bf16 and fp16; fp32 and CUDA clean
body:
## Summary

On Intel Arc (B70, `level_zero`), `torch` 2.12.0+xpu returns **non-finite (NaN)
results for `Conv1d`, `Conv2d` and raw `matmul` in both bfloat16 and float16**.
The identical code and identical shapes are clean on CUDA, and fp32 is clean on
the same XPU device. This makes reduced precision unusable on Arc for any model
whose forward pass contains a convolution or an attention matmul.

`nn.Linear`, `softmax`, `gelu` and `layernorm` are all clean on the same device
and in the same run, so this is not a general "XPU reduced precision is broken"
result — it is specific to a subset of kernels.

This is not a model-specific issue. It was found while trying to run
`Qwen2_5OmniForConditionalGeneration` (Ovis-Omni-Embedding-3B) on an Arc Pro B70,
but the reproduction below involves no model at all.

## Versions

| | |
|---|---|
| torch (failing) | `2.12.0+xpu` (`torch.version.xpu = 20250302`) |
| GPU | `Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B70 Graphics`, 31.9 GiB, `level_zero` backend |
| torch (control) | `2.13.0+cu130` (CUDA 13.0) |
| GPU (control) | `NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti`, compute capability 12.0, driver 595.91.07 |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS |
| Kernel | 7.0.6-2-pve |

## Reproduction

Runs on either device, so the control ships with the repro:

```bash
/opt/intel-venv/bin/python             scripts/repro-xpu-reduced-precision.py xpu
/models/nvidia_5060ti-venv/bin/python  scripts/repro-xpu-reduced-precision.py cuda
```

## Results — XPU (B70), `torch 2.12.0+xpu`

### bfloat16

| case | result |
|---|---|
| conv1d 128->1280 k3 s2 L=30000 | **NaN** |
| conv1d 128->1280 k3 s2 L=512 | **NaN** |
| conv1d 128->1280 k3 s2 L=64 | ok |
| conv1d 8->16 k3 s1 L=32 | ok |
| conv2d 3->64 k3 L=64 | **NaN** |
| linear 1280->1280 | ok |
| linear 8->8 | ok |
| matmul 1280x1280 (raw) | **NaN** |
| softmax | ok |
| gelu | ok |
| layernorm 1280 | ok |

### float16

| case | result |
|---|---|
| conv1d 128->1280 k3 s2 L=30000 | **NaN** |
| conv1d 128->1280 k3 s2 L=512 | **NaN** |
| conv1d 128->1280 k3 s2 L=64 | **NaN** |
| conv1d 8->16 k3 s1 L=32 | ok |
| conv2d 3->64 k3 L=64 | **NaN** |
| linear 1280->1280 | ok |
| linear 8->8 | ok |
| matmul 1280x1280 (raw) | **NaN** |
| softmax | ok |
| gelu | ok |
| layernorm 1280 | ok |

### float32 — all clean

Every case above, including conv1d 128->1280 k3 s2 L=30000, conv2d, and the raw
1280x1280 matmul, is finite in fp32.

## Results — CUDA control (5060 Ti), `torch 2.13.0+cu130`

Every case in all three dtypes is finite. `modules non-finite in at least one
dtype: 0`.

## Observations that may help

- **bf16 and fp16 both fail, fp32 passes** on the same device and same weights,
  which points at the reduced-precision kernel path rather than a bad cast or a
  missing scale.
- **The failure is length-dependent and not monotonic.** For the same
  `conv1d 128->1280 k3 s2`, L=30000 fails in bf16 while L=64 is fine; in fp16 all
  three lengths fail. `conv1d 8->16 k3 s1 L=32` (small channel count) is clean in
  both. That pattern is consistent with a reduction or accumulation issue that
  depends on tensor size, and it means a small test case can easily pass and hide
  the bug — the "tiny" case here is clean while the real shapes are not.
- **`nn.Linear` is clean at 1280->1280, but a raw `matmul` of the same 1280x1280
  is not.** Whatever `F.linear` does differently from `torch.matmul` on this
  backend is likely where the divergence is.
- The additive attention mask is all zeros for a single chunk and therefore
  cannot be the source of an overflow here, so I have ruled that out as a
  confound.

## Impact

Any Arc configuration that assumes reduced precision is usable will silently
produce NaN. In our case this forced a 5.5B-parameter model from bf16 (11.2 GB)
to fp32 (22.4 GB), roughly halving the model size that fits on the card. Silent
NaN is the dangerous part: it surfaces far from its cause as a
`expected mat1 and mat2 to have the same dtype` error or a garbage decode, not as
an arithmetic fault at the convolution.

Because `nn.Linear`, `softmax`, `gelu` and `layernorm` are all clean, it would be
useful to know whether there is a narrower characterization of the affected
kernels, and whether a smaller repro (single `conv1d`, no model) is enough to
bisect it.

body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

In `torch/distributed/elastic/agent/server/api.py`, the `Worker` class docstring lists `id (Any)` under its `Args:` block, but `Worker.__init__` does not accept an `id` argument. It only takes the rank and world-size ints, and `self.id` is set internally (the agent assigns it later). Following the documented signature gives:

```
TypeError: Worker.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'id'
```

Minimal repro:

```python
from torch.distributed.elastic.agent.server.api import Worker

Worker(id=1, local_rank=0, global_rank=0, role_rank=0, world_size=1, role_world_size=1)
```

I also compared the docstring with the real signature: the Args block documents `local_rank, global_rank, role_rank, world_size, role_world_size, id`, while `__init__` takes all of those except `id`. The prose above the Args block already describes `id` correctly as an attribute assigned by the agent, so the fix is just dropping that one line from the Args block.

A one-line fix for this was in #198900, which got closed with a note to open an issue first. #199255 fixes the same line and is linked here, so I'll leave #198900 closed instead of opening a duplicate.

Note: this issue text was drafted with help from an AI assistant; I verified the mismatch and the repro myself on current `main`.

### Versions

PyTorch version: current `main` branch (checked on 2026-10-01)
How you installed PyTorch: found by reading the source on GitHub; no install needed for a docstring mismatch
Python version: not relevant here (docs-only issue)
OS: macOS

title: [Inductor][PDL] triton.enable_pdl: a kernel loads a buffer written two kernels back before gdc_wait() when the kernel in between is store-only, giving wrong results
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug The analysis was done with assistance of AI and was reviewed by me. With `torch.compile(..., options={"triton.enable_pdl": True})`, a kernel's first load of a buffer written *two kernels back* is emitted before `tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait()` when the kernel in between does not touch that buffer. If the kernel in between is store-only (a zero fill, `full`, `arange` …), it never calls `gdc_wait()` and triggers its dependents as soon as its CTAs exit. So the third kernel can start, and load, while the first is still computing. Inductor places `index_put_`/`scatter_add`/`index_add` zero-fill inits right before their consumer, so this chain arises naturally. Results are wrong on every call after the first here; exact with `triton.enable_pdl=False` or `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`. Reproduced on nightly 2.15.0.dev20260930+cu132 (git 89ac0527b15d) and on 2.14.0, NVIDIA GB10 (sm_121): ```python import torch R, C, K = 64, 256, 64 # few, slow CTAs, so the producer leaves SMs free def f(x): y = x for _ in range(K): y = torch.sin(y) * 1.5 y = y.sum(-1) # K0: slow persistent reduction writes y idx = torch.arange(R // 2, device=x.device) # half the rows, so K2 cannot fuse into K0 # K1: zero fill (store-only); K2: loads y before its gdc_wait() return x.new_zeros(R // 2 + 5).index_put_((idx,), y[: R // 2] * 3.0) pdl = torch.compile(f, options={"triton.enable_pdl": True}) ref = torch.compile(f, options={"triton.enable_pdl": False}) print(torch.__version__, torch.version.git_version[:12], torch.cuda.get_device_name(), torch.cuda.get_device_capability()) g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0) errs = [] for _ in range(20): x = torch.randn(R, C, generator=g).cuda() out = pdl(x) # PDL first, so a stale read cannot pick up ref's output torch.cuda.synchronize() errs.append((out - ref(x)).abs().max().item()) print(f"{sum(e > 1e-3 for e in errs)}/20 calls wrong; max |pdl - ref| per call:") print(" ".join(f"{e:.2g}" for e in errs)) ``` Output on the nightly: ``` 2.15.0.dev20260930+cu132 89ac0527b15d NVIDIA GB10 (12, 1) 20/20 calls wrong; max |pdl - ref| per call: 1.8e+02 1.2e+02 3.7e+02 1.1e+03 3.2e+03 9.6e+03 2.9e+04 8.6e+04 2.6e+05 7.8e+05 2.3e+06 7e+06 2.1e+07 6.3e+07 1.9e+08 5.7e+08 1.7e+09 5.1e+09 1.5e+10 4.6e+10 ``` With `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`: `0/20 calls wrong`, every error 0. The error triples on each call because the early load reads a reused allocation that still holds the previous call's `y`, which the kernel multiplies by 3. The producer must leave SMs free for its dependents: with 2048 or more rows it fills the GPU and every call passed. Generated code (nightly, `TORCH_LOGS=output_code`; loads, stores and PDL calls only): ```python # call() triton_per_fused_mul_sin_sum_0.run(arg0_1, buf1, 64, 256, stream=raw_stream0) # K0 writes y (buf1) triton_poi_fused_new_zeros_1.run(buf2, 37, stream=raw_stream0) # K1: store-only triton_poi_fused_arange_index_put_mul_new_zeros_slice_2.run(buf1, buf2, 32, stream=raw_stream0) # K2 reads y # K0 triton_per_fused_mul_sin_sum_0 tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait() tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (r0_1 + 256*x0), xmask, eviction_policy='evict_first', other=0.0) tl.extra.cuda.gdc_launch_dependents() # K1 may start now; K0 then computes 64 sin() and stores y tl.store(out_ptr1 + (x0), tmp133, xmask) # K1 triton_poi_fused_new_zeros_1: no gdc_wait, no gdc_launch_dependents (implicit trigger on exit) tl.store(out_ptr0 + (x0), tmp0, xmask) # K2 triton_poi_fused_arange_index_put_mul_new_zeros_slice_2 tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (x0), xmask) # y, loaded BEFORE the wait tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait() tl.extra.cuda.gdc_launch_dependents() tl.store(out_ptr0 + (x0), tmp2, xmask) ``` Cause: Since #166741 (712bfd126be0), `_handle_pdl_before_access` moves the wait in front of a load only if `scheduler.previous_node` writes that buffer; otherwise the wait comes after the kernel's first load. That is safe only if the previous kernel itself waited for everything before it. Store-only kernels never wait, and CUDA documents `griddepcontrol.wait` / `cudaGridDependencySynchronize` as waiting for the kernel's *direct* grid dependencies only. So K2's early load of K0's output is not ordered after K0. ### Versions

title: [Inductor][PDL] triton.enable_pdl: a kernel loads a buffer the previous kernel mutated in place before gdc_wait(), giving wrong results
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug The analysis was done with the assistance of AI and reviewed by me. With `torch.compile(..., options={"triton.enable_pdl": True})`, a kernel that reads a buffer the immediately preceding kernel mutated *in place* (`index_put_`, an indexed store, scatter, an in-place fill) issues that load *before* `tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait()`. The preceding kernel calls `gdc_launch_dependents()` after its last load, i.e. before its stores/atomics, so the reader can run while those stores are still landing and reads a partly updated buffer. Results are wrong on a fraction of calls after the first; they are exact with `triton.enable_pdl=False` or `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`. Reproduced on nightly 2.15.0.dev20260930+cu132 (git 89ac0527b15d) and on 2.14.0, NVIDIA GB10 (sm_121): ```python import torch M, D, L = 4096, 256, 8192 # the mutating kernel must span several waves of CTAs def scatter_add(idx, src): # index_put_ with accumulate: atomic adds return src.new_zeros(M, D).index_put_((idx,), src, accumulate=True) * 2.0 def scatter_store(idx, src, base): # plain indexed stores, no atomics a = base.clone() a[idx] = src return a * 2.0 def add_args(g): return torch.randint(0, M, (L,), generator=g).cuda(), torch.randn(L, D, generator=g).cuda() def store_args(g): idx = torch.randperm(M, generator=g)[: M // 2] return idx.cuda(), torch.randn(M // 2, D, generator=g).cuda(), torch.randn(M, D, generator=g).cuda() def check(fn, make_args, calls=100): pdl = torch.compile(fn, options={"triton.enable_pdl": True}) ref = torch.compile(fn, options={"triton.enable_pdl": False}) g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0) errs = [] for _ in range(calls): args = make_args(g) out = pdl(*args) # PDL first, so a stale read cannot pick up ref's output torch.cuda.synchronize() errs.append((out - ref(*args)).abs().max().item()) wrong = sum(e > 1e-3 for e in errs) print(f"{fn.__name__}: {wrong}/{calls} calls wrong, max |pdl - ref| = {max(errs):.3g}") print(torch.__version__, torch.version.git_version[:12], torch.cuda.get_device_name(), torch.cuda.get_device_capability()) check(scatter_add, add_args) check(scatter_store, store_args) ``` Output on the nightly: ``` 2.15.0.dev20260930+cu132 89ac0527b15d NVIDIA GB10 (12, 1) scatter_add: 33/100 calls wrong, max |pdl - ref| = 16.9 scatter_store: 23/100 calls wrong, max |pdl - ref| = 12.6 ``` With `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` (20 calls each): `scatter_add: 0/20 calls wrong, max |pdl - ref| = 3.81e-06` (atomic-add rounding) and `scatter_store: 0/20 calls wrong, max |pdl - ref| = 0`. The rate varies between runs (5/20 and 3/20 in a 20-call run; 91/100 and 88/100 on 2.14 with an fp64 variant of this script); the first call is usually right, because autotuning runs each kernel synchronously. The mutating kernel has to span several waves of CTAs: with small sizes (e.g. `M=256, D=64, L=512`) every call passed. Generated code (nightly, `TORCH_LOGS=output_code`, `scatter_add`; loads, stores and PDL calls only): ```python # call() triton_poi_fused_new_zeros_0.run(buf0, 1048576, stream=raw_stream0) triton_poi_fused_index_put_new_zeros_1.run(arg1_1, arg0_1, buf0, 2097152, stream=raw_stream0) # mutates buf0 triton_poi_fused_mul_2.run(buf0, buf2, 1048576, stream=raw_stream0) # reads buf0 # triton_poi_fused_index_put_new_zeros_1 tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (x1), None, eviction_policy='evict_last') tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait() tmp6 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (x2), None) tl.extra.cuda.gdc_launch_dependents() # dependents released here ... tl.atomic_add(out_ptr0 + (x0 + 256*tmp4), tmp6, None, sem='relaxed') # ... before the atomics into buf0 # triton_poi_fused_mul_2 tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (x0), None) # buf0, loaded BEFORE the wait tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait() tl.extra.cuda.gdc_launch_dependents() tl.store(out_ptr0 + (x0), tmp2, None) ``` Cause: `TritonKernel._handle_pdl_before_access` (`torch/_inductor/codegen/triton.py`) moves the wait in front of an access only if `matching_dep` finds the buffer among the previous node's writes: ```python return any( dep == current_node.mutation_renames.get(w.name, w.name) for w in prev_deps ) ``` For a buffer mutated in place, the two sides use different names: the reader passes the real buffer name (`buf0`; codegen only uses real names), while the previous node's write is recorded under the mutation name (`buf1`). `current_node.mutation_renames` maps real → mutated (`{'buf0': 'buf1'}`), so applying it to `w.name`, which is already `buf1`, never yields `buf0`. Traced on 2.14 (the code is identical on the nightly and on main `b881c29e`): ``` cur=op4 deps=('buf0',) prev=op1_op3 writes=['buf1','buf3'] cur.mutation_renames={'buf0':'buf1','buf2':'buf3'} ``` Stores have the mirror mismatch (a mutating store passes the mutated name while the previous node writes the real one), so a store-only in-place kernel right after its producer gets no wait, and the producer's late stores can overwrite it (e.g. `a = base * 1.5; a[torch.arange(0, M, 3)] = 0`). ### Versions

title: [XPU] boolean-mask indexing silently returns empty on Intel Arc B580
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Related to #199157 — same workload (DeepSeek-V2-based MoE on an Intel Arc
B580 with torch-xpu), same family of broken position/index handling. Filing
separately since it's a different op with a different failure mode.

Comparing CPU vs XPU on the same tensors: CPU returns all 24 selected rows,
XPU returns an empty tensor. On tensors produced by prior ops it can instead
abort outright.

> **AI disclosure:** I used an AI coding assistant to help minimize the
> reproducer below and to check for existing reports. I ran every snippet
> myself on my own B580, confirmed the outputs match, and I understand and
> stand behind the analysis.

import torch
t = torch.ones(24, 8, device='xpu', dtype=torch.bfloat16)
m = torch.ones(24, device='xpu', dtype=torch.bool)  # all True
print(t[m].shape)  # torch.Size([0, 8]) — WRONG, expect (24, 8)

On computed (non-fresh) tensors the same pattern can fail loudly instead:
  RuntimeError: numel: integer multiplication overflow

Expected masked selection to return the selected rows, as on CPU. Actual:
silently empty (worse than a crash — downstream code proceeds with missing
data), occasionally the overflow error.


I have this B580 on hand and can test any fix.

title: [XPU] torch.nonzero returns empty tensor on Intel Arc B580
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I'm running a DeepSeek-V2-based MoE model on an Intel Arc B580 with torch-xpu
and getting wrong outputs. Comparing CPU vs XPU on the same tensors, I traced
it down to `nonzero`: CPU finds 12 matching positions, XPU returns none.

> **AI disclosure:** I used an AI coding assistant to help minimize the
> reproducer below and to check for existing reports. I ran every snippet
> myself on my own B580, confirmed the outputs match, and I understand and
> stand behind the analysis.

import torch
idx = torch.tensor([0,0,0,1,2,0,3,1]*3, device='xpu')
print("eq sum (xpu):", (idx == 0).sum().item())          # 12, correct
print("nonzero (xpu):", (idx == 0).nonzero().numel())    # 0, WRONG
print("nonzero (cpu):", (idx == 0).cpu().nonzero().numel())  # 12, correct

Expected `nonzero` on XPU to return the 12 matching positions, as on CPU.
Actual: empty tensor. Note the comparison itself works (sum is 12) — only the
position materialization is broken.

This breaks index-routing code (in my case MoE expert dispatch). Workaround
that proves the data path is fine: move the bool mask to CPU, `nonzero`
there, move indices back, then `index_select` on XPU — verified value-correct.

title: deserialize_torch_artifact retries every `weights_only=True` failure with `weights_only=False`
body:
I was reading `deserialize_torch_artifact` on main (`2581b459d5546d212ad4a660bb57d163d436de35`). The first `torch.load` does not decide what gets loaded.

### Describe the bug

`deserialize_torch_artifact` in `torch/_export/serde/serialize.py` does this:

```python
try:
    artifact = torch.load(buffer, weights_only=True)
except Exception as e:
    buffer.seek(0)
    artifact = torch.load(buffer, weights_only=False)
```

The `except` is bare `Exception`. That includes the `UnpicklingError` the weights-only unpickler raises when an object is not allowlisted. That error is a normal outcome of the first call, and the helper treats it as the signal to rewind the buffer and load the same bytes with `weights_only=False`.

The comment says the second call exists so custom objects such as `ScriptObject` still load. Callers that need those objects can ask for that load themselves. As written, the first call does not change the result: if it fails, including the expected rejection, the second call runs. Why is the weights-only load there if it is designed to fail open?

The helper then checks that the object is a tuple or dict. That check is after the second `torch.load` has already returned.

[#158247](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/158247) ("Fix: Improve fallback behavior in `deserialize_torch_artifact`") added this try/except retry. It is in 2.10.0 and later. Before that, [#132348](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/132348) ("Set weights_only=False in export `deserialize_torch_artifact`") pinned the flag so export could keep loading custom objects such as `ScriptObject` after `torch.load` started defaulting to `weights_only=True`. From that PR (2.5.0) through 2.9.1 the function did not try `weights_only=True` at all:

```python
artifact = torch.load(buffer, weights_only=False)
```

`torch.export.load` calls `load_pt2`. `_load_exported_programs` reads `archive/data/sample_inputs/<model>.pt` and `GraphModuleDeserializer` passes those bytes into this helper. The same helper also receives the raw bytes for the legacy `weights/<model>.pt` and `constants/<model>.pt` members. A current `package_pt2` / `torch.export.save` archive stores the sample-inputs member as raw `torch.save` bytes, so that member is enough to reach the second load. From 2.10.0 the `torch.export.load` docstring says the loader uses pickle (#167557). That sentence is about the `ScriptObject` path. It does not say that a failed weights-only load is what selects `weights_only=False`.

### Expected behavior

The weights-only load is either the load, or it is not. Today it is neither.

`weights_only=True` exists to restrict what `torch.load` will reconstitute. `UnpicklingError` is how that restriction reports "this object is not allowlisted." Catching that error and immediately calling `torch.load` again with `weights_only=False` means the restriction never applies: the rejection is the condition for dropping it. A caller cannot observe the first result, cannot tell an allowlist rejection from a legacy `ScriptObject` failure, and cannot stop the second load. The tuple/dict check afterward only inspects whatever the second load already returned.

The expected behavior is one `torch.load`, with an explicit `weights_only` argument that defaults to `True`. An allowlist rejection should propagate. Archives that embed `ScriptObject` or other non-tensor objects should pass `weights_only=False` at `torch.export.load` / `load_pt2`, instead of the helper treating every failure as that request.

### Suggested change

Delete the `except` retry and thread the flag from `load_pt2` / `torch.export.load` into this helper for sample inputs, constants, and state-dict bytes.

```python
def deserialize_torch_artifact(
    serialized: dict[str, Any] | tuple[Any, ...] | bytes,
    *,
    weights_only: bool = True,
):
    if isinstance(serialized, (dict, tuple)):
        return serialized
    if len(serialized) == 0:
        return {}
    buffer = io.BytesIO(serialized)
    artifact = torch.load(buffer, weights_only=weights_only)
    if not isinstance(artifact, (tuple, dict)):
        raise AssertionError(f"expected tuple or dict, got {type(artifact).__name__}")
    return artifact
```

`torch.export.load` and `load_pt2` take the same keyword, default `True`, and pass it through `ExportedProgramDeserializer.deserialize` into each call:

```python
self.constants = deserialize_torch_artifact(constants, weights_only=weights_only)
self.example_inputs = deserialize_torch_artifact(example_inputs, weights_only=weights_only)
state_dict = deserialize_torch_artifact(serialized_state_dict, weights_only=weights_only)
```

### Versions

- Control flow checked on `2.15.0a0+git2581b45` (`2581b459d5546d212ad4a660bb57d163d436de35`).
- 2.10.0 and later: try `weights_only=True`, then `weights_only=False` on any exception (#158247).
- 2.5.0 through 2.9.1: `weights_only=False` directly (#132348).

`collect_env.py` output is not included. This is in the Python loader and does not depend on CUDA.

title: [dynamo] CPU flash-attention decomposition changes output strides for a contiguous query tensor
body:
### 🐛

this  [PR #134656](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/134656/changes) changes [CPU flash attention decomposition ](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/9debb84606380679698bef8fb04746a5c762089e/torch/_decomp/decompositions.py#L5866)

to always convert output to MHA query layout. this is inconsistent of the shape metadata provided by [`meta__scaled_dot_product_flash_attention_for_cpu`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/9debb84606380679698bef8fb04746a5c762089e/torch/_meta_registrations.py#L6684) when input query are in contiguous format or BERT model format.

## Native/meta contract and related PR

[PR #134656](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/134656/changes) changed native CPU flash attention and its meta implementation to derive the output layout from the query using `empty_like(query)`.

The relevant allocation in [`meta__scaled_dot_product_flash_attention_for_cpu`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/9debb84606380679698bef8fb04746a5c762089e/torch/_meta_registrations.py#L6684) is:

```python
attention = torch.empty_like(query)
```

Meta execution supplies stride information as well as shape and dtype. 

The decomposition instead forces one fixed storage order. PR #134656 establishes the query-dependent native/meta behavior relevant to this issue; its diff does not introduce the permutation block discussed below.

## MHA-style and BERT-style queries

Let:

- `N`: batch size
- `H`: number of attention heads
- `L`: sequence length
- `A`: width of each head, also commonly named `E`

Both query styles have logical shape `(N, H, L, A)`, but their underlying dense storage orders differ:

```python
# MHA-style: projection starts in sequence-first order.
query = projected.view(L, N, H, A).permute(1, 2, 0, 3)
# Shape:   (N, H, L, A)
# Strides: (H*A, A, N*H*A, 1)
# Storage order: [L, N, H, A]

# BERT-style: projection starts in batch-first order.
query = projected.view(N, L, H, A).transpose(1, 2)
# Shape:   (N, H, L, A)
# Strides: (L*H*A, A, H*A, 1)
# Storage order: [N, L, H, A]
```

These are representative tensor constructions, not model classifications. Both are generally non-contiguous in their logical `(N, H, L, A)` dimensions. A fully contiguous query is a third layout, with strides `(H*L*A, L*A, A, 1)`.

## How the decomposition changes the layout

The [decomposition](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/9debb84606380679698bef8fb04746a5c762089e/torch/_decomp/decompositions.py#L5866) first invokes:

```python
output, attn = aten._scaled_dot_product_attention_math.default(
    query,
    key,
    value,
    attn_mask=attn_mask,
    dropout_p=dropout_p,
    is_causal=is_causal,
    dropout_mask=None,
    scale=scale,
    enable_gqa=query.size(1) != key.size(1),
)
```

For the dense query constructions above, this math call produces:

| Input query style | Math output shape | Math output strides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contiguous | `(N, H, L, A)` | `(H*L*A, L*A, A, 1)` |
| MHA-style | `(N, H, L, A)` | `(H*L*A, L*A, A, 1)` |
| BERT-style | `(N, H, L, A)` | `(H*L*A, L*A, A, 1)` |

The decomposition then applies:

```python
output = (
    output.permute(2, 0, 1, 3)
    .contiguous(memory_format=torch.contiguous_format)
    .permute(1, 2, 0, 3)
)
```

This transforms the output as follows:

| Step | Logical shape | Strides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Math output | `(N, H, L, A)` | `(H*L*A, L*A, A, 1)` |
| First permutation | `(L, N, H, A)` | `(A, H*L*A, L*A, 1)` |
| Contiguous copy | `(L, N, H, A)` | `(N*H*A, H*A, A, 1)` |
| Final permutation | `(N, H, L, A)` | `(H*A, A, N*H*A, 1)` |

The final permutation restores the logical shape but retains the storage order established by the copy: `[L, N, H, A]`.

The existing comment explains why this is needed for the MHA-style case. However, applying this layout universally disagrees with native/meta for other queries:

| Query style | Native/meta expected output strides | Decomposition output strides | Matches? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Contiguous | `(H*L*A, L*A, A, 1)` | `(H*A, A, N*H*A, 1)` | No |
| MHA-style | `(H*A, A, N*H*A, 1)` | `(H*A, A, N*H*A, 1)` | Yes |
| BERT-style | `(L*H*A, A, H*A, 1)` | `(H*A, A, N*H*A, 1)` | No |

These comparisons assume ordinary non-singleton dimensions, as in the reproducer below.

## Minimal reproducer

```python
import torch
from torch._decomp.decompositions import (
    scaled_dot_product_flash_attention_for_cpu,
)

N, H, L, A = 3, 4, 5, 32
inputs = tuple(torch.randn(N, H, L, A) for _ in range(3))
op = torch.ops.aten._scaled_dot_product_flash_attention_for_cpu.default

native, _ = op(*inputs)
meta, _ = op(*(tensor.to("meta") for tensor in inputs))
decomposed, _ = scaled_dot_product_flash_attention_for_cpu(*inputs)

print("Query:", inputs[0].shape, inputs[0].stride())
print("Native:", native.shape, native.stride())
print("Meta:", meta.shape, meta.stride())
print("Decomposition:", decomposed.shape, decomposed.stride())

torch.testing.assert_close(decomposed, native, atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-5)

native.view(N * H * L, A)      # Succeeds.
decomposed.view(N * H * L, A)  # Fails: incompatible strides.
```

Observed strides, with shape `(3, 4, 5, 32)` in every case:

```text
Query:         (640, 160, 32, 1)
Native:        (640, 160, 32, 1)
Meta:          (640, 160, 32, 1)
Decomposition: (128, 32, 384, 1)
```

During export, a consumer such as `output.contiguous().view(...)` can lose the redundant `contiguous()` because native/meta output is already contiguous. Replacing attention with this decomposition then changes the strides and makes the recorded `view()` invalid.

## Expected behavior

The decomposition should preserve the output layout predicted by `empty_like(query)`, rather than impose a fixed sequence-first layout.

Regression coverage should compare native/meta and decomposed layouts for contiguous, MHA-style, and BERT-style queries, and verify downstream views through `torch.export.export(...).run_decompositions()`.


### Versions

- PyTorch: `2.12.0+cpu`
- PyTorch revision: `7661cd9c6b841b62b7f411aa52ec51f05457263b`
- Python: `3.12.3`
- Platform: Linux AArch64

title: PerChannelMinMaxObserver.reset_min_max_vals() drops the dtype passed via factory_kwargs
body:
*Disclosure (per the AI policy): I prepared this report with help from Claude (an AI assistant). I ran the snippet below myself in the environment listed under Versions and pasted its output unmodified.*

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`PerChannelMinMaxObserver.reset_min_max_vals()` (also used by `MovingAveragePerChannelMinMaxObserver`) replaces `min_val` / `max_val` with a new `torch.rand(0)`, so a dtype passed through `factory_kwargs` is lost after a reset. `MinMaxObserver.reset_min_max_vals()` resets in place and keeps the dtype.

```python
import torch
from torch.ao.quantization.observer import PerChannelMinMaxObserver, MinMaxObserver

fk = {"dtype": torch.float64}

o = PerChannelMinMaxObserver(ch_axis=0, factory_kwargs=fk)
print("PerChannel after init :", o.min_val.dtype, o.max_val.dtype)
o.reset_min_max_vals()
print("PerChannel after reset:", o.min_val.dtype, o.max_val.dtype)

m = MinMaxObserver(factory_kwargs=fk)
m.reset_min_max_vals()
print("MinMax     after reset:", m.min_val.dtype, m.max_val.dtype)

o = PerChannelMinMaxObserver(ch_axis=0, factory_kwargs=fk)
o(torch.randn(3, 4, dtype=torch.float64))
print("PerChannel observed float64 input:", o.min_val.dtype)
o.reset_min_max_vals()
o(torch.randn(3, 4, dtype=torch.float64))
print("PerChannel observed float64 input after reset:", o.min_val.dtype)
```

Output:

```
PerChannel after init : torch.float64 torch.float64
PerChannel after reset: torch.float32 torch.float32
MinMax     after reset: torch.float64 torch.float64
PerChannel observed float64 input: torch.float64
PerChannel observed float64 input after reset: torch.float32
```

Expected: the buffers keep their configured dtype after `reset_min_max_vals()`, as `MinMaxObserver` does.

The code responsible is on `main` today: [`observer.py` `PerChannelMinMaxObserver.reset_min_max_vals`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/ao/quantization/observer.py#L884-L892) assigns `torch.rand(0,)`, which is always CPU/float32. I have not tested a CUDA observer (no CUDA build here), so I am only reporting the dtype behavior I observed.

title: [Feature Request] multiple dimensions support for `torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity`
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

The current `torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity` only accepts a single dimension (int) as input (torch 2.14.0).

```python
TypeError: cosine_similarity(): argument 'dim' must be int, not tuple
```

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/9debb84606380679698bef8fb04746a5c762089e/aten/src/ATen/native/Distance.cpp#L273

For an image pair with shape `(B, C, H, W)`, it may be useful to compute cosine similarity over `(C, H, W)` in some applications. With the current API, the pipeline may need to flatten the reduction dimensions to use `cosine_similarity`.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

B, C, H, W = 4, 16, 64, 64
shape = (B, C, H, W)

x1 = torch.randn(shape)
x2 = torch.randn(shape)

eps = 1e-8

x1, x2 = torch.broadcast_tensors(x1, x2)

# (B,)
cos_sim = F.cosine_similarity(
    x1.flatten(1),
    x2.flatten(1),
    dim=-1,
    eps=eps,
)
```

Alternatively, `cosine_similarity` can be reproduced using other operations that support multiple dimensions directly:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

B, C, H, W = 4, 16, 64, 64
shape = (B, C, H, W)

x1 = torch.randn(shape)
x2 = torch.randn(shape)

eps = 1e-8
reduce_dims = (1, 2, 3)

x1, x2 = torch.broadcast_tensors(x1, x2)

x1_normalized = F.normalize(x1, p=2, dim=reduce_dims, eps=eps)
x2_normalized = F.normalize(x2, p=2, dim=reduce_dims, eps=eps)

# (B,)
cos_sim = (x1_normalized * x2_normalized).sum(dim=reduce_dims)
```

This approach can also be useful when the reduction dimensions are non-consecutive. However, it essentially reimplements `cosine_similarity` at the Python API level. Supporting multidim `cosine_similarity` could make these cases cleaner and clearer.


### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

title: sort/topk dtype check errors say "on CPU" for CUDA tensors
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.sort` and `torch.topk` on a CUDA tensor with an unsupported dtype raise an error that says "on CPU", even though the tensor is on the GPU. Each call below run on its own:

```python
import torch
x = torch.tensor([1+1j, 2+0j], device="cuda")
torch.sort(x)     # TypeError: Sort does not support complex dtypes on CPU
torch.topk(x, 1)  # TypeError: topk does not support complex dtypes on CPU
torch.topk(torch.tensor([True, False], device="cuda"), 1)  # NotImplementedError: topk does not support bool dtypes on CPU
```

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "repro.py", line 3, in <module>
    torch.sort(x)
TypeError:  Sort does not support complex dtypes on CPU
```

Expected: the error should not mention CPU, e.g. `Sort does not support complex dtypes`.

The checks are in the meta functions for topk and sort in `aten/src/ATen/native/Sorting.cpp` (lines 65, 66 and 82), added in #159556. Meta functions run for every device, so the "on CPU" wording is misleading for CUDA tensors. Two of the messages also start with a stray space.

Suggested fix: drop "on CPU" from the three messages. I'd be happy to submit this as my first pull request.

title: Inductor StaticallyLaunchedTritonKernel finalization can invalidate CUDA graph capture via cuModuleUnload
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug `torch.compile(..., mode="max-autotune")`can leave static Inductor CUDA kernels whose Python finalizers run during a later CUDA graph capture. When this happens, `cuModuleUnload` is called while capture is active and invalidates the graph. The visible failure is: ```text RuntimeError: info.status != cudaStreamCaptureStatusInvalidated INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:2213 Invalid stream capture status ``` With CUDA driver logging enabled : ```text Returning 900 (CUDA_ERROR_STREAM_CAPTURE_UNSUPPORTED) from cuModuleUnload RuntimeError: ... INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:2213 ... Invalid stream capture status Returning 901 (CUDA_ERROR_STREAM_CAPTURE_INVALIDATED) from cuStreamEndCapture ``` `cuModuleUnload` fails first (900) and invalidates the capture. The next allocation then hits the allocator assertion, and ending the capture reports 901. Background: I originally encountered the issue during cross-validation with repeated `torch.compile` calls using `mode="max-autotune"`. The crash was nondeterministic: one fold could complete while a later fold failed during its initial capture, and rerunning could pass the same point. I diagnosed and isolated the problem into a standalone PyTorch-only reproducer using GPT-6 Astra Medium. It: - compiles and runs a simple `sin + cos` function with `mode="max-autotune"` - drops the compiled object while cyclic GC is disabled - starts an unrelated CUDA graph capture - re-enables automatic cyclic GC during capture - triggers GC using ordinary Python allocations There is no explicit `gc.collect()` inside the capture. Diagnostic tracing shows loaded static kernels being finalized while CUDA capture is active: ```text FINALIZER class=StaticallyLaunchedCudaKernel kernel=triton_poi_fused_add_cos_sin_0 module_loaded=True gc_active=True generation=0 capturing=True ``` The observed path is: ```text automatic Python GC -> StaticallyLaunchedTritonKernel.__del__() -> close() -> _unload_kernel(mod) -> cuModuleUnload -> CUDA error 900 -> capture invalidated -> allocator/capture-end errors ``` Keeping cyclic GC disabled during capture makes the same reproducer pass. The low GC threshold in the reproducer is intentional: it makes a normally timing-dependent GC event deterministic. ### Ablation - `mode="max-autotune"`: reproduces - `max-autotune` + GC deferred during capture: passes - `mode="default"`: passes in this reproducer - `mode="reduce-overhead"`: passes in this reproducer Tested with PyTorch `2.13.0+cu132`, CUDA `13.2`, on H100 80GB and RTX 4050. ### Repro Scripts
gc_module_unload.py (attached in ZIP) ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Standalone PyTorch/CUDA reproducer. Requires only PyTorch and the stdlib.""" import argparse import gc import os import tempfile def capture(torch, x, stream): graph = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph() with torch.inference_mode(), torch.cuda.graph( graph, stream=stream, capture_error_mode="thread_local" ): # Trigger automatic cyclic GC while capturing (no explicit collect). gc.set_threshold(1, 1, 1) garbage = [[] for _ in range(3000)] y = x + 1 graph.replay() torch.testing.assert_close(y, x + 1) print("PASS: capture and replay match eager output", flush=True) def main(): parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__) parser.add_argument( "--defer-gc", action="store_true", help="Run the passing control", ) parser.add_argument( "--mode", default="max-autotune", choices=("default", "reduce-overhead", "max-autotune"), ) args = parser.parse_args() # A warm compiler cache can avoid creating the discarded kernel objects. with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="gc-capture-repro-") as cache: os.environ["TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR"] = os.path.join(cache, "inductor") os.environ["TRITON_CACHE_DIR"] = os.path.join(cache, "triton") import torch print( f"PyTorch={torch.__version__}, CUDA={torch.version.cuda}", flush=True, ) gc.collect() gc.disable() x = torch.randn(1024, device="cuda") compiled = torch.compile( lambda x: x.sin() + x.cos(), mode=args.mode, ) with torch.inference_mode(): for _ in range(3): compiled(x).cpu() del compiled torch.compiler.reset() # Keep cyclic garbage pending until capture starts. gc.set_threshold(10**9, 10**9, 10**9) if not args.defer_gc: gc.enable() capture(torch, x, torch.cuda.Stream()) if __name__ == "__main__": main() ```

title: [Windows] 2.13+ wheels need VCRUNTIME140_THREADS.dll (VC++ >= 14.38), but the redist preflight check does not probe it
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Since 2.13, the Windows wheels import `VCRUNTIME140_THREADS.dll`, which only ships with the VC++ Redistributable 14.38 (VS 2022 17.8) and later. The redistributable check in `torch/__init__.py` (`_load_dll_libraries`) only probes `vcruntime140.dll`, `msvcp140.dll` and `vcruntime140_1.dll`. Those three exist in every 14.x redist, so on a machine with an older redist the check passes silently and the user gets a bare `WinError 126` / `WinError 1114` naming some unrelated DLL, with no hint to update the redistributable.

I hit this while setting up a CPU-only Windows env to run SDPA checks with the attention shapes of Spark-X2.5 (GQA 8/2 and 16/4, head_dim 256, sliding window 512). System redist is 14.32.31326.

**Where the dependency comes from**

```python
import pefile
pe = pefile.PE(r"...\torch\lib\torch_cpu.dll", fast_load=True)
pe.parse_data_directories(directories=[1])
for e in pe.DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT:
    if b"THREADS" in e.dll.upper():
        print(e.dll, [i.name for i in e.imports])
# b'VCRUNTIME140_THREADS.dll' [cnd_wait, cnd_signal, cnd_init, thrd_join, cnd_destroy,
#   cnd_broadcast, mtx_unlock, mtx_lock, thrd_create, mtx_init, mtx_destroy]
```

These are C11 `<threads.h>` functions. #178201 switched `third_party/pthreadpool` to google/pthreadpool, which uses `<threads.h>` when `PTHREADPOOL_USE_PTHREADS` is 0, and that is the default on `_WIN32` (`src/threadpool-common.h`). `release/2.12` still pins the old pthreadpool (`4fe0e1e`); `release/2.13` and `release/2.14` pin `a56dcd7`.

**Repro** (torch 2.14.0+cpu, Python 3.11, VC++ redist 14.32 installed)

1. `import torch` as-is: fails with `[WinError 1114] ... c10.dll`. That part is the `constexpr std::mutex` problem from #169429, being addressed in #196987. No redist hint is printed.
2. To simulate a machine where the mutex issue is fixed (or #196987 is in), put a 14.44 `msvcp140.dll` / `vcruntime140.dll` / `vcruntime140_1.dll` next to `torch\lib\c10.dll`, still without `vcruntime140_threads.dll`:

```
OSError: [WinError 126] The specified module could not be found. Error loading "...\torch\lib\shm.dll" or one of its dependencies.
```

Again no hint. The DLL it names is `shm.dll` (first in glob order that depends on `torch_cpu.dll`), which is misleading.

3. Adding `vcruntime140_threads.dll` (14.44) as well: `import torch` works.

So even after #196987 lands, redist 14.32 to 14.37 still can't load 2.13+ wheels, and the preflight check says nothing about it.

**Proposed fix**

Probe `vcruntime140_threads.dll` in the same `try` block, and word the message as "not installed or is outdated" since the redist is usually present, just too old. I verified locally that with this change both scenarios above print the redist download hint before the `OSError`, and a machine with the DLL present imports normally. I'll open a PR.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0+cpu
Is debug build: False
CUDA used to build PyTorch: None
Python version: 3.11.15 (main, Jun 11 2026, 04:59:07) [MSC v.1944 64 bit (AMD64)] (64-bit runtime)
Python platform: Windows-10-10.0.26200-SP0
Is CUDA available: False
CPU: Intel(R) Core(TM) Ultra 5 125H
System msvcp140.dll / vcruntime140.dll: 14.32.31326.0, no vcruntime140_threads.dll
```

title: fbgemm_gpu-1.8.0+cpu: download-r2.pytorch.org serves different wheels than the sha256 advertised in the index (11/16 files)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

# Summary

For `fbgemm_gpu==1.8.0+cpu`, the index at https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu/fbgemm-gpu/ links each wheel to download-r2.pytorch.org with a `#sha256=` fragment. For 11 of the 16 wheels, the R2 copy doesn't match that hash. The same filename on download.pytorch.org (S3/CloudFront) does match. This looks like the same kind of S3/R2 inconsistency as #179554.


# Impact

* Hash-checking installers (`pip --require-hashes`, `uv` with a lockfile) fail with a hash mismatch.
* Anything that fetches the index link without checking the hash gets a different build. This includes caching proxies such as Cloudsmith, Artifactory and similar mirrors, which cache the R2 bytes while advertising the index hash. For the cp312 x86_64 wheel, that build fails to load against torch==2.13.0+cpu:
```
OSError: Could not load this library: .../site-packages/fbgemm_gpu/fbgemm_gpu_tbe_utils.so
```
We found unresolved c10/at/torch symbols in the R2 build's libraries that aren't in the S3 build, so it appears to be built against a different torch ABI.

# Scan (2026-09-30)

"advertised" is the hash in the index; "s3" and "r2" are the sha256 of the file actually downloaded from each host (first 12 hex characters shown):

```
MISMATCH adv=6c817c14c399 s3=6c817c14c399 r2=e767cd6f370f cp310-cp310-manylinux_2_28_aarch64
MISMATCH adv=698c9a35e016 s3=698c9a35e016 r2=78f00673f746 cp310-cp310-manylinux_2_28_x86_64
MISMATCH adv=b53a5088b43c s3=b53a5088b43c r2=a33586093e69 cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_28_aarch64
MISMATCH adv=a2b8b7eaa39b s3=a2b8b7eaa39b r2=db2602b4316e cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_28_x86_64
MISMATCH adv=766fcff5ed69 s3=766fcff5ed69 r2=8ad4f286b2cf cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_aarch64
MISMATCH adv=661715c6141c s3=661715c6141c r2=e22e7753e567 cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_x86_64
MISMATCH adv=50df0524af49 s3=50df0524af49 r2=f79e2ec2cd9f cp313-cp313-manylinux_2_28_aarch64
OK       adv=4be9112a19c2 s3=4be9112a19c2 r2=4be9112a19c2 cp313-cp313-manylinux_2_28_x86_64
MISMATCH adv=58ae2a1d1023 s3=58ae2a1d1023 r2=0f66e746615e cp314-cp314-manylinux_2_28_aarch64
MISMATCH adv=d823bfea5c8a s3=d823bfea5c8a r2=9666026d417e cp314-cp314-manylinux_2_28_x86_64
MISMATCH adv=2a7355b49b3f s3=2a7355b49b3f r2=e820017ff32a cp314-cp314t-manylinux_2_28_aarch64
MISMATCH adv=e40c05b4bd8f s3=e40c05b4bd8f r2=396c83bd08d5 cp314-cp314t-manylinux_2_28_x86_64
OK       (cp315 / cp315t, x86_64 and aarch64: all 4 match)
```

Reproduce

```
F=fbgemm_gpu-1.8.0%2Bcpu-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl
curl -s https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu/fbgemm-gpu/ | grep -o "$F#sha256=[0-9a-f]*"   # advertised: 661715c6...
curl -sL https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu/$F    | sha256sum                            # 661715c6...
curl -sL https://download-r2.pytorch.org/whl/cpu/$F | sha256sum                            # e22e7753...
```

# Ask

Re-sync the R2 objects for whl/cpu/fbgemm_gpu-1.8.0+cpu-* from S3 (the S3 copies match the advertised hashes).
It may be worth running the S3-vs-R2 scan from #179554 over the other fbgemm_gpu versions and CUDA variants (for example whl/cu128, whl/cu130), since we saw this per-artifact rather than per-release.


### Versions

We noticed this issue from `fbgemm_gpu==1.8.0+cpu`.
This seems to be a PyTorch wheel repository, not specific to Python or torch versions.

title: cholesky_solve gives a nonzero derivative to the triangle of the factor it does not read
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.cholesky_solve(B, L)` reads only the lower triangle of `L` (the upper one when `upper=True`), but its backward and forward AD formulas treat `L` as dense. The unread triangle gets a nonzero gradient and tangent even though changing it does not change the output.

```python
import torch

L = torch.linalg.cholesky(torch.tensor([[4.0, 2.0], [2.0, 3.0]], dtype=torch.float64))
b = torch.tensor([[1.0], [2.0]], dtype=torch.float64)
E = torch.tensor([[0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 0.0]], dtype=torch.float64)  # upper triangle, not read

f = lambda L: torch.cholesky_solve(b, L)
print("changes x:", not torch.equal(f(L), f(L + E)))
print("reverse, grad at L[0, 1]:", torch.func.grad(lambda L: f(L).sum())(L)[0, 1].item())
print("forward, jvp along E:", torch.func.jvp(f, (L,), (E,))[1].flatten().tolist())
```

```
changes x: False
reverse, grad at L[0, 1]: -0.08838834764831849
forward, jvp along E: [-0.4419417382415921, 0.3535533905932737]
```

Expected `0.0` and `[0.0, 0.0]`.

`cholesky_solve_backward` and `cholesky_solve_jvp` in `torch/csrc/autograd/FunctionsManual.cpp` both build `dA = dL L^H + L dL^H` from the full `dL`. Applying `tril` (or `triu` when `upper=True`) to `grad_input2` in backward and to `dL` in the JVP makes both modes match `cholesky_solve(b, L.tril())`. I checked this for float64 and complex128 with both values of `upper`. `triangular_solve_backward` already restricts its gradient this way.

The OpInfo gradient tests miss this because the `cholesky_solve` entry uses `gradcheck_wrapper_triangular_input`, which applies `tril` before calling the op. The wrapper can be removed once the formulas are fixed, as #198602 does for `triangular_solve`.

Related: #198017, #196694.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.15.0a0+gitc0fd0be (#198602 head; both formulas build dA the same way on main)
OS: macOS 26.6.2 (arm64)
Python version: 3.13.13
Is CUDA available: False
```

title: Ability to download prebolt binaries for nightly builds
body:
PyTorch publishes nightly wheels at https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly. This contains all the artifacts that are installed when PyTorch is built but leaves out everything else in the `build/` tree. This behavior is generally desirable.

However, some artifacts that are produced in the build tree can be useful for other purposes. For example, since enabling BOLT optimization for PyTorch, we keep the unoptimized libraries at `build/lib/prebolt`. These libraries can be used to profile PyTorch and generate profile data to be used for BOLT optimization.

Currently that data is generated using NVIDIA's internal builds since we need prebolt binaries for profiling. The ability to use builds from the PyTorch CI will help us generate better BOLT profile data and eventually help in profiling within PyTorch CI itself.

These binaries can also be helpful when trying to investigate performance regressions as pre-bolt binaries are not affected by staleness of the BOLT profile data.

I would like to request some way of downloading those pre-bolt artifacts. To avoid increasing load on PyTorch infra, we can have a short retention period for those libraries.

Related-to: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/188602
