title: [MPS][FlexAttention] Potential ~3× forward throughput improvement on M4 (sampled workloads)
body:
I'm building a llm for the purpose of learning using FlexAttentions, and noticed how it's slower than other approaches such as SDPA, codex also suggested a different kernel that it's claiming to be 3x the throughput in many attention scenarios. I'm fairly new to this and surprised that a gap like this could exist, so maybe it's missing something obvious, just thought it may still be useful to report.

> ## Summary
>
> **AI disclosure:** This report, the benchmark code, and the experimental patch
> were primarily written by Codex with human direction and feedback. The reported
> measurements come from local benchmark executions, not AI estimates. The analysis
> and experimental code may still contain mistakes; this is a request for guidance,
> not an independently validated or merge-ready fix.
>
> I'm learning GPU kernel programming and may have missed an obvious limitation
> or made an unfair comparison. On my M4, compiled FlexAttention was slower than
> an eager blockwise SDPA reference for equivalent sliding-window attention.
> An experimental cooperative rewrite also improved the sampled workloads, but
> regressed some small-head cases. Is this expected, or worth investigating?
>
> This is a **performance issue/question, not a PR**. The patch is exploratory;
> I haven't established a version-to-version regression or an end-to-end speedup.
>
> ## Environment and reproduction
>
> - Apple M4 (10 GPU cores, 16 GiB), macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Python 3.12.14 arm64.
> - PyTorch 2.14.0, git `08187d9e0fba026dc8217405802ab5381dc88d90`.
> - MPS fallback, fast-math and prefer-Metal environment flags unset.
> - Forward only; FlexAttention uses Inductor, `fullgraph=True`, `dynamic=False`.
>   SDPA is eager. No dropout, autograd or timed compilation.
>
> Save the self-contained script below as `minimal_repro.py` and run **`python minimal_repro.py`**.
> It contains both implementations and correctness checks; no custom kernel,
> model or dataset is required. The mask is `0 <= q - k < 256`; SDPA uses explicit
> offset Boolean masks, not rectangular `is_causal=True`.
>
> <details>
> <summary>Self-contained reproduction (stock PyTorch; AI-assisted code)</summary>
>
> ```python
> """Stock PyTorch only. Apple Silicon MPS. Forward-only latency reproduction."""
> import random
> import statistics
> import time
>
> import torch
> import torch.nn.functional as F
> from torch.nn.attention.flex_attention import create_block_mask, flex_attention
>
>
> @torch.no_grad()
> def main():
>     assert torch.backends.mps.is_available(), "Run on an MPS-capable Mac"
>     print("torch:", torch.__version__, "git:", torch.version.git_version)
>     torch.manual_seed(91626)
>     B, H, T, D, W = 1, 8, 2048, 96, 256
>     q, k, v = [torch.randn(B, T, H, D, device="mps").transpose(1, 2)
>                for _ in range(3)]
>
>     def mask_mod(b, h, qi, ki):
>         return (qi >= ki) & (qi - ki < W)
>
>     mask = create_block_mask(mask_mod, None, None, T, T,
>                              device="cpu", BLOCK_SIZE=128).to("mps")
>     compiled = torch.compile(flex_attention, backend="inductor",
>                              fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)
>     methods = {"compiled_flex": lambda: compiled(q, k, v, block_mask=mask)}
>     for block_size in (128, 256):
>         blocks = []
>         for start in range(0, T, block_size):
>             end, left = min(T, start + block_size), max(0, start - W + 1)
>             distance = (torch.arange(start, end, device="mps")[:, None]
>                         - torch.arange(left, end, device="mps")[None, :])
>             blocks.append((start, end, left, (distance >= 0) & (distance < W)))
>
>         def blockwise(blocks=blocks):
>             return torch.cat([F.scaled_dot_product_attention(
>                 q[:, :, start:end], k[:, :, left:end], v[:, :, left:end],
>                 attn_mask=allowed, dropout_p=0.0, is_causal=False,
>             ) for start, end, left, allowed in blocks], dim=2)
>
>         methods[f"block_sdpa_{block_size}"] = blockwise
>     reference = methods["block_sdpa_256"]()
>     for fn in methods.values():
>         torch.testing.assert_close(fn(), reference, atol=8e-5, rtol=1e-3)
>         for _ in range(5):
>             fn()
>     torch.mps.synchronize()
>     samples = {name: [] for name in methods}
>     rng = random.Random(91626)
>     with torch.compiler.set_stance("fail_on_recompile"):
>         for _ in range(17):
>             names = list(methods)
>             rng.shuffle(names)
>             for name in names:
>                 torch.mps.synchronize()
>                 start = time.perf_counter()
>                 output = methods[name]()
>                 torch.mps.synchronize()
>                 samples[name].append((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000)
>                 del output
>     for name, values in samples.items():
>         print(f"{name}: median={statistics.median(values):.3f} ms")
>
>
> if __name__ == "__main__":
>     main()
> ```
>
> </details>
>
> ## Measurements
>
> **Stock-only reproduction:** FP32, B1/H8/T2048/D96, window256, sparse-mask
> block128. Median synchronized latency from 17 randomized rounds, five warmups:
>
> | Implementation | Latency |
> |---|---:|
> | Compiled FlexAttention | 30.196 ms |
> | Eager SDPA, query block128 | 3.398 ms |
> | Eager SDPA, query block256 | 2.706 ms |
>
> **Stock versus experimental FlexAttention:** selected matched-workload
> throughput results below combine the mask and dimension sweeps. Both are
> compiled; defaults are B1/H8/T2048, transposed layout, sparse-mask block128.
> Sliding-window rows use window256. Rates are **thousands of completed attention
> input tokens/s**, not generated tokens/s, and are measured separately from latency.
>
> | Run | Workload | Dtype / head width | Stock k tokens/s | Experiment k tokens/s | Ratio |
> |---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
> | Q | Sliding window | FP16 / 96 | 153.69 | 492.76 | 3.21× |
> | Q | Full causal | FP16 / 96 | 50.16 | 177.41 | 3.54× |
> | Q | Dense | FP16 / 96 | 38.56 | 92.50 | 2.40× |
> | Q | Uneven packed documents | FP16 / 96 | 192.64 | 624.49 | 3.24× |
> | Q | Prefix LM | FP16 / 96 | 47.94 | 174.71 | 3.64× |
> | Q | Dense | FP16 / 256 | 2.87 | 36.30 | 12.64× |
> | L | Sliding window | FP32 / 96 | 62.27 | 529.80 | 8.505× [8.504–8.512] |
> | L | Sliding window | FP16 / 256 | 19.34 | 215.54 | 11.135× [11.032–11.155] |
> | L | Sliding window | FP32 / 512 | 5.50 | 61.52 | 11.246× [11.140–11.345] |
>
> - **Q — quick mask checks (September 21):** exact clean patch; one >=5-second
>   window per method, not repeated medians or confidence intervals.
> - **L — longer dimension sweep (September 19):** earlier prototype; seven
>   randomized >=10-second windows after bounded stabilization. Rates are medians;
>   paired ratios include IQR. Clean/prototype executable shader tokens matched
>   in 112 generation checks, which does not prove identical compiled performance.
> - Both use three resident input sets and synchronize after bursts of 16 calls.
>   Timing includes dispatch, allocation and synchronization, but excludes
>   compilation, mask construction and transfers. Throughput is `calls * B * T / seconds`.
>
> The broader prototype **regressed FP16/D32** (0.817× at B1; 0.758× at B4), so
> the clean patch excludes these cases. Full results, separate latency samples
> and bounded batch/queue searches with fresh 30-second confirmations are retained
> locally, not included in the patch attachment. Those operating points are **not**
> matched-workload speedups or demonstrated maximum throughput.
>
> ## Experimental change and limitations
>
> The rewrite assigns 128 threads to eight query rows, shares key work and
> distributes softmax/value accumulation across lanes. It retains tile-level
> online-softmax rescaling and uses vector QK dot products, not matrix-engine QK.
> Its provisional guard selects FP16/FP32 equal QK/V widths 48–768 with unit
> feature stride; other cases retain stock. This is evidence from one GPU,
> not a recommended universal dispatch rule.
>
> - All 13 corrected mask workloads passed both reference checks. The separate
>   clean-patch suite had 73 passes and two feature-strided cases failing for
>   both stock and experiment, with no new failures.
> - The first mask harness attempt failed its CPU oracle before timing; the
>   corrected transfer and failed records are retained. Tolerances were unchanged.
> - **GPU saturation is unverified:** Instruments profiling failed, so there is
>   no usable GPU timeline. The quick checks do not establish thermal stability;
>   the desktop was not exclusively reserved.
> - No backward, dynamic-shape, other-GPU or upstream-main binary validation.
>   Installed PyTorch files were unchanged; experimental tests used process-local
>   compiler hooks. The patch is not merge-ready.
>
> ## Attachments
>
> - **`minimal_repro.py`** — standalone stock-only FlexAttention/SDPA reproduction.
>   [Download minimal_repro.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32488584/minimal_repro.py)
> - **`cooperative_mps_patch.py`** — experimental patch as readable Python source,
>   primarily AI-written as disclosed above; not an archive or a benchmark harness.
>   [Download cooperative_mps_patch.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32488896/cooperative_mps_patch.py)
>   Running without arguments prints the exact audited diff. `--check /path/to/pytorch`
>   verifies its pinned source hashes; `--apply` and `--reverse` are explicit opt-in
>   commands for a matching source checkout. It downloads nothing and is not needed
>   for the stock-only reproduction. Review before running; not merge-ready.
>
> Could someone check whether I'm using the MPS path as intended and suggest the
> most useful next measurement or profile? I'd welcome corrections to the setup
> or my interpretation. Thank you.

title: [inductor] torch._foreach_add_([x], [x.flip(0)]) reads x while writing it: silent wrong results (CUDA and CPU)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

An in-place foreach op whose other operand is computed from the same tensor at other positions gives wrong values under `torch.compile`. Eager is fine, and so is the plain `x.add_(x.flip(0))`.

```python
import torch


def f(x):
    torch._foreach_add_([x], [x.flip(0)])
    return x


device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
compiled = torch.compile(f)
for shape in ((8, 8), (1024, 1024)):
    x = torch.rand(*shape, device=device)
    want = f(x.clone())
    print(shape, [int((compiled(x.clone()) != want).sum()) for _ in range(5)])
```

CUDA, 2.14.0+cu130, RTX 4070 (2.9.1 is the same): right at the small shape, wrong at the large one.

```
(8, 8) [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
(1024, 1024) [496640, 495296, 496560, 495504, 496512]
```

CPU, 2.14.0 and nightly 2.15.0.dev20260921: wrong at any size.

```
(8, 8) [32, 32, 32, 32, 32]
(1024, 1024) [524204, 524184, 524192, 524136, 524244]
```

The kernel gets `x` as input and as output, and reads the mirrored row while it is being written:

```python
    tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (x2), xmask)
    tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (56 + x0 + ((-8)*x1)), xmask)
    tmp2 = tmp0 + tmp1
    tl.store(out_ptr0 + (x2), tmp2, xmask)

triton_poi_fused_0.run(arg0_1, arg0_1, 64, stream=raw_stream0)
```

Same with `x.roll(1, 0)`, `x.T.clone()` or `x.flip(0) * 2.0` as the other operand, with `_foreach_mul_`, `_foreach_copy_` and `_foreach_addcdiv_`, and with lists of more than one tensor.

`register_foreach_inplace` in `torch/_inductor/lowering.py` lowers the op as the out-of-place one followed by `mutate_to(arg, result, unsafe_alias=True)`. With `unsafe_alias`, `realize_into` skips the copy and gives the pointwise that computes `result` the layout `MutationLayoutSHOULDREMOVE(arg)`, which is only safe when `result` reads `arg` at the position it writes. Would checking the read indices there, and falling back to `unsafe_alias=False` otherwise, be the right fix? I can send it.

title: [inductor] y = x.clone(); op(y, x) becomes op(x, x) for custom ops and user-defined Triton kernels that mutate x: silent wrong results
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Same root cause as #197829 and #156786, a third way in: custom ops and user-defined Triton kernels. When the user passes a clone of the tensor the op mutates, the clone is removed and the op gets the same tensor twice.

```python
import torch


@torch.library.custom_op("mylib::reverse_into", mutates_args=("dst",))
def reverse_into(src: torch.Tensor, dst: torch.Tensor) -> None:
    n = src.shape[0]
    for k in range(n):
        dst[n - 1 - k] = src[k]


def f(x):
    y = x.clone()
    reverse_into(y, x)
    return x * 2.0


x = torch.arange(8.0)
a, b = x.clone(), x.clone()
f(a)
torch.compile(f)(b)
print(a.tolist())
print(b.tolist())
```

```
[7.0, 6.0, 5.0, 4.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.0]
[0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.0]
```

CPU, 2.14.0 and nightly 2.15.0.dev20260921, with `enable_auto_functionalized_v2` on or off. The generated code calls `torch.ops.mylib.reverse_into.default(arg0_1, arg0_1)`.

With a Triton kernel it is a race between program instances, so it only shows once the tensor is large enough:

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def reverse_kernel(src, dst, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    offs = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offs < n
    tl.store(dst + (n - 1 - offs), tl.load(src + offs, mask=mask), mask=mask)


def f(x):
    y = x.clone()
    n = x.numel()
    reverse_kernel[(triton.cdiv(n, 1024),)](y, x, n, BLOCK=1024)
    return x * 2.0


compiled = torch.compile(f)
for n in (4096, 1 << 21):
    x = torch.rand(n, device="cuda")
    want = f(x.clone())
    print(n, [int((compiled(x.clone()) != want).sum()) for _ in range(5)])
```

2.14.0+cu130, RTX 4070:

```
4096 [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
2097152 [870624, 851048, 850368, 840736, 862704]
```

```python
reverse_kernel_0.run(arg0_1, arg0_1, 4096, 4, 1, 1, stream=raw_stream0)
```

`remove_noop_ops` drops the clone, which is fine while the graph is functional. `reinplace_and_refine_tensors_to_clone` then decides `x` needs no clone because nothing uses it after the node. It doesn't look at the other arguments of the same node, so `functional_op(src=x, dst=x)` becomes the mutating op on `x`.

I have a patch that keeps the clone of a mutated argument when another argument of the node overlaps what the op writes (for v2, the mutated views rather than the whole base). What it costs: a call the user wrote as `op(x, x)` is no longer done in place, since after `remove_noop_ops` it is the same graph. Would you rather have that, or keep the clone in `remove_noop_ops` when its consumer mutates the source? I can send either.

title: ☂️ Forward-mode and higher-order AD return wrong derivatives
body:
Umbrella tracking issue for a **class** of bugs: `torch.func.jvp` / `torch.autograd.forward_ad`, nested (second-order) forward AD, `jacfwd`, and `hessian` return **numerically wrong derivatives** for ops whose first-order backward is correct. No error is raised; the wrong number flows into an optimizer, an implicit-layer solve or a physics model and surfaces as a training problem rather than a stack trace.

This is the forward-mode sibling of the eager-vs-compiled correctness umbrellas (#195547, #197554). If the repro only misbehaves under `torch.compile`, it belongs on `oncall: pt2`, not here.

### The shared root cause

Every member is a **per-op formula bug in a hand-written derivative rule** (`tools/autograd/derivatives.yaml` / `torch/csrc/autograd/FunctionsManual.cpp`), not an infrastructure bug in the forward-AD machinery:

- a JVP written with the factors in the wrong order for a non-commutative product (`cholesky_inverse`, `cholesky_solve`);
- a second-order term dropped when the JVP rule is itself differentiated (`linalg.solve`, `det`, `slogdet`, `householder_product`, `batch_norm`, `layer_norm`);
- a rule that is only right on the generic branch and wrong at a boundary the sample inputs never hit (`cumprod` at a zero factor, `scatter_reduce(prod)` with a zero, `triangular_solve(unitriangular=True)`, `logcumsumexp` with an underflowing prefix, `sinc` / `logaddexp` at a removable singularity);
- a custom `autograd.Function` whose `jvp` is not re-entered for higher derivatives (#197867).

Each one needs its own derivation and a float64 / complex128 finite-difference check. They are cheap to fix individually, but that is exactly why they keep coming back: the class is **under-tested**, so each fix only covers the op somebody happened to sweep.

### Why CI did not catch these

All of the affected ops declare `supports_forward_ad=True` and `supports_fwgrad_bwgrad=True` in their `OpInfo`, and none of the second-order ones carry a skip. The gap is in what the harness checks:

| Order | What is tested today | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| first-order JVP | `test_forward_mode_AD` (`gradcheck(check_forward_ad=True)`) | finite differences |
| reverse-over-forward | `test_fn_fwgrad_bwgrad` | finite differences |
| reverse-over-reverse | `test_fn_gradgrad` | finite differences |
| **forward-over-forward** (nested JVP) | `functorch` `test_jvpjvpvmap` only | **vmap-vs-loop consistency, no numerical reference**, and only over `autograd_function_db` |

So a wrong second-order JVP passes CI as long as it is wrong the same way with and without `vmap`. The first-order members slipped through a different hole: `sample_inputs` never exercise the failing regime (zero factors, `unitriangular=True`, underflowing prefixes), and `cholesky_solve` has `test_forward_mode_AD` skipped outright.

### What would close the class

**Not one PR per op.** Per-op fixes are welcome (two are already up) and each member stays open as the record for its reproducer, but the ask that actually closes the class is test infrastructure:

- [ ] an `OpInfo` test that checks **forward-over-forward** against a finite-difference reference (`gradcheck` already has `check_forward_ad`; add a nested variant or extend `gradgradcheck` with a `check_fwd_over_fwd` mode) and turn it on for every op with `supports_forward_ad=True`;
- [ ] audit ops whose forward-AD tests are skipped or whose `sample_inputs` avoid the singular / boundary regime, and add `error_inputs`-style boundary samples for derivative checks;
- [ ] for `autograd.Function`, a test that `jvp` composes with itself (`jacfwd(jacfwd(f))`) over `autograd_function_db`.

### Members

**Batch of 2026-09-11 (all forward-AD formula bugs, float64 finite-difference reproducers in each):**

- [ ] #196682 — `cholesky_inverse` JVP places the inverse on the wrong side of the tangent (fix: #197010)
- [ ] #196694 — `cholesky_solve` propagates an incorrect tangent through the Cholesky factor
- [ ] #196695 — `linalg.solve` loses a second-order term under nested forward AD
- [ ] #196696 — `det` second derivative wrong under nested JVP
- [ ] #196697 — `linalg.slogdet` returns zero instead of a nonzero second-order JVP
- [ ] #196698 — `linalg.householder_product` nested JVP wrong
- [ ] #196699 — `nn.functional.batch_norm` second-order JVP wrong
- [ ] #196700 — `nn.functional.layer_norm` second-order JVP wrong
- [ ] #196701 — `cumprod` nested JVP wrong at a zero factor
- [ ] #196702 — `scatter_reduce(reduce="prod")` returns a zero JVP for a nonconstant polynomial
- [ ] #196703 — `sinc` second derivative is NaN at its removable singularity
- [ ] #196704 — `logaddexp` second-order AD is NaN for finite logits
- [ ] #196705 — `logcumsumexp` drops an early-prefix first-order JVP contribution (fix: #196741)
- [ ] #196707 — `triangular_solve(unitriangular=True)` differentiates the ignored diagonal

**Other reports of the same class:**

- [ ] #197867 — nested `jacfwd` through a custom `autograd.Function` returns 0 for higher derivatives

**Already fixed, listed as a prior instance:** #196680 (`ldexp` dropped the derivative contribution of a negative exponent).

The list is seeded from the 2026-09 triage sweep; comment here with a short float64 reproducer and it will be added.

### Out of scope

- Forward AD **raising** `NotImplementedError` / "not supported" for an op (a missing rule, not a wrong one), e.g. #182641, #182661, #182842, #191787.
- Low-precision `inf`/`nan` in a derivative where the float64 formula is right (dynamic range, not a formula bug).
- Wrong derivatives that appear only under `torch.compile` (e.g. #190855) — `oncall: pt2`.
- First-order **backward** formula bugs; those go on their own tracker.

title: saved_tensors_hooks: document the (non-)ordering contract for unpack_hook calls
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

**Request: document the ordering contract (if any) for `unpack_hook` calls in `torch.autograd.graph.saved_tensors_hooks`, or provide an opt-in stricter mode.**

The docs describe when `pack_hook` runs (at save time, forward) and when `unpack_hook` runs (when the saved tensor is needed, backward), but say nothing about the *order* of `unpack_hook` calls relative to pack order, or about how stable that order is.

This matters for a real class of hooks: memory-bounded training implementations that do not store large saved tensors at all, but store small "deltas" from which each saved tensor can be reconstructed *from its successor state*. Such a hook maintains one live buffer and walks it backwards one step per unpack. Correctness then depends on the engine requesting saved tensors in (approximately) reverse pack order.

We maintain such an implementation in [awslabs/keys_values](https://github.com/awslabs/keys_values) (chunked backward over long sequences with evicting KV caches; the hooks reconstruct intermediate cache-buffer states from scatter deltas instead of storing them). We observed empirically that the request order is workload-dependent:

- for an LM cross-entropy training graph, saved buffers were requested exactly in reverse pack order (thousands of unpacks, zero violations);
- for a GRPO/RL policy-gradient graph over the same model code, requests arrived up to several "steps" ahead of, and also behind, the reverse order — including a request for a state the walk had already passed (`torch==2.9/2.11`, both with FlexAttention and with plain SDPA; also reproduced under `_aot_autograd` with activation checkpointing at 36 layers / ~1500 chunks);
- the deviation did not reproduce on small models (576-config sweep over depth/width/GQA/chunking on a 2-layer model): it appears only at scale, which makes it look like flaky infrastructure until the invariant is identified.

We fixed our side by making reconstruction order-independent (awslabs/keys_values#149: apply deltas in whatever order is requested; keep a CPU copy of a state only while a consumer for it provably remains outstanding). So this issue is not a blocker for us. But while debugging we could not find any statement about what IS guaranteed, and the answer changes what implementations like ours may rely on.

**Ask (any of these would help, in descending order of usefulness):**
1. A documented statement in the `saved_tensors_hooks` docs: "no ordering is guaranteed between unpack calls of different nodes" (if that is the intent) — one sentence would have saved us several weeks;
2. optionally, a documented *weak* guarantee, e.g. all `unpack_hook` calls for one autograd node happen together at that node's execution;
3. optionally, an opt-in debug/strict mode that makes the engine's choice among ready nodes deterministic (reverse `sequence_nr`), analogous in spirit to `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms`, accepting the performance cost.

I am happy to contribute the documentation change for (1)/(2) if a maintainer can state the intended contract, and to provide traces or a repro harness for the orderings described above.

### Alternatives

- Making the hook implementation order-independent (done, our side; costs bounded CPU copies).
- Forcing coarse ordering with per-slice `backward(inputs=...)` calls or finer checkpointing granularity — works, but retraverses the graph / multiplies checkpoints.
- Relying on observed ordering — what we did originally; it holds for some graphs and silently breaks for others, which is the reason for this request.

### Additional context

Observed on torch 2.9.1+cu126 and 2.11.0+cu130, single GPU (L40S/A100). The engine behavior itself looks entirely reasonable (topological readiness + internal priority); the request is only about documenting what user code may assume.

title: Multinomial.entropy() evaluates lgamma(total_count + 1) in the default dtype, and expand() drops _binomial so the expanded distribution has no entropy()
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.distributions.Multinomial` has two problems in `torch/distributions/multinomial.py`, both around `entropy()`.

**1. `entropy()` of a double distribution carries a float32 error that grows with `total_count`.**

`entropy()` builds `n = torch.tensor(self.total_count)`, an int64 scalar, and evaluates `torch.lgamma(n + 1)`. `lgamma` of an integer tensor is computed in the default dtype, so with the default float32 the term `log(total_count!)` is off by about `1e-7 * log(n!)` even when `probs` is float64 and the result is a float64 tensor. Compared with `scipy.stats.multinomial.entropy` (float64):

```python
import torch, numpy as np, scipy.stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for n in (10, 100, 1000, 10000):
    p = rng.dirichlet(np.ones(6))
    d = torch.distributions.Multinomial(n, torch.tensor(p))  # float64 probs, default dtype float32
    print(n, d.entropy().dtype, abs(d.entropy().item() - scipy.stats.multinomial(n, p).entropy()))
```

```text
10    torch.float64 4.59e-07
100   torch.float64 4.33e-06
1000  torch.float64 2.39e-04
10000 torch.float64 1.85e-03
```

With `torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)` the same code agrees with scipy to 5e-15, 2e-12, 9e-10 and 7e-08, which is what a float64 result should give. The existing `test_multinomial_1d_log_prob_and_entropy` does not see this because it runs under `set_default_dtype_if_supported(torch.double)` with `total_count=10` and `atol=1e-3`.

**2. `expand()` does not copy `_binomial`, so an expanded `Multinomial` has no `entropy()`.**

```python
d = torch.distributions.Multinomial(10, torch.tensor([0.2, 0.3, 0.5]))
d.expand(torch.Size([4])).entropy()
# AttributeError: 'Multinomial' object has no attribute '_binomial'
```

`expand()` sets `new._categorical` but not `new._binomial`, which `entropy()` reads. `test_distribution_expand` checks `mean` and `variance` of the expanded distribution but not `entropy`, so this went unnoticed.

**Fix.** `n = torch.tensor(self.total_count, dtype=self.probs.dtype, device=self.probs.device)` in `entropy()`, and `new._binomial = self._binomial.expand(batch_shape + self.event_shape)` in `expand()`. Tests: a new `test_multinomial_entropy_double` (float64 probs, default float32, `total_count=1000`, compared with scipy at the default tolerance, plus the expanded distribution), and an `entropy()` check added to `test_distribution_expand` next to `mean` and `variance`, which covers every distribution in the example list. On the current `main` version of the file both new checks fail (`AttributeError`, and `2.39e-04` against an allowed `1e-07`); with the change `pytest test/distributions/test_distributions.py -k "multinomial or distribution_expand or entropy"` gives 15 passed, and the whole file 248 passed, 6 skipped, 2 failed, the 2 being `TestKL::test_compile_kl_multivariate_normal` which fails the same way without the change on this torch build (Dynamo `_infer_size` with SymInt).

Happy to open the PR with the diff below if this looks right to you.

### Patch

The complete change is below so that nobody has to redo it; I will open it as the PR as soon as a maintainer confirms the direction.

<details>
<summary>2 files, +27 -1</summary>

```diff
diff --git a/test/distributions/test_distributions.py b/test/distributions/test_distributions.py
index 4677ff9..d6affeb 100644
--- a/test/distributions/test_distributions.py
+++ b/test/distributions/test_distributions.py
@@ -1537,6 +1537,12 @@ class TestDistributions(DistributionsTestCase):
                         )
                     except NotImplementedError:
                         pass
+                    try:
+                        self.assertEqual(
+                            expanded.entropy(), d.entropy().expand(expanded_shape)
+                        )
+                    except NotImplementedError:
+                        pass
 
     @expectedFailureMPS
     def test_distribution_subclass_expand(self):

title: [Windows] os.execv in rocm_sdk_core/_cli.py fails when the installation path contains spaces
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When installing the experimental ROCm SDK wheels on Windows (e.g., rocm_sdk_core and rocm_sdk_libraries_custom), the trampoline console scripts fail to execute underlying binaries (like offload-arch.exe) if the Python virtual environment is located in a path that contains spaces.

This causes a fatal ModuleNotFoundError when attempting to import torch.distributed.tensor or related modules, as the subprocess call to offload-arch fails because the unquoted path gets split at the space by the OS.

Reproducing Example
Create a Python virtual environment in a path with spaces (e.g., C:\My Folder\AI\_venvs\audio-venv).
Install PyTorch with ROCm for Windows using the AMD repo:
bash

pip install https://repo.radeon.com/rocm/windows/rocm-rel-7.2.1/rocm_sdk_core-7.2.1-py3-none-win_amd64.whl
pip install https://repo.radeon.com/rocm/windows/rocm-rel-7.2.1/rocm_sdk_libraries_custom-7.2.1-py3-none-win_amd64.whl
pip install https://repo.radeon.com/rocm/windows/rocm-rel-7.2.1/torch-2.9.1%2Brocm7.2.1-cp312-cp312-win_amd64.whl
Run Python and try to import PyTorch:
python

import torch
Error message
text

AI: Unknown command line argument 'My Folder\_venvs\audio-venv\Lib\site-packages\_rocm_sdk_core\lib\llvm\bin\offload-arch.exe'.  Try: 'C:\My Folder\AI --help'
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
  File "C:\My Folder\AI\_venvs\audio-venv\Lib\site-packages\rocm_sdk_core\_dist_info.py", line 123, in get_offload_arch
    result = subprocess.check_output(["offload-arch"], env=env, text=True)
...
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch._C._distributed_c10d'; 'torch._C' is not a package
(Note that offload-arch.exe incorrectly parses the unquoted path C:\My Folder\AI\... as the command C:\My and the argument Folder\AI\...)

Root Cause & Proposed Fix
In both rocm_sdk_core/_cli.py and rocm_sdk_libraries_custom/_cli.py, the _exec function uses os.execv without quoting the full_path. However, even when explicitly quoting argv[0], Windows os.execv (via the C runtime _wexecv) can sometimes fail to pass the quotes robustly to the underlying CreateProcess call.

python

def _exec(relpath: str):
    full_path = PLATFORM_PATH / (relpath + exe_suffix)
    # BUG: If full_path contains spaces, Windows C-runtime will split argv[0] at the space
    os.execv(full_path, [str(full_path)] + sys.argv[1:])
Fix: The most robust fix for Windows is to completely replace os.execv with subprocess.call(), which correctly handles all Windows command-line escaping rules via list2cmdline:

python

import subprocess
import sys
def _exec(relpath: str):
    full_path = PLATFORM_PATH / (relpath + exe_suffix)
    sys.exit(subprocess.call([str(full_path)] + sys.argv[1:]))

title: [dynamo] Mutations of a closure-captured list/dict are silently dropped when they happen in a method of a locally defined class instantiated inside the compiled function (`fullgraph=True`, no graph break)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** When a compiled function instantiates a locally defined class and calls a method that mutates a list or dict captured from the enclosing scope, eager mutates it on every call and `torch.compile` never does: `list.append`, `dict[k] = v` and `dict[k] += 1` leave the container unchanged, while the tensor result is correct (torch 2.14.0 and nightly; `backend="eager"` with `fullgraph=True` is enough). A helper object that counts calls or records shapes leaves an empty log after compiling, with no graph break and no error, and a context manager written this way loses its state. Because the mutation is replayed correctly when the object is created outside the compiled function or a nested function is used rather than a method, the loss is specific to method closures of objects created while tracing.

```python
import torch

def make(kind):
    state = {"n": 0} if kind.startswith("dict") else []
    class Helper:
        def touch(self):
            if kind == "dict +=":
                state["n"] += 1
            elif kind == "dict setitem":
                state["k"] = 1
            elif kind == "list append":
                state.append(1)
            elif kind == "list +=":
                state.extend([1])
    def f(x):
        Helper().touch()
        return x + 1
    return f, state

for kind in ("dict +=", "dict setitem", "list append", "list +="):
    res = []
    for comp in (False, True):
        torch._dynamo.reset()
        f, state = make(kind)
        g = torch.compile(f, backend="eager", fullgraph=True) if comp else f
        g(torch.ones(1)); g(torch.ones(1))
        res.append(str(state))
    print(f"{kind:13s} eager {res[0]:18s} compiled {res[1]}")
```

```
dict +=       eager {'n': 2}           compiled {'n': 0}
dict setitem  eager {'n': 0, 'k': 1}   compiled {'n': 0}
list append   eager [1, 1]             compiled []
list +=       eager [1, 1]             compiled []
```

Forms that behave correctly with the same `Helper` and the same `state` (from `closure_mutation_minimal.py`):

| call inside the compiled function | compiled result |
|---|---|
| `Helper().touch()` (object created inside `f`) | **mutation lost** |
| `outer.touch()` with `outer = Helper()` created outside `f` | correct |
| a nested function `helper_fn()` that performs the same mutation | correct |
| class and state at module level | correct |

The same defect makes a locally defined context manager lose its side effects:

```python
def run():
    log = []
    class CM:
        def __enter__(self): log.append("enter"); return self
        def __exit__(self, *a): log.append("exit"); return False
    def f(x):
        with CM():
            y = x + 1
        return y * 2
    torch.compile(f, backend="eager")(torch.ones(2))
    return log          # eager: ['enter', 'exit']   compiled: []
```

Expected: the mutation is replayed after the graph runs, as it is for the other three forms; or, if Dynamo cannot track the closure cell of a method of an object without a source, a graph break (an error under `fullgraph=True`) instead of silently dropping the effect.

A likely place to look: the receiver is a `UserDefinedObjectVariable` created during tracing and therefore has no source; the closure cell reached through its method appears to be tracked as a fresh local object rather than as the pre-existing cell of the enclosing frame, so its mutation is never registered with `SideEffects` for replay.

### Error logs

No error and no graph break; the side effect is missing as shown above.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0+cpu
OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Pro for Workstations (10.0.26200 64-bit)
Python version: 3.14.7 (64-bit runtime)
Is CUDA available: False
CPU: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-11900T @ 1.50GHz
[pip3] numpy==2.5.2
[pip3] torch==2.14.0+cpu
```

Same output on nightly (2.15.0.dev20260911 on Windows, 2.15.0.dev20260920 on Linux) and on Linux with 2.14.0 (Python 3.12), so it does not depend on the Python version or the platform.

title: [inductor] Floating-point floor division is off by one: `torch.compile` makes `1.0 // 0.1` return `10.0` (eager and Python: `9.0`)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** `a // b`, `torch.floor_divide` and `torch.div(..., rounding_mode="floor")` on floating-point tensors do not agree between eager and Inductor when the exact quotient lies just below an integer: for `1.0 // 0.1` eager returns `9.0`, as Python does, and Inductor returns `10.0`; the same happens for `0.5 // 0.1` and `6.0 // 0.2` in float32 and float64 (torch 2.14.0 and nightly, CPU and CUDA, Windows and Linux; `aot_eager` matches eager). A user who bins values or computes indices with `//` gets a bucket that is one too high after adding `torch.compile`, with no warning. Because Inductor lowers floating floor division to `floor(div_rn(a, b))` rather than to eager's fmod-based algorithm, every quotient that rounds up to an integer in floating point is affected, on every device that shares this lowering.

```python
import torch

print("python   :", 1.0 // 0.1, 0.5 // 0.1, 6.0 // 0.2)
for dtype in (torch.float32, torch.float64):
    a = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.5, 6.0, 1.0], dtype=dtype)
    b = torch.tensor([0.1, 0.1, 0.2, 1 / 3], dtype=dtype)
    for name, fn in (("a // b", lambda a, b: a // b), ("div(floor)", lambda a, b: torch.div(a, b, rounding_mode="floor"))):
        torch._dynamo.reset()
        print(f"{str(dtype):14s} {name:11s} eager {fn(a, b).tolist()}  inductor {torch.compile(fn)(a, b).tolist()}")
```

```
python   : 9.0 4.0 29.0
torch.float32  a // b      eager [9.0, 4.0, 29.0, 2.0]  inductor [10.0, 5.0, 30.0, 3.0]
torch.float32  div(floor)  eager [9.0, 4.0, 29.0, 2.0]  inductor [10.0, 5.0, 30.0, 3.0]
torch.float64  a // b      eager [9.0, 4.0, 29.0, 3.0]  inductor [10.0, 5.0, 30.0, 3.0]
torch.float64  div(floor)  eager [9.0, 4.0, 29.0, 3.0]  inductor [10.0, 5.0, 30.0, 3.0]
```

`0.1` is stored as a value slightly larger than one tenth, so the exact quotient `1.0 / 0.1` is slightly below 10 and its floor is 9; the correctly rounded floating-point quotient is exactly `10.0`, and flooring that gives 10.

**Root cause.** `torch/_inductor/lowering.py`:

```python
def _floor_div_floating(a, b):
    ...
    def fn(a, b, nan, neg_one, zero):
        quotient = ops.div_rn(a, b)
        result = ops.floor(quotient)
```

Eager (`c10::div_floor_floating`) and `torch._refs` compute `mod = fmod(a, b); div = (a - mod) / b; ...; floor(div)`, which is exact for these inputs. `cpp_prefix.h` already contains a vector implementation of that algorithm (`div_floor_floating_vec`), so the C++ backend can call it (and the scalar `c10::div_floor_floating`) instead of `floor(div_rn(...))`; for Triton the same fmod-based sequence can be emitted. This is the mirror image of #184408 (truncating division off by one on CUDA): that report notes that the floor path was switched to `div_rn`; `div_rn` fixes quotients that were rounded *down* by an approximate reciprocal, but not quotients whose correctly rounded value is already past the integer.

### Error logs

No error is raised; the values differ as shown above.

### Versions

```

OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Pro for Workstations (10.0.26200 64-bit)
MSVC: Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19.44.35228 for x64
Python version: 3.14.7 (64-bit runtime)
Is CUDA available: False
CPU: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-11900T @ 1.50GHz
[pip3] numpy==2.5.2
[pip3] torch==2.14.0+cpu
```

title: [fx] Generated code for `operator.pow(-2, x)` is `-2 ** x`, which Python evaluates as `-(2 ** x)`: `GraphModule.forward` returns the wrong sign (`Interpreter` is correct); reachable from `torch.compile(dynamic=True)` via `(-1) ** x.shape[0]`
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** For an FX node `operator.pow(-2, x)`, `torch.fx.Interpreter` computes `(-2) ** x`, while the Python source that `GraphModule` generates is `pow_1 = -2 ** x`, which Python parses as `-(2 ** x)`, so `gm(2)` returns `-4` instead of `4` (torch 2.14.0 and nightly). Any program that raises a negative constant to a traced power silently gets the wrong sign for even exponents: under `torch.compile(dynamic=True)` with `backend="eager"` or `"aot_eager"`, the alternating-sign idiom `x * (-1) ** x.shape[0]` returns `-x` for every length, and `torch.fx.symbolic_trace` is wrong too. Because the code generator formats the template `"{} ** {}"` with the plain `repr` of each argument rather than parenthesising it, and `**` binds tighter than unary minus, every negative literal used as the base of `pow` is affected.

```python
import operator
import torch, torch.fx

g = torch.fx.Graph()
x = g.placeholder("x")
g.output(g.call_function(operator.pow, (-2, x)))
gm = torch.fx.GraphModule(torch.nn.Module(), g)
print(gm.code.strip())
print("Interpreter:", torch.fx.Interpreter(gm).run(2), " GraphModule.forward:", gm(2), " Python (-2) ** 2:", (-2) ** 2)

def alternating_sign(x):
    return x * (-1) ** x.shape[0]

for backend in ("eager", "aot_eager"):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    f = torch.compile(alternating_sign, backend=backend, dynamic=True)
    print(backend, [(n, alternating_sign(torch.ones(n))[0].item(), f(torch.ones(n))[0].item()) for n in (2, 3, 4)], "  # (n, eager, compiled)")
```

```
def forward(self, x):
    pow_1 = -2 ** x;  x = None
    return pow_1
Interpreter: 4  GraphModule.forward: -4  Python (-2) ** 2: 4
eager [(2, 1.0, -1.0), (3, -1.0, -1.0), (4, 1.0, -1.0)]   # (n, eager, compiled)
aot_eager [(2, 1.0, -1.0), (3, -1.0, -1.0), (4, 1.0, -1.0)]   # (n, eager, compiled)
```

The Dynamo graph for the second program is `pow_1 = -1 ** s77; mul = l_x_ * pow_1`. With `backend="inductor"` the same program does not return a wrong value but fails to compile (`InductorError: RecursionError` while generating code for `ops.index_expr(PowByNatural(-1, s77), torch.float32)`), which is a separate problem.

**Root cause and fix.** `torch/fx/graph.py`, in the "pretty print operators" branch of the code generator:

```python
f"{magic_methods[node.target.__name__].format(*(_get_repr(a) for a in node.args))}"
```

with `magic_methods["pow"] = "{} ** {}"`. Wrapping a literal first operand of `pow` in parentheses when it is a negative number (or always emitting `({}) ** {}` for non-`Node` arguments) fixes it; `neg`, `sub`, `mod`, `floordiv`, shifts and bitwise templates do not have the problem because unary minus binds tighter than those operators.

title: [inductor] `x + 0` / `x * 1` / `x / 1.0` as a graph output returns the input tensor itself (`out is x`), so an in-place update of the result silently corrupts the input
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** For a function whose output is `x / temperature`, `buf * momentum` or `x + bias` called with the neutral value (`1.0`, `1.0`, `0`), eager and `aot_eager` return a fresh tensor, while Inductor returns the input object itself (`out is x`; with `requires_grad`, another object on the same storage), on torch 2.14.0 and nightly, CPU and CUDA. A caller that then updates the result in place (`new_buf.add_(g)`, `logits.clamp_(...)`) overwrites its own input with no error, only for the value that makes the operation a no-op: the same code is correct for `temperature=0.9` and wrong for `temperature=1.0`. Because `joint_graph.remove_no_ops` replaces the node by its operand without the check that `post_grad.remove_noop_ops` has ("Don't introduce new aliasing between inputs and outputs"), every graph that returns such a no-op of an input is affected.

```python
import torch

def scale(logits, temperature):
    return logits / temperature

def momentum_step(buf, momentum):
    return buf * momentum

def add_bias(x, bias):
    return x + bias

for name, f, arg in (("logits / 1.0", scale, 1.0), ("logits / 0.9", scale, 0.9),
                     ("buf * 1.0", momentum_step, 1.0), ("x + 0", add_bias, 0)):
    for backend in ("eager (no compile)", "aot_eager", "inductor"):
        torch._dynamo.reset()
        g = f if backend.startswith("eager") else torch.compile(f, backend=backend)
        x = torch.ones(3)
        out = g(x, arg)
        same = out is x
        out.add_(5)                     # the caller updates the *result* in place
        print(f"{name:13s} {backend:19s} out is x: {str(same):5s}  x afterwards: {x.tolist()}")
```

```
logits / 1.0  eager (no compile)  out is x: False  x afterwards: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
logits / 1.0  aot_eager           out is x: False  x afterwards: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
logits / 1.0  inductor            out is x: True   x afterwards: [6.0, 6.0, 6.0]
logits / 0.9  eager (no compile)  out is x: False  x afterwards: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
logits / 0.9  aot_eager           out is x: False  x afterwards: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
logits / 0.9  inductor            out is x: False  x afterwards: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
buf * 1.0     eager (no compile)  out is x: False  x afterwards: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
buf * 1.0     aot_eager           out is x: False  x afterwards: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
buf * 1.0     inductor            out is x: True   x afterwards: [6.0, 6.0, 6.0]
x + 0         eager (no compile)  out is x: False  x afterwards: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
x + 0         aot_eager           out is x: False  x afterwards: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
x + 0         inductor            out is x: True   x afterwards: [6.0, 6.0, 6.0]
```

Also affected: `0 + x`, `x - 0`, `x + 0.0`, `torch.add(x, 0)`, `(x + 0) + 0`, the same operations with a constant tensor built inside the function (`x * torch.ones(3)`, `x + torch.zeros(3)`, `x - torch.zeros_like(x)`, `x / torch.ones_like(x)`, `x * torch.full_like(x, 1.0)`), integer dtypes, an `nn.Module` whose `forward` is `logits / self.t` with `self.t = 1.0`, and inputs with `requires_grad=True` (there `out is x` is `False` but `out.data_ptr() == x.data_ptr()`, so `out.detach().mul_(2)` doubles `x`). Not affected: `x ** 1`, `x // 1`, `x.clone()`, `x + torch.zeros(())`.

A second, smaller consequence of the same elimination: `x + 0` no longer normalises negative zero (`torch.tensor(-0.0) + 0` is `0.` in eager and `-0.` compiled).

**Root cause and possible fix.** `torch/_inductor/fx_passes/joint_graph.py::remove_no_ops` → `replace_no_op` does `node.replace_all_uses_with(replacement)` whenever shape/dtype/device match and the replacement is not mutated (the guard added for #174187). When `replacement` is a placeholder and `node` feeds the graph output, the compiled graph returns its input, but AOTAutograd has already recorded that output as a non-alias, so the runtime wrapper hands the input tensor back to the caller as if it were fresh. `post_grad.py::remove_noop_ops` avoids the same situation with

```python
# Don't introduce new aliasing between inputs and outputs.
if (not node_is_view and node_storage in output_storages
        and (src_storage in input_storages or src_storage in output_storages)):
    continue
```

Applying the same condition in `replace_no_op` (skip, or replace the node by `aten.clone(replacement)` so the arithmetic still disappears) restores eager semantics; the check also has to cover two outputs that would become the same tensor (`return x * 1, x + 0`).

### Error logs

No error is raised.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0+cpu
OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Pro for Workstations (10.0.26200 64-bit)
MSVC: Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19.44.35228 for x64
Python version: 3.14.7 (64-bit runtime)
Is CUDA available: False
CPU: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-11900T @ 1.50GHz
[pip3] numpy==2.5.2
[pip3] torch==2.14.0+cpu
```

Same output on nightly (2.15.0.dev20260911 on Windows, 2.15.0.dev20260920 on Linux), on Linux CPU with 2.14.0, and on CUDA (Tesla T4, 2.14.0+cu130), so the behaviour comes from the shared FX pass and not from a backend.

title: [pt2] Python float argument that changes between calls goes stale in the cached graph (residual of #194976): norm `eps`, `huber_loss` delta, SDPA `scale`, `interpolate(scale_factor=...)` keep an earlier value (`interpolate`: old output shape)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** For `f(x, s)` that uses a Python float as `x * s` and, through arithmetic, as a float parameter of an operator (`F.rms_norm(x * s, (4,), eps=s + 1e-3)`), eager and `aot_eager` use the current `s`, while the default `torch.compile` keeps the parameter computed from the second `s` for all later values (torch 2.14.0 and nightly 2026-09-21, CPU and CUDA). A schedule that varies a loss `delta`, a `label_smoothing`, an attention `scale` or an `interpolate` scale factor computes with an old value, with no error, and `interpolate` returns the old shape. Because fake-tensor propagation specialises the symbolic float with a ShapeEnv guard rather than a graph input, AOT bakes the constant while the Dynamo graph stays identical for every `s`, so after each recompile AOTAutogradCache returns the first artifact.

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
x, y = torch.randn(4, 4), torch.randn(4, 4)
programs = {
    "rms_norm(x * s, eps=s + 1e-3)":          lambda s: F.rms_norm(x * s, (4,), eps=s + 1e-3),
    "huber_loss(x * s, y, delta=s + 0.1)":    lambda s: F.huber_loss(x * s, y, delta=s + 0.1),
    "interpolate(x * s, scale_factor=1 + s)": lambda s: F.interpolate((x * s)[None], scale_factor=1.0 + s),
}
for name, f in programs.items():
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    cf = torch.compile(f)
    print(name)
    for s in (0.9, 0.5, 0.25, 2.0):
        want, got = f(s), cf(s)
        same = want.shape == got.shape and torch.allclose(want, got)
        print(f"    s={s:<5} eager shape {tuple(want.shape)}  compiled shape {tuple(got.shape)}  " + ("ok" if same else "WRONG" + ("" if want.shape != got.shape else f" (max abs diff {(want - got).abs().max().item():.3f})")))
```

```
rms_norm(x * s, eps=s + 1e-3)
    s=0.9   eager shape (4, 4)  compiled shape (4, 4)  ok
    s=0.5   eager shape (4, 4)  compiled shape (4, 4)  ok
    s=0.25  eager shape (4, 4)  compiled shape (4, 4)  WRONG (max abs diff 0.218)
    s=2.0   eager shape (4, 4)  compiled shape (4, 4)  WRONG (max abs diff 0.348)
huber_loss(x * s, y, delta=s + 0.1)
    s=0.9   eager shape ()  compiled shape ()  ok
    s=0.5   eager shape ()  compiled shape ()  ok
    s=0.25  eager shape ()  compiled shape ()  WRONG (max abs diff 0.120)
    s=2.0   eager shape ()  compiled shape ()  WRONG (max abs diff 0.731)
interpolate(x * s, scale_factor=1 + s)
    s=0.9   eager shape (1, 4, 7)  compiled shape (1, 4, 7)  ok
    s=0.5   eager shape (1, 4, 6)  compiled shape (1, 4, 6)  ok
    s=0.25  eager shape (1, 4, 5)  compiled shape (1, 4, 6)  WRONG
    s=2.0   eager shape (1, 4, 12)  compiled shape (1, 4, 6)  WRONG
```

The first call specialises `s` (static), the second makes it automatically dynamic and is still right, and every value after that reuses the parameter of the second call: for `rms_norm` the compiled result equals eager's result with `eps = 0.5 + 1e-3` exactly. With `TORCHINDUCTOR_FX_GRAPH_CACHE=0` or `TORCHINDUCTOR_AUTOGRAD_CACHE=0` (either one), and with `backend="aot_eager"`, all rows are `ok`.

Of 51 operators with a float parameter that I tried in this shape, 18 are affected on nightly: `rms_norm`, `layer_norm`, `group_norm`, `batch_norm`, `instance_norm` (eps) and `batch_norm` momentum, `cosine_similarity` eps, `pairwise_distance` / `cdist` p, `quantile` q, `interpolate` scale_factor (nearest and linear), `smooth_l1_loss` beta, `huber_loss` delta, `cross_entropy` label_smoothing, `poisson_nll_loss` eps, `triplet_margin_loss` margin, and `scaled_dot_product_attention` scale. Pointwise ops whose scalar is tensorified (`clamp`, `leaky_relu`, `elu`, `hardtanh`, `threshold`, `addcmul`, `lerp`, `where`, `pow`, …) are correct on nightly; on 2.14.0, which predates the fix for #194976, many of those are wrong as well (`torch.add(x * s, y, alpha=1 - s)`, the EMA update, among them).

**Root cause.** `TORCH_LOGS=graph_code,aot_graphs,recompiles` for the `rms_norm` program:

```
[0/1] Dynamo graph:   item = l_s_.item(); mul = l_x_ * item; add = item + 0.001; rms_norm = torch.rms_norm(mul, (4,), None, add)
[0/1] AOT graph:      mul = aten.mul.Tensor(arg0_1, _local_scalar_dense) ... add_1 = aten.add.Scalar(mean, 0.5009999871253967)
[0/2] recompile:      guard failure  (0.001 + s) == 0.501   # functional.py: rms_norm (_dynamo/utils.py in run_node)
[0/2] Dynamo graph:   identical text to [0/1]
[0/2] AOT graph:      "Forward graph (from cache)" ... add_1 = aten.add.Scalar(mean, 0.5009999871253967)
```

The operator takes a C++ `double`, so tracing it on fake tensors specialises the expression `zf + 0.001` and records the ShapeEnv guard `(0.001 + s) == 0.501`; the value is burned into the AOT graph, but the Dynamo graph still carries the symbolic expression. The guard works (the third call recompiles), but the recompile produces the same Dynamo graph, AOTAutogradCache keys on that graph and prunes guards over symbols that are not placeholder SymInts, and the artifact with `0.501` inside comes back. This is the mechanism described in #195040, which closed it for the final sweep of `_tensorify_python_scalars.py`; specialisation that happens earlier, during Dynamo's fake-tensor propagation of an op with a float schema argument, is not covered.

**Possible fix.** Treat a float symbol that gets specialised during tracing the same way #195040 treats one specialised in the tensorify sweep: mark it with `TensorifyState.specialize` and restart analysis so that Dynamo bakes the value into its own output graph (the value then is part of the cache key); or, more narrowly, make AOTAutogradCache bypass / miss when the ShapeEnv holds an equality guard over a float symbol that is not a graph input.

### Error logs

No error. The recompile log shows the guard failing and the forward graph being served from cache.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0+cpu
OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Pro for Workstations (10.0.26200 64-bit)
MSVC: Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19.44.35228 for x64
Python version: 3.14.7 (64-bit runtime)
Is CUDA available: False
CPU: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-11900T @ 1.50GHz
[pip3] numpy==2.5.2
[pip3] torch==2.14.0+cpu
```

Same result on nightly (2.15.0.dev20260911 on Windows, 2.15.0.dev20260921 on Linux), on Linux CPU with 2.14.0, and on CUDA (Tesla T4, 2.14.0+cu130 and nightly 2.15.0.dev20260921+cu130).

title: `adaptive_max_pool3d_backward` and `fractional_max_pool{2,3}d_backward` read a non-contiguous `indices` tensor as if it were contiguous: silently wrong gradients, reached from `torch.compile` with `channels_last_3d` inputs
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** For `F.adaptive_max_pool3d` on a `channels_last_3d` input, eager and `aot_eager` compute the same input gradient, and Inductor computes a different one: the forward values and indices are identical, but `backward()` scatters the gradient to the wrong positions (max difference 282 in the example below; torch 2.14.0 and nightly). A 3-D CNN that follows the memory-format recommendation and is then compiled trains with silently wrong gradients through every adaptive max pool. Because the CPU kernels of `adaptive_max_pool3d_backward`, `fractional_max_pool2d_backward`, and `fractional_max_pool3d_backward` make `grad_output` contiguous but read `indices` through its raw data pointer, any caller that passes non-contiguous indices gets a wrong result; eager autograd never does, Inductor does as soon as it lays the saved indices out in the input's memory format.

User-level reproduction (needs Inductor):

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
f = lambda t: F.adaptive_max_pool3d(t, (2, 3, 5))
x = torch.randperm(1 * 4 * 4 * 6 * 5).float().reshape(1, 4, 4, 6, 5)
for name, xin in (("contiguous", x), ("channels_last_3d", x.contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last_3d))):
    grads = []
    for backend in (None, "aot_eager", "inductor"):
        torch._dynamo.reset()
        t = xin.detach().clone(memory_format=torch.preserve_format).requires_grad_()
        out = (f if backend is None else torch.compile(f, backend=backend))(t)
        (out * torch.arange(1.0, out.numel() + 1).reshape(out.shape)).sum().backward()
        grads.append(t.grad.clone())
    print(f"{name:17s} aot_eager == eager: {torch.equal(grads[0], grads[1])}   inductor == eager: {torch.equal(grads[0], grads[2])}"
          f"   max diff {(grads[0] - grads[2]).abs().max().item():.0f}")
```

```
contiguous        aot_eager == eager: True   inductor == eager: True   max diff 0
channels_last_3d  aot_eager == eager: True   inductor == eager: False   max diff 282
```

Kernel-level reproduction (eager only, no compiler involved): the same values in `indices`, once contiguous and once with `channels_last` strides.

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
A = torch.ops.aten
x3 = torch.randperm(240).float().reshape(1, 4, 4, 3, 5)
x3w = torch.cat([x3, x3], 3)
x2 = torch.randperm(120).float().reshape(1, 4, 6, 5)
rs2, rs3 = torch.full((1, 4, 2), 0.5), torch.full((1, 4, 3), 0.5)
cases = []
v, i = F.adaptive_max_pool3d(x3, (2, 3, 5), return_indices=True)
cases.append(("adaptive_max_pool3d_backward", lambda go, idx: A.adaptive_max_pool3d_backward(go, x3, idx), v, i, torch.channels_last_3d))
v, i = F.adaptive_max_pool2d(x2, (3, 5), return_indices=True)
cases.append(("adaptive_max_pool2d_backward", lambda go, idx: A.adaptive_max_pool2d_backward(go, x2, idx), v, i, torch.channels_last))
v, i = F.max_pool3d(x3, 2, 1, return_indices=True)
cases.append(("max_pool3d_with_indices_backward", lambda go, idx: A.max_pool3d_with_indices_backward(go, x3, [2, 2, 2], [1, 1, 1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1], False, idx), v, i, torch.channels_last_3d))
v, i = F.fractional_max_pool2d(x2, 2, output_size=(3, 3), return_indices=True, _random_samples=rs2)
cases.append(("fractional_max_pool2d_backward", lambda go, idx: A.fractional_max_pool2d_backward(go, x2, [2, 2], [3, 3], idx), v, i, torch.channels_last))
v, i = F.fractional_max_pool3d(x3w, 2, output_size=(2, 2, 2), return_indices=True, _random_samples=rs3)
cases.append(("fractional_max_pool3d_backward", lambda go, idx: A.fractional_max_pool3d_backward(go, x3w, [2, 2, 2], [2, 2, 2], idx), v, i, torch.channels_last_3d))
for name, fn, v, idx, fmt in cases:
    go = torch.arange(1.0, v.numel() + 1).reshape(v.shape)
    idx_nc = idx.contiguous(memory_format=fmt)                      # equal values, channels_last strides
    same = torch.equal(fn(go, idx), fn(go, idx_nc))
    print(f"{name:34s} indices strides {str(tuple(idx_nc.stride())):22s} same gradient as with contiguous indices: {same}")
```

```
adaptive_max_pool3d_backward       indices strides (120, 1, 60, 20, 4)    same gradient as with contiguous indices: False
adaptive_max_pool2d_backward       indices strides (60, 1, 20, 4)         same gradient as with contiguous indices: True
max_pool3d_with_indices_backward   indices strides (96, 1, 32, 16, 4)     same gradient as with contiguous indices: True
fractional_max_pool2d_backward     indices strides (36, 1, 12, 4)         same gradient as with contiguous indices: False
fractional_max_pool3d_backward     indices strides (32, 1, 16, 8, 4)      same gradient as with contiguous indices: False
```

`adaptive_max_pool2d_backward` and `max_pool{2,3}d_with_indices_backward` normalize `indices` and are correct; the other three are not. Passing a channels_last `grad_output` or `self` to the affected kernels is handled correctly, only `indices` is read without `.contiguous()`.

**Possible fix.** In `aten/src/ATen/native/AdaptiveMaxPooling3d.cpp`, `FractionalMaxPool2d.cpp`, and `FractionalMaxPool3d.cpp` (backward, CPU; the CUDA counterparts are worth the same look), take `indices.contiguous()` next to the existing `gradOutput.contiguous()`; the 2-D adaptive kernel and the `max_pool{2,3}d_with_indices_backward` kernels are correct in the table above, so they evidently normalize the argument already. Independently, Inductor's fallback for these ops could `require_contiguous` the `indices` argument. This belongs to the class tracked in #195547 (a precondition the kernel relies on but never establishes).

### Error logs

No error is raised; the gradients differ as shown above.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0+cpu
OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Pro for Workstations (10.0.26200 64-bit)
MSVC: Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19.44.35228 for x64
Python version: 3.14.7 (64-bit runtime)
Is CUDA available: False
CPU: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-11900T @ 1.50GHz
[pip3] numpy==2.5.2
[pip3] torch==2.14.0+cpu
```

Same output on nightly (2.15.0.dev20260911 on Windows, 2.15.0.dev20260920 on Linux) and on Linux with 2.14.0. On CUDA (Tesla T4, 2.14.0+cu130) the compiled gradient matches eager, so only the CPU kernels are affected.

title: [inductor] Autograd's "modified by an inplace operation" check is lost when a view of a graph input is saved for backward: `x @ w`, `bmm`, `einsum`, 3-D `F.linear` silently return wrong gradients after `x` is modified in place
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** When a tensor that backward needs is modified in place between forward and backward, eager and `aot_eager` raise "one of the variables needed for gradient computation has been modified by an inplace operation", while `backend="inductor"` raises nothing for `mm`, `bmm`, `einsum`, `addmm`, 3-D `F.linear` and slicing, and `backward()` returns a gradient computed from the modified input (torch 2.14.0 and nightly, CPU and CUDA). A training loop that reuses its input buffer before `backward()` (`x.copy_(next_batch)`) is stopped by eager, but keeps running under `torch.compile` with gradients of no executed forward pass. Because the saved tensor is a view that Inductor rebuilds with `reinterpret_tensor` rather than the input itself, it no longer shares the input's version counter, and the check disappears for every graph whose backward saves a view of an input.

```python
import torch

def f(x, w):
    return x @ w

x = torch.arange(6.).reshape(2, 3) / 7
w = (torch.arange(9.).reshape(3, 3) / 5).requires_grad_()
true_grad = x.clone().t() @ torch.ones(2, 3)          # dL/dw of the forward that actually runs

for backend in (None, "aot_eager", "inductor"):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    xb, wb = x.clone(), w.detach().clone().requires_grad_()
    g = f if backend is None else torch.compile(f, backend=backend)
    out = g(xb, wb)
    xb.add_(1)                                        # input modified between forward and backward
    try:
        out.sum().backward()
        print(backend, "-> no error, grad correct:", torch.allclose(wb.grad, true_grad), wb.grad[0].tolist())
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(backend, "-> raises:", str(e)[:70])
```

```
None      -> raises: one of the variables needed for gradient computation has been modified
aot_eager -> raises: one of the variables needed for gradient computation has been modified
inductor  -> no error, grad correct: False [2.4285714626312256, 2.4285714626312256, 2.4285714626312256]
```

The correct gradient row is `[0.4286, 0.4286, 0.4286]`; Inductor returns the gradient of `(x + 1) @ w`, a forward pass that never ran.

Each (program, backend) below ran in a fresh interpreter (`saved_view_variants.py`); "raises" is the eager error above:

| forward (then `x.add_(1)`, then `backward()`) | eager | aot_eager | inductor |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x @ p` | raises | raises | **silent, wrong grad (max err 2)** |
| `torch.bmm(x, p)` | raises | raises | **silent, wrong grad** |
| `torch.einsum('ij,jk->ik', x, p)` | raises | raises | **silent, wrong grad** |
| `F.linear(x, p)` with 3-D `x` | raises | raises | **silent, wrong grad (max err 4)** |
| `torch.matmul(x, p)` with 3-D `x` | raises | raises | **silent, wrong grad** |
| `torch.addmm(p.sum(0), x, p)` | raises | raises | **silent, wrong grad** |
| `x[0] * p` | raises | raises | **silent, wrong grad** |
| `softmax(x @ p, -1) @ x.t()[:3].t()` | raises | raises | **silent, wrong grad** |
| `x.t() @ p`, `x.view(3, 2) * p`, `x * p`, `x.expand(4, 2, 3) * p`, 2-D `F.linear`, `conv2d`, a small MLP | raises | raises | raises |

**Root cause.** For `x @ w` the AOT forward graph saves a *view of the input* for backward:

```
def forward(primals_1, primals_2):
    mm = aten.mm.default(primals_1, primals_2)
    permute = aten.permute.default(primals_1, [1, 0])
    return (mm, permute)            # permute: SavedForBackwardsAOTOutput(idx=0)
```

With `aot_eager` the saved `permute` is produced by a real `aten.permute` call, so it shares `primals_1`'s version counter and the saved-variable check fires. Inductor's wrapper returns the view as a new tensor on the same storage (`reinterpret_tensor`) with its **own version counter**, so modifying `x` afterwards no longer bumps the version of what was saved. This is directly observable:

```python
out = torch.compile(lambda x, w: x @ w, backend=backend)(x, w)
saved = out.grad_fn.saved_tensors[0]
x.add_(1)
print(saved.untyped_storage().data_ptr() == x.untyped_storage().data_ptr(), x._version, saved._version)
# aot_eager: True 1 1      inductor: True 1 0
``` The min-cut partitioner is not involved (`aot_eager_decomp_partition` raises). Programs whose backward saves the input itself (2-D `linear`, `mul`, `conv2d`) keep the check.

**Possible fix.** Either (a) have AOTAutograd's runtime wrapper regenerate saved-for-backward tensors that alias a graph input from that input, the way user-visible outputs that alias inputs are already regenerated with `gen_alias_from_base`, or (b) make Inductor's `reinterpret_tensor` wrapper share the base tensor's version counter when the result escapes the graph (`torch._C._autograd._unsafe_set_version_counter`), or (c) record the input's `_version` at forward time in `CompiledFunction` and compare it in `backward`.

Expected: the same `RuntimeError` as eager and `aot_eager` (or, at the very least, a gradient that belongs to the forward pass that ran).

### Error logs

_No response_

### Versions

No error is raised under `backend="inductor"`; that is the defect. Eager / `aot_eager` raise:

```
RuntimeError: one of the variables needed for gradient computation has been modified by an inplace operation: [torch.FloatTensor [3, 2]] is at version 1; expected version 0 instead.
```

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0+cpu
Is debug build: False
CUDA used to build PyTorch: None
ROCM used to build PyTorch: N/A

OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Pro for Workstations (10.0.26200 64-bit)
MSVC: Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19.44.35228 for x64 (used by Inductor's C++ backend)

Python version: 3.14.7 (tags/v3.14.7:823f032, Aug  5 2026, 10:51:32) [MSC v.1944 64 bit (AMD64)] (64-bit runtime)
Python platform: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0
Is CUDA available: False

CPU:
Name: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-11900T @ 1.50GHz

Versions of relevant libraries:
[pip3] numpy==2.5.2
[pip3] torch==2.14.0+cpu
```

The table above is identical on nightly 2.15.0.dev20260911+cpu (Windows), on Linux CPU with 2.14.0 and nightly 2.15.0.dev20260919, and on CUDA (Tesla T4, 2.14.0+cu130, Triton path), so it is neither platform- nor device-specific.

body:
Platforms: rocm

title: [MPS] segment_reduce is not implemented
body:
### The feature, motivation and pitch
Add native MPS support for `torch.segment_reduce`, including its backward implementation.

`segment_reduce` combines consecutive, variable-length groups using `sum`, `mean`, `min`, `max`, or `prod`. It is useful for pooling packed token embeddings into sentence/document embeddings and aggregating ragged feature groups without padding each group to the same length.

The existing operator has CPU, CUDA, and XPU implementations, but the base
of pytorch has no native MPS dispatch. On the installed runtime, this minimal example raises `NotImplementedError` when MPS fallback is disabled:

```python
 # Run with PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=0
import torch

 print(torch.__version__, torch.version.git_version)
 data = torch.tensor([1., 2., 3., 4., 5., 6.], device="mps")
lengths = torch.tensor([2, 1, 3], device="mps")
torch.segment_reduce(data, "sum", lengths=lengths)
# Expected: tensor([3., 3., 15.], device="mps:0")
# Actual: NotImplementedError: aten::segment_reduce is not currently
# implemented for the MPS device.
```


The requested scope is FP32/FP16/BF16 data, INT32/INT64 lengths and offsets,  and first-order gradients using the existing operator schema. Indices-based  reduction is not part of this request.

 ### Additional context

 An initial implementation is under review in pytorch/pytorch#197014. Feedback on the scope and preferred test coverage would help prepare it for merging.

title: [DTensor] Shard._select_split_tensor SymInt path computes a negative shard length for uneven splits
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Shard._select_split_tensor has a SymInt fast path (index is a torch.SymInt and with_padding=False) that assumes only the last shard is short and this branch is taken when index is not a Python int and with_padding=False.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/b6131af877449b1d3af5700b93b4a3bcbe8348fa/torch/distributed/tensor/placement_types.py#L281-L289

That is wrong when the first n-1 full chunks do not fit, for example when dim_size=5, num_chunks=4: 
- split_size=  (5 + 4 -1)//4 =2
-  last_split= ( 5 -2*(4-1))= -1
-  So the implied length is [2,2,2,-1] which is wrong.

The Python-int path (_split_tensor) returns [2, 2, 1, 0] as _custom_chunk already clamps this correctly:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/b6131af877449b1d3af5700b93b4a3bcbe8348fa/torch/distributed/tensor/placement_types.py#L330-L336

```
python 

import torch
from torch.distributed.tensor import Shard
from torch.fx.experimental.symbolic_shapes import ShapeEnv

t = torch.arange(20).reshape(5, 4)
index = ShapeEnv().create_unbacked_symint()
Shard(0)._select_split_tensor(
    t,
    num_chunks=4,
    index=index,
    with_padding=False,
    clone=False,
    contiguous=False,
)

```

title: dp_knapsack_sliding_hirschberg can return solutions exceeding max_memory
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`dp_knapsack_sliding_hirschberg` is an alternative implementation of the same quantized 0/1 knapsack as `dp_knapsack`, selectable via `torch._functorch.config.activation_memory_budget_solver = "dp_knapsack_sliding_hirschberg"`. It can return a saved set whose memory exceeds `max_memory`.

This happens even when every weight is an exact multiple of the solver's quantization step (1e-4), so the inputs map exactly to integer weights in the solver's quantized representation and the failure is not caused by quantization error. `dp_knapsack` returns a feasible (and, in all cases below, optimal) solution for the same inputs.

### Expected behavior

The returned saved set's quantized memory usage should be <= the quantized `max_memory`, the same constraint `dp_knapsack` satisfies. For the minimal example below (three 1-unit items, 1-unit budget), the maximum feasible runtime is 1.0.

### Actual behavior

`dp_knapsack_sliding_hirschberg` returns a solution that violates the solver's own quantized capacity constraint. In the minimal example it returns `[0, 1]`, which uses 2 quantization units against a 1-unit budget, reporting runtime 2.0. On 1000 random small instances with exact-unit weights, it exceeded the budget 46 times; `dp_knapsack` never did. The repro prints three of those failing cases in full (e.g. 73 units used against a 72-unit budget).

### Cause

In the split step, `capacity` is first incremented to the DP profile length (`capacity = capacity + 1`). The right profile is then reversed, so index `best_split` corresponds to right-half weight `capacity - 1 - best_split`. The code assigns `right_capacity = capacity - best_split`, giving the right subproblem one excess unit of capacity at each split. Because each recursive right subproblem is assigned one extra quantization unit, the returned solution can become infeasible with respect to the original capacity.

Proposed fix:

```diff
-        right_capacity = capacity - best_split
+        right_capacity = capacity - 1 - best_split
```

The fix preserves the DP profile indexing while ensuring the two recursively assigned capacities sum to the original quantized capacity.

With this change, the repro below reports 0 budget violations for both solvers, and the existing `test/functorch/test_ac_knapsack.py` still passes. I have a one-line fix with regression tests ready and will send a PR once this is triaged.

### Repro

```python
import itertools
import random

import torch
from torch._functorch._activation_checkpointing.knapsack import (
    dp_knapsack,
    dp_knapsack_sliding_hirschberg,
)

S = 10000  # quantization scale used by both solvers


def used_units(memory, saved):
    return sum(round(memory[i] * S) for i in saved)


def brute_force(memory, runtime, budget):
    # exact optimum over all subsets, in quantized units
    q, cap = [round(m * S) for m in memory], round(budget * S)
    return max(
        sum(r for r, b in zip(runtime, mask) if b)
        for mask in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=len(q))
        if sum(w for w, b in zip(q, mask) if b) <= cap
    )


print("torch", torch.__version__)

# 1) Minimal case: three 1-unit items, 1-unit budget (no rounding involved)
memory, runtime, budget = [1e-4, 1e-4, 1e-4], [1.0, 1.0, 1.0], 1e-4
print(f"\nmemory={memory} runtime={runtime} budget={budget}")
print(f"quantized weights={[round(m * S) for m in memory]} quantized budget={round(budget * S)}")
for solver in (dp_knapsack, dp_knapsack_sliding_hirschberg):
    rt, saved, _ = solver(memory, runtime, budget)
    print(f"{solver.__name__:31s} saved={saved} runtime={rt} "
          f"units used={used_units(memory, saved)}")
print(f"{'brute-force optimum':31s} runtime={brute_force(memory, runtime, budget)}")

# 2) Random small instances with weights that are exact multiples of 1/S
rng = random.Random(0)
trials, over = 1000, {dp_knapsack: 0, dp_knapsack_sliding_hirschberg: 0}
examples = []
for _ in range(trials):
    n = rng.randint(2, 10)
    memory = [rng.randint(1, 30) / S for _ in range(n)]
    runtime = [float(rng.randint(1, 50)) for _ in range(n)]
    budget = rng.randint(0, round(sum(memory) * S)) / S
    results = {}
    for solver in over:
        rt, saved, _ = solver(memory, runtime, budget)
        results[solver] = (rt, saved)
        over[solver] += used_units(memory, saved) > round(budget * S)
    _, h_saved = results[dp_knapsack_sliding_hirschberg]
    if used_units(memory, h_saved) > round(budget * S) and len(examples) < 3:
        examples.append((memory, runtime, budget, results))

print(f"\nrandom instances with exact-unit weights: {trials}")
for solver, count in over.items():
    print(f"{solver.__name__:31s} results exceeding budget: {count}")

print("\nfirst 3 failing random instances:")
for memory, runtime, budget, results in examples:
    print(f"\nquantized weights={[round(m * S) for m in memory]} "
          f"quantized budget={round(budget * S)}")
    print(f"runtime={runtime}")
    for solver, (rt, saved) in results.items():
        print(f"{solver.__name__:31s} saved={saved} runtime={rt} "
              f"units used={used_units(memory, saved)}")
    print(f"{'brute-force optimum':31s} runtime={brute_force(memory, runtime, budget)}")
```

title: [Inductor][ROCm] Comprehensive padding is skipped when an intermediate buffer is frozen under a user-visible consumer
body:
### Bug description

On ROCm/HIP, TorchInductor can incorrectly skip comprehensive padding for an intermediate tensor.

The intermediate buffer is produced by `add`, but it is frozen while the current FX node is its consumer `mm`. Since the final `mm` is a user-visible output and has `dislike_padding=True`, `_pad_strides()` incorrectly applies the consumer's padding preference to the producer buffer.

### Minimal reproduction

```python
import torch
from torch._inductor import config, metrics


def f(x, y):
    x = torch.matmul(x, y)
    x = x + 1
    return torch.matmul(x, y)


torch.manual_seed(0)

x = torch.randn(2, 16, 2047, device="cuda")
y = torch.randn(2047, 2047, device="cuda")

ref = f(x, y)

metrics.reset()

with config.patch(
    {
        "comprehensive_padding": True,
        "padding_alignment_bytes": 128,
        "padding_stride_threshold": 1024,
        "triton.cudagraphs": False,
    }
):
    compiled = torch.compile(f, fullgraph=True)
    out = compiled(x, y)

torch.testing.assert_close(ref, out, atol=1e-2, rtol=1e-2)

print("num_comprehensive_padding:", metrics.num_comprehensive_padding)
assert metrics.num_comprehensive_padding > 0
```

### Actual behavior

```text
num_comprehensive_padding: 0
AssertionError
```

The intermediate `[2, 16, 2047]` tensor has stride:

```text
[32752, 2047, 1]
```

With float32 and 128-byte alignment, it should be padded to:

```text
[32768, 2048, 1]
```

but the original stride is kept.

### Expected behavior

The intermediate tensor should be comprehensively padded, while the final user-visible output should still preserve its required stride.

`metrics.num_comprehensive_padding` should therefore be greater than zero.

### Root cause

Tracing the layout freeze shows:

```text
buffer: buf1
producer: add
producer target: aten.add.Tensor
producer dislike_padding: False

current node: mm_1
current target: aten.mm.default
current dislike_padding: True
```

When `_pad_strides()` runs:

```text
current node: mm_1
current dislike_padding: True
input stride:  [32752, 2047, 1]
output stride: [32752, 2047, 1]
```

So the buffer belongs to `add`, but the padding decision is made using the consumer `mm_1`.

`Layout._pad_strides()` currently uses `V.get_current_node()` to check `dislike_padding`, which in this case refers to the consumer rather than the origin node of the buffer being frozen.

### A/B verification

As a local experiment, running the layout freeze under the buffer's origin FX node:

```python
origin = buf.get_origin_node()

with V.set_current_node(origin):
    ...
```

changes the result to:

```text
num_comprehensive_padding: 1
PASS
```

No other behavior was changed.

### Proposed fix location

The relevant location appears to be:

```text
torch/_inductor/ir.py
ExternKernel.convert_to_reinterpret_view()
```

This function already obtains:

```python
x_unwrap_view_fx_node = buf.get_origin_node()
```

but layout freezing still runs under the existing `V.current_node`.

Using the buffer's origin node as the current node while calling `freeze_layout()` / `freeze_layout_with_same_order()` appears to avoid incorrectly inheriting `dislike_padding` from the consumer.

### Environment

- PyTorch: 2.14.0
- Backend: ROCm / HIP
- `torch.compile` / TorchInductor
- AMD GPU
